lead: Both readings are about the care owed to those who are young in faith. Paul writes as a father to the Corinthians: he begot them in Christ through the Gospel, and he asks them to imitate him, warning that the kingdom of God is a matter of power, not of talk. In Matthew, Jesus speaks with unusual severity about anyone who makes one of his little ones stumble. On the memorial of St Justin, a philosopher who found in Christ the truth he had been seeking and gave his life for it, the Church hears that faith is proved not by clever words but by a life given.

r.h: I became your father through the gospel
set: These verses close the first part of the letter (chapters 1 to 4), in which Paul has dealt with the parties at Corinth, some saying “I belong to Paul”, others “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). He has just spoken with sharp irony of the Corinthians who think themselves already rich and wise, while the apostles are treated as the rubbish of the world (4:8–13). Now his tone changes: “I am not writing this to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children” (4:14).
str: v. 15: many guardians, but only one father: Paul begot them in Christ through the Gospel.
vv. 16–17: be imitators of me; Timothy is sent to remind them of Paul’s ways in Christ.
vv. 18–20: some are arrogant, thinking he will not come; he will come and test their power, not their talk.
v. 21: a choice: shall he come with a stick, or with love and gentleness?
kw: In a Greek household this was the slave who took a boy to school and watched over his conduct. He could be strict and useful, but he was not the father. Paul uses the same word for the Law in Galatians 3:24.
The word behind our “mimic”. Paul does not ask to be admired but copied, because he himself imitates Christ (11:1). Faith is passed on by example as much as by teaching.
Not force of personality but the working of God’s Spirit, the same power Paul spoke of in 2:4: his preaching came “with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power”.
vv: For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
“Ten thousand” is a deliberate exaggeration. Teachers can be many; the one who first brought them to new life in Christ stands in a unique place. On calling anyone “father”, see the question below.
For this reason I sent you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord
Timothy is Paul’s spiritual son too (Philippians 2:22). Paul sends someone formed by him, who will remind them of a way of life, not only of ideas.
For the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.
Paul rarely speaks of the kingdom of God, and here he defines it by what it does. Clever speech was prized in Corinth; Paul says the kingdom is known where God changes lives.
Am I to come to you with a stick, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
The stick was the rod of correction used by a father or teacher. Paul would rather come gently, but a true father does not ignore wrongdoing. Chapter 5 will show the correction he has in mind.
ch: The Church sees in Paul the pattern of every shepherd who begets and forms souls in Christ. The Second Vatican Council says that priests, as fathers and teachers among the people of God, should bring up their faithful as spiritual children in Christ, and that they do so above all by the example of their lives (Presbyterorum Ordinis 6 and 9, in substance). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, notes that Paul did not say “I gave you teaching” but “I begot you”, the language of the deepest love (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 13).

r.h: Do not make the little ones stumble
set: Matthew 18 is the fourth of the five great discourses of Jesus in this Gospel, often called the discourse on the community. It begins when the disciples ask who is the greatest, and Jesus puts a child among them: whoever welcomes such a child welcomes him (18:1–5). Today’s verses follow at once. The “little ones” are children, and also all the humble and weak believers in the community, whose faith can be easily wounded.
str: v. 6: whoever makes one of these little ones stumble: better a millstone and the sea.
v. 7: woe to the world because of stumbling blocks; they will come, but woe to the one through whom they come.
vv. 8–9: if hand, foot or eye makes you stumble, cut it off; better to enter life maimed than be thrown into the fire.
kw: Originally the stick that springs a trap, then any obstacle that makes someone trip. To “scandalise” in the Gospel is not merely to shock but to lead another into sin or out of faith.
Those who are small in the world’s eyes. In Matthew the word marks the disciples who are humble and vulnerable (10:42; 18:10, 14). The Father does not want one of them to be lost.
From the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a place of terrible idolatry (Jeremiah 7:31). The name became a picture of final ruin, the loss of God.
vv: If any of you put a stumbling block before one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for you if a great millstone were fastened around your neck and you were drowned in the depth of the sea.
The Greek speaks of a millstone turned by a donkey, far heavier than a hand mill. The picture is meant to shock: harming the faith of the weak is worse than death.
Occasions for stumbling are bound to come, but woe to the one by whom the stumbling block comes!
Jesus is realistic: in a fallen world scandals will happen. That does not excuse the one who causes them.
If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away
Jesus now turns from the scandal we give to others to the occasions of sin in ourselves. The language is a vivid way of speaking, not a command to harm the body (see the question below).
ch: The Catechism defines scandal as an attitude or behaviour which leads another to do evil, and teaches that it is especially grave when it comes from those who have authority over others or affects the weak; it is this that prompted the Lord’s words about the millstone (CCC 2284–2285). The Church applies the warning with humility to herself, above all where the young or vulnerable have been harmed by those who should have protected them. St Augustine, explaining the cutting off of hand and eye, says they stand for anything dear to us, even a friend or a habit, which draws us away from God (in substance, On the Sermon on the Mount 1.13).

qa: Jesus said, “Call no one your father on earth” (Matthew 23:9). Why does Paul call himself a father, and why do we call priests “Father”?

Jesus is warning against seeking titles that put a teacher in the place of God, the one Father from whom all fatherhood comes. He is not forbidding the word, for he himself teaches “Honor your father and your mother” (Matthew 15:4), and Stephen addresses the elders as “brothers and fathers” (Acts 7:2). Paul, filled with the Spirit, says plainly that he became the Corinthians’ father in Christ. Christians have used the title for spiritual fathers from the earliest times, as a sign that the life of grace is passed on through those God sends.
Does Jesus really mean that we should cut off a hand or tear out an eye?

No. Jesus is using a strong figure of speech, as teachers of his time often did, to show how seriously we must deal with what leads us into sin. The Church has always understood it this way and teaches that deliberately mutilating the body is against the moral law (CCC 2297). What must be cut off is the occasion of sin: a habit, a place, a screen, a relationship that draws us away from God.
rite: St Justin was born around the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis, the ancient Shechem in Samaria. He searched for truth among the philosophers and found it in Christ, and afterwards taught the faith in Rome while still wearing the philosopher’s cloak. He was beheaded there with several companions around 165. His First Apology gives the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist outside the New Testament: the reading of the memoirs of the apostles and the prophets, the homily, the prayers, the bread and wine brought, the thanksgiving and the people’s Amen (chapters 65 to 67, quoted in CCC 1345). Every Holy Qurbana still follows that shape.
study: Paul says the kingdom of God “depends not on talk but on power”. Where in my life does my faith remain only talk, and where can people see God’s power at work?
Who are the “little ones” around me whose faith I could help or harm by my words and example?

lead: Today’s readings are about faith that shines and spreads. Paul asks the Philippians to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, because God himself is at work in them, so that they may shine like stars in a crooked generation. In John, the Samaritan woman’s testimony brings her townspeople to Jesus, and once they have heard him for themselves they confess him as the Saviour of the world. In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns that every witness, however weak, is meant to lead others to meet Christ in person.

r.h: Shine like stars in the world
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison (1:13), the community in Macedonia he loved perhaps more than any other. He has just set before them the great hymn of Christ who emptied himself, became obedient unto death on a cross, and was exalted by the Father (2:6–11). “Therefore” in verse 12 draws the consequence: what Christ did must now take shape in their lives.
str: vv. 12–13: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for God is at work in you.
vv. 14–15: do all things without murmuring, so as to be blameless children of God, shining like stars.
v. 16: hold fast to the word of life, so that Paul’s labour will not have been in vain.
kw: A verb for bringing something to completion. Salvation is God’s gift, but the believer must let it grow to its full fruit in daily life.
The word behind our “energy”. God is not an onlooker; he works within the will and the action of the believer. Our working is the fruit of his.
The word used in the Greek Old Testament for the lights in the sky (Genesis 1:14). Paul echoes Daniel 12:3, where the wise shine like the brightness of the sky.
vv: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling
“Fear and trembling” is not anxiety about whether God is good, but the reverence of someone who knows that salvation is precious and can be lost through carelessness.
for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
This verse is the key. We do not work in order to make God act; we work because he is already acting in us. Both the wanting and the doing are his gift.
Do all things without murmuring and arguing
“Murmuring” recalls Israel grumbling in the desert (Exodus 16:7–8). In the next verse Paul borrows the words “crooked and perverse generation” from Deuteronomy 32:5.
in which you shine like stars in the world.
The Christians of Philippi were a small group in a Roman colony. Paul does not tell them to withdraw from the world but to shine in it.
ch: The Church reads these verses as a clear statement of how grace and human freedom work together. The Catechism teaches that God’s gracious initiative calls for a human response made in freedom, and that our merits are themselves the gifts of God (CCC 2002, 2009). It quotes St Augustine: God created us without us, but he did not will to save us without us (CCC 1847). The Council of Trent, against the idea that we are merely passive, taught that grace moves the will without destroying its freedom.

r.h: This is truly the Saviour of the world
set: At Jacob’s well near the Samaritan town of Sychar, Jesus has spoken with a woman who came to draw water at noon. He told her of living water, revealed that he knew her life, and said to her, “I am he,” the Messiah (4:26). She left her water jar and went back to the town, saying, “Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done!” (4:29). Meanwhile Jesus told his disciples that the fields were already white for harvest (4:35). These verses show that harvest.
str: v. 39: many Samaritans believe because of the woman’s testimony.
v. 40: they ask Jesus to stay; he stays two days.
v. 41: many more believe because of his own word.
v. 42: their confession: we have heard for ourselves; this is truly the Saviour of the world.
kw: The woman bears witness, the same word used of John the Baptist (1:7) and of the beloved disciple (21:24). A woman with a troubled past becomes the first to bring a whole town to Christ in this Gospel.
A favourite word in John. The disciples first asked Jesus where he was staying and stayed with him (1:38–39). Now the Samaritans ask him to stay, and faith grows in his company.
This title appears only here and in 1 John 4:14. In the Roman world it was sometimes given to emperors. People whom many in Judea kept at a distance are the ones who give Jesus this universal title.
vv: Many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me everything I have ever done.”
She does not preach a sermon; she tells what happened to her. Being known by Jesus, and not rejected, has made her a witness.
So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days.
Jesus, a Jew, accepts the hospitality of Samaritans, crossing a long-standing division (4:9). His staying is itself a message.
It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.
This is the path of all faith: it often begins with someone else’s word and becomes our own in a personal meeting with Christ.
ch: St Augustine saw in this passage the pattern of the Church’s mission: people first hear of Christ through the Church, as the Samaritans heard through the woman, and then they come to believe because of Christ himself (in substance, Tractates on John 15). The Catechism teaches that faith is a personal act, the response a person makes in freedom to God who reveals himself, and yet never an isolated act, because we receive it from others and pass it on (CCC 166). Pope Francis, speaking of the Samaritan woman, noted that she became a missionary straight after her encounter with Jesus (Evangelii Gaudium 120).

study: Paul says that God is at work in me “both to will and to work”. Where have I noticed God moving my desires as well as my actions?
The Samaritans’ faith began with a woman’s word and became their own when they met Jesus. Who first spoke to me of Christ, and to whom can I speak of him?

lead: Both readings use the picture of seed and soil. Paul tells the quarrelling Corinthians that he planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth, and that they are God’s field. In Luke, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains it: the seed is the word of God, and only the heart that holds it fast with patience bears fruit. The Church hears today that ministers are only servants of the growth, and that every hearer must become good soil.

r.h: You are God’s field
set: In chapter 2 Paul has spoken of the hidden wisdom of God, revealed by the Spirit to those who are spiritual (2:6–16). Now he turns to the Corinthians themselves. They prided themselves on wisdom and spiritual gifts, but their rivalries over preachers show that they are still beginners. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who taught in Corinth after Paul had founded the church there (Acts 18:24–28).
str: vv. 1–2: Paul could not speak to them as spiritual people; he gave them milk, not solid food.
vv. 3–4: their jealousy and slogans (“I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”) show they are still of the flesh.
vv. 5–7: Paul and Apollos are only servants; one planted, one watered, but God gave the growth.
vv. 8–9: planter and waterer work together and each receives his wage; you are God’s field, God’s building.
kw: Not people who have bodies, but those whose thinking and behaviour are still ruled by merely human ways. For Paul “flesh” is human nature left to itself, closed to the Spirit.

Little children who cannot yet take solid food. The Corinthians thought themselves mature; Paul says they are babies in Christ, which is no shame for a beginner but is a shame for those who should have grown.
Literally “co-workers”. Paul and Apollos are God’s fellow workers and also co-workers with each other: not rivals but labourers in the same field.
vv: I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for solid food.
A good teacher gives what the hearers can receive. The Letter to the Hebrews uses the same picture (Hebrews 5:12–14).
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.
The first two verbs describe single past actions; the third, in the Greek imperfect tense, suggests that God kept on giving growth. The ministers came and went; God’s work continued.
For we are God’s servants, working together; you are God’s field, God’s building.
Three times in one verse Paul says “God’s”. The Church does not belong to its preachers. The next verses develop the picture of the building, with Christ as its only foundation (3:11).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, describing the Church through images drawn from Scripture, calls her the cultivated field, the tillage of God, and also God’s building, quoting this verse (Lumen Gentium 6; CCC 755–756). The Church has always applied Paul’s words to her ministers: they are servants through whom God acts, and the fruit is his. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, observes that Paul makes himself and Apollos small so that the Corinthians would stop dividing over them (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 8).

r.h: The seed is the word of God
set: Luke has just described Jesus going through cities and villages proclaiming the good news, with the Twelve and certain women who provided for them out of their resources (8:1–3). Large crowds are now gathering. The parable of the sower appears in Matthew, Mark and Luke, each with an explanation; Luke’s telling is shorter and lays special stress on hearing the word and holding it fast.
str: v. 4: a great crowd from town after town.
vv. 5–8: the parable: seed on the path, on rock, among thorns, in good soil; “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
vv. 9–10: the disciples ask its meaning; the secrets of the kingdom are given to them.
vv. 11–15: the explanation: the seed is the word of God; four kinds of hearers.
kw: Not puzzles but God’s plan, once hidden and now being revealed in Jesus. It is given as a gift to those who come close and ask, as the disciples do here.
Literally “beautiful and good”, a Greek phrase for a person of noble character. In Luke the good soil is a heart that is sincere and well disposed.
Steadfastness that holds on under pressure. Luke alone adds that the good soil bears fruit “with patient endurance”: fruit does not come in a day.
vv: A sower went out to sow his seed
In Palestine seed was often scattered broadly, sometimes before ploughing. The sower is generous; he does not first measure the soil.
The seed is the word of God.
Luke states plainly what the seed is. The same word of God that Jesus sows will later spread through the apostles, so that in Acts “the word of God continued to spread” (Acts 6:7).
they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
The thorns are not great crimes but ordinary cares and comforts. They do not kill the seed at once; they slowly crowd it out.
these are the ones who, when they hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.

Hearing, holding fast, bearing fruit with endurance: Luke gives a whole programme of discipleship in one sentence. A little later he will show Jesus’ true family as “those who hear the word of God and do it” (8:21).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, quoted in the Catechism, compares the word of the Lord to a seed sown in a field: those who hear it with faith and are numbered among Christ’s little flock have truly received the kingdom (Lumen Gentium 5; CCC 543). The Catechism adds that Jesus’ parables call for a decision, and that for those who stay outside, everything remains enigmatic (CCC 546). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, admitted that his hearers might be surprised that the Lord calls riches thorns, and explained that riches wound the mind with cares and choke the word (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 15).

qa: Jesus says he speaks in parables “so that ‘looking they may not perceive’”. Does he want some people not to understand?

Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9–10, where God tells the prophet that his preaching will meet hardened hearts. The words describe the result of preaching to those who refuse to listen, not God’s wish that anyone be lost. Parables reveal to those who come close and ask, like the disciples, and they remain closed to those who stand at a distance. The Catechism says that through his parables Jesus invites people to the feast of the kingdom but also asks for a radical choice (CCC 546).
study: Paul says that God gives the growth. In my work for the parish or family, do I sometimes act as if the fruit depends only on me?
Which of the four soils best describes my hearing of God’s word this week, and what thorns need clearing?

lead: On the feast of the Sacred Heart the four readings lead us step by step into the heart of God. In Genesis, Abram shows a large and peaceful heart: rather than quarrel with his nephew Lot, he lets him choose first, and God renews the promise to the one who gave way. In Isaiah, the Servant of the Lord is wounded for our transgressions, and by his bruises we are healed. Paul, his heart aching for his own people, teaches that one believes with the heart and is justified. And in John, a soldier’s spear opens the side of the crucified Jesus, and at once blood and water flow out.

The Heart of Jesus is not a sentimental picture but the whole of his love, human and divine, given to the end. The Fathers saw the Church and her sacraments born from that opened side. Today we are invited to look on the one whom they pierced, and to let our own hearts be made like his.

r.h: Let there be no strife between you and me
set: Abram has come back from Egypt to the hill country of Bethel, where he had built an altar at the start of his journey (13:3–4; 12:8). Both he and his nephew Lot have grown rich in flocks, herds and tents, and the land cannot support them both; their herdsmen quarrel (13:5–7). Abram is the elder, and the land has been promised to him (12:7). By custom he could have chosen first.

Instead he offers Lot the choice. Lot looks down on the plain of the Jordan, green and well watered, and takes it, moving towards Sodom. Only after Lot has gone does God speak to Abram, and the promise that seemed to be given away comes back to him enlarged.
str: vv. 8–9: Abram’s proposal: no strife, for we are kindred; the whole land is before you, choose.
vv. 10–11: Lot looks, sees the well-watered plain, and chooses it for himself.
vv. 12–13: Abram stays in Canaan; Lot settles near Sodom, whose people were wicked.
vv. 14–17: God renews the promise: look in every direction; the land and countless descendants.
v. 18: Abram moves his tent to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
kw: A quarrel, a dispute. The same word names the place where Israel later quarrelled with God in the desert (Exodus 17:7). Abram refuses to let possessions divide a family.
Literally “brothers”. Lot is Abram’s nephew, but Hebrew uses “brother” for close relatives. The word makes Abram’s argument: family is worth more than pasture.
Great trees near Hebron, a place of worship. Here Abram will later welcome three visitors and receive the promise of a son (18:1). His life moves from altar to altar.
vv: Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.
Abram does not wait for Lot to make peace. The one with the stronger claim takes the first step.
Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me.
He gives up his right of choice. This is not weakness but trust: Abram knows the land is God’s gift, not something to be seized.
Lot looked about him, and saw that the plain of the Jordan was well watered everywhere like the garden of the Lord
Lot chooses by what his eyes see. The narrator adds a warning at once: this was before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.
Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward
Lot lifted his eyes to choose for himself; now God tells Abram to lift his eyes and receive. What Abram let go, God gives back in every direction.
So Abram moved his tent, and came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron; and there he built an altar to the Lord.
Abram answers the promise with worship. Tents move, but the altar marks where God is honoured.
ch: The Catechism describes Abraham’s heart as entirely submissive to the word of God, and notes that his prayer is expressed first by deeds: a man of silence, he builds an altar to the Lord at each stage of his journey (CCC 2570). The Letter to the Hebrews sees in his life in tents a sign that he was looking forward to a city whose builder is God (Hebrews 11:9–10). On this feast the Church hears in Abram’s generosity an echo of the Heart that is “gentle and humble” (Matthew 11:29): the one who gives way in love loses nothing that God wants to give.

r.h: He was wounded for our transgressions
set: This is the fourth and greatest of the Servant Songs in the second part of Isaiah (the others are 42:1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–9). These chapters (40 to 55) speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ, announcing comfort and return. Many scholars think they come from a prophet of that time who stood in the tradition of Isaiah of Jerusalem.

Who is the Servant? Within the book he is sometimes Israel itself (41:8; 49:3), and Jewish tradition has often read this song of the people of Israel in their sufferings. Others have seen a prophet or a future figure. From the beginning Christians have recognised in this Servant Jesus, who suffered for the sins of others: the deacon Philip explains this passage to the Ethiopian official as the good news of Jesus (Acts 8:32–35).
str: 52:13–15: God speaks: my servant shall be exalted; many were appalled at his disfigured form; kings will be silent.
53:1–3: a group speaks (“we”): he grew up like a root in dry ground; despised and rejected.
53:4–6: the turning point: he bore our infirmities; wounded for our transgressions; the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all.
53:7–9: he was silent like a lamb; taken away by injustice; his grave with the wicked though he had done no violence.
kw: A title of honour, given to Moses and David. The Servant belongs wholly to God and carries out his will, even through suffering.
The verb means both to act wisely and to succeed. The song begins with the end: the one who seems a failure is the one whose work succeeds.
A singular noun, literally “his bruise” or “stripe”, the mark of a blow. 1 Peter 2:24 quotes this verse: “by his wounds you have been healed.”
vv: See, my servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
The same verbs are used of God himself in Isaiah’s vision (6:1). John’s Gospel speaks of Jesus being “lifted up” on the cross, which is already his glory (John 12:32–33).
He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity
People turned their faces away. The Servant knows the loneliness of every sufferer.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.
The heart of the song. “We” thought he was punished for his own sins (v. 4); now “we” see that he carried ours. The wounds of the Servant become the place of our healing.
like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.
Jesus was silent before the high priest and before Pilate (Mark 14:61; 15:5). John the Baptist calls him “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Scriptures foretold God’s plan of salvation through the death of “the righteous one, my servant”, as a mystery of universal redemption (CCC 601, quoting Isaiah 53:11). It explains that when John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, he reveals him as both the suffering Servant who silently lets himself be led to the slaughter and the Paschal Lamb (CCC 608). St Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, quoted this whole song to show that the prophets had foretold the sufferings of Christ (in substance, First Apology 50–51). The Gospels apply it to Jesus’ healing (Matthew 8:17) and his Passion (Luke 22:37).

r.h: One believes with the heart
set: Chapters 9 to 11 of Romans are Paul’s long reflection on his own people, Israel, most of whom had not accepted Jesus as Messiah. He begins with deep grief: he would be willing to be cut off from Christ for the sake of his kindred (9:3). He insists that to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship and the promises, and from them comes the Messiah (9:4–5).

In these verses Paul contrasts two ways of seeking righteousness: by one’s own achievement under the law, and by faith in what God has done in Christ. He takes words of Moses from Deuteronomy 30:12–14, which said that God’s commandment is not far away in heaven or across the sea, and applies them to the word of faith: Christ has already come down and been raised.
str: vv. 1–3: Paul’s prayer for Israel’s salvation; their zeal for God, not according to knowledge.
v. 4: Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes.
vv. 5–8: two kinds of righteousness; the word is near you, on your lips and in your heart.
vv. 9–10: confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord, believe in your heart that God raised him: you will be saved.
kw: Ardent devotion. Paul had it himself as a Pharisee, so much that he persecuted the Church (Philippians 3:6). He speaks of his people’s zeal with respect, as one who knows it from within.
Both “end” and “goal”. Christ is the goal toward which the law was leading and its fulfilment, not its cancellation (compare Matthew 5:17).
One of the earliest Christian confessions (1 Corinthians 12:3). In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios stands for the holy Name of God. To call Jesus Lord is to confess him as divine.
vv: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
Paul’s argument begins with love and prayer. He does not write about Israel as an outsider but as one of them (11:1).
For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
“Everyone”: the righteousness given in Christ is offered to Jew and Gentile alike (10:12).
The word is near you, on your lips and in your heart
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:14. God does not ask us to climb to heaven; in Christ he has come close.
because if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
Lips and heart: faith is both inward and spoken. The order of verse 9 follows Deuteronomy’s words (“lips” then “heart”); verse 10 puts the heart first.
For one believes with the heart and so is justified, and one confesses with the mouth and so is saved.
In the Bible the heart is not only feelings but the centre of the person, where decisions are made. On this feast we remember that Christ first gave us his own Heart.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 4 to teach that the moral law finds its fullness and unity in Christ, who is the end of the law because he alone teaches and gives the righteousness of God (CCC 1953). It explains that by giving Jesus the divine title “Lord”, the first confessions of the Church’s faith affirmed that the honour due to God the Father is due also to him (CCC 449). It calls the heart the dwelling place where I am, our hidden centre, the place of decision and of covenant (CCC 2563). And it reminds us that the gifts and calling of God to the Jewish people are irrevocable, as Paul himself says in this same section (Romans 11:29; CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: They will look on the one whom they have pierced
set: Jesus has been crucified at Golgotha. He has entrusted his mother to the beloved disciple and the disciple to her (19:26–27), and has said, “I am thirsty,” receiving sour wine on a branch of hyssop (19:28–29). Now he dies.

John has told us that this was the day of Preparation for the Passover (19:14), the day the Passover lambs were slain in the Temple. The Law of Moses required that the body of an executed man not remain hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and this sabbath was the great feast. The Roman practice of breaking the legs of the crucified hastened death, because they could no longer push themselves up to breathe.
str: v. 30: Jesus receives the wine, says “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit.
vv. 31–33: the request to remove the bodies; the soldiers break the legs of the other two, but not of Jesus, already dead.
v. 34: a soldier pierces his side with a spear; at once blood and water come out.
v. 35: the eyewitness’s solemn testimony, so that you also may believe.
vv. 36–37: two Scriptures fulfilled: no bone broken; they will look on the one whom they have pierced.
kw: From telos, end and goal. Not “it is over” but “it is accomplished”: the work the Father gave him is brought to completion (17:4), and he loved his own “to the end” (13:1).

The word for Jesus’ side is the same word used in the Greek Old Testament for the rib taken from the side of the sleeping Adam, from which Eve was formed (Genesis 2:21–22). The Fathers built much on this.

The verb John uses to render Zechariah 12:10 from the Hebrew, where God says that the inhabitants of Jerusalem will look on the one they have pierced and mourn for him. John sees in the soldier’s spear the fulfilment of that prophecy of grief and grace.
vv: When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
Literally “he handed over the spirit”. He is not overcome by death; he lays down his life of his own accord (10:18). Many have also seen here a first hint of the gift of the Holy Spirit.
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.
The detail points to the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46).
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

Jesus had promised that rivers of living water would flow from within him, and John explained this of the Spirit (7:38–39). Blood and water recall the Eucharist and Baptism, by which the Church lives.
He who saw this has testified so that you also may believe. His testimony is true
The evangelist steps forward to vouch for what he saw, as he does at the end of the Gospel (21:24). This is the purpose of the whole book: “that you may come to believe” (20:31).
None of his bones shall be broken.
This recalls the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12) and also the righteous sufferer whom God protects (Psalm 34:20).
And again another passage of scripture says, “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
Zechariah 12:10 continues: they will mourn for him as for an only child. Looking on the pierced Christ leads to sorrow for sin and to the fountain that cleanses (Zechariah 13:1).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus knew and loved each of us during his life, his agony and his Passion, and that his Sacred Heart, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is rightly considered the chief sign and symbol of the love with which he loves the Father and all people (CCC 478). The Church, it says, was born primarily of Christ’s total self-giving, anticipated in the Last Supper and realised on the cross, symbolised by the blood and water flowing from his opened side (CCC 766). The blood and water are types of Baptism and the Eucharist (CCC 1225).

St John Chrysostom taught that the Church was formed from the side of Christ as Eve was formed from the side of Adam, and that water and blood are the symbols of Baptism and the holy mysteries (in substance, Baptismal Catecheses 3). St Augustine observed that the evangelist chose his word carefully: the soldier opened his side, so that the door of life might be opened, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed (in substance, Tractates on John 120.2). Pope Pius XII took the title of his encyclical on the Sacred Heart from Isaiah 12:3, “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Haurietis Aquas, 1956), and Pope Francis returned to the theme in Dilexit Nos (2024).

qa: Why does the Church honour Jesus’ heart? Is this not just a sentimental image?

In the Bible the heart means the centre of the person, where love, thought and choice meet (CCC 2563). To honour the Heart of Jesus is to honour the whole person of the incarnate Son in his love, which is both human and divine. The Catechism calls his pierced Heart the chief sign and symbol of that love (CCC 478). The devotion grew in the Middle Ages and was spread especially after the visions given to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial in France in the 1670s. Pope Pius IX extended the feast to the whole Latin Church in 1856.
John says that “the Jews” asked for the legs to be broken. Does the Gospel blame the Jewish people?

No. In John’s Passion “the Jews” usually means the Temple authorities who acted against Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus himself, his mother, the beloved disciple and all the first disciples were Jews. Here the request even comes from a concern to keep God’s Law about the dead (Deuteronomy 21:22–23) and to honour the feast. The Church teaches that Christ’s death cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that all sinners were the authors of his Passion (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
Is Isaiah 53 really about Jesus, or about Israel?

Both readings have a long history. Within Isaiah, the Servant is at times Israel, and Jewish interpreters have often read this song of the sufferings of their people, a reading Christians should respect. The New Testament, from Philip’s words to the Ethiopian (Acts 8:35) to 1 Peter 2:22–25, sees its fullest meaning in Jesus, the one innocent man who suffered for the sins of many. The Church holds that the Old Testament keeps its own value and that its full meaning is revealed in Christ (CCC 128–129).
rite: Many Syro-Malabar families keep a picture of the Sacred Heart in the place of prayer at home and have consecrated their family to it, and the First Friday devotion, with confession and Holy Qurbana, is loved in our parishes. The feast falls in the Season of the Apostles: the Church born from the opened side is the Church sent out on mission, as Mar Thoma Shleeha was sent to our land.

Our East Syriac tradition loves to set the cross beside the tree of life. Mar Ephrem, meditating on the Passion, speaks of entering through the pierced side of Christ into the garden that had been closed by the sword since Adam’s sin (in substance, Commentary on the Diatessaron 21). The fountain that flows from the side of the second Adam reopens Paradise. Each time we receive the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Holy Qurbana, we drink from that fountain.
study: Abram let Lot choose first rather than quarrel. In which relationship in my family or parish am I being asked to give way for the sake of peace?
Isaiah says “by his bruises we are healed”. What wound in my life do I need to bring to the wounds of Christ?
Paul says we believe with the heart and confess with the lips. Is there a place where my faith stays hidden in my heart and needs to be spoken?
John asks us to look on the one whom they pierced. How could my family spend a few minutes before the image of the Sacred Heart this week?

lead: The day after the feast of the Sacred Heart, the Church turns to the Heart of the Mother. The four readings trace how God prepared and filled that heart. In Genesis, God gives Sarai a new name and promises that the barren woman will become the mother of nations, the bearer of the covenant child. In Isaiah, when King Ahaz refuses to trust, God himself gives a sign: a young woman will bear a son called Immanuel. Ephesians blesses the Father who chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love. And in Luke, after three days of searching, Mary finds her Son in the Temple, does not fully understand his words, and treasures all these things in her heart.

Mary’s heart is called immaculate because God preserved it from every stain of sin from the first moment of her existence, by the merits of her Son. But Luke shows us that this pure heart was not spared sorrow, searching or the effort of faith. It is a heart that keeps God’s word and ponders it, and so it is the model for ours.

r.h: Sarah shall give rise to nations
set: Genesis 17 tells of God’s covenant with Abraham when he was ninety-nine years old (17:1). God changes his name from Abram to Abraham, “ancestor of a multitude” (17:5), and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant. Abraham already has a son, Ishmael, born to Sarai’s servant Hagar, now thirteen years old (16:15–16; 17:25). Many years have passed since the first promise, and Sarai is far past the age of childbearing.
In today’s verses the promise becomes precise: the covenant child will be born of Sarah herself, and he will be called Isaac.
str: vv. 15–16: Sarai is renamed Sarah; God will bless her and give Abraham a son by her; she will become nations.
v. 17: Abraham falls on his face and laughs: can a man of a hundred and a woman of ninety have a child?
v. 18: Abraham’s plea for Ishmael.
vv. 19–21: God’s answer: Sarah will bear a son, Isaac, heir of the everlasting covenant; Ishmael too will be blessed.
v. 22: God goes up from Abraham.
kw: Both Sarai and Sarah are usually understood as forms of the word for “princess”. The new name marks a new mission: she will be the mother of kings.
Abraham laughs in disbelief (v. 17), and Sarah will laugh too (18:12). God gives the child a name that turns their laughter into joy: “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6).
A covenant without end, binding God to Abraham’s descendants. God’s faithfulness does not depend on human possibility.
vv: As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.
God names Sarah himself. In this chapter she is no longer only Abraham’s wife; she has her own place in the covenant.
I will bless her, and she shall give rise to nations; kings of peoples shall come from her.
Twice God says “I will bless her”. The woman who seemed to have no future becomes a mother of peoples.
Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?

Abraham’s laughter is not mockery but astonishment. The question will be answered at Mamre: “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (18:14), words echoed by the angel to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall name him Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.
The covenant passes through a child born not by human strength but by God’s promise. Paul will say that believers in Christ are, like Isaac, “children of the promise” (Galatians 4:28).
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him and make him fruitful and exceedingly numerous
God hears the father’s prayer for his other son. Ishmael is not rejected; he too receives a blessing and will become a great nation.
ch: The Catechism teaches that throughout the Old Covenant the mission of many holy women prepared for that of Mary, and names Sarah among them: by virtue of God’s promise, she conceives a son in spite of her old age (CCC 489). God chooses those who seem powerless to show his faithfulness. Sarah’s late motherhood and Mary’s virginal motherhood are both signs that the child of the covenant is God’s gift. Mary in her Magnificat praises the God who keeps the promise “to Abraham and to his descendants forever” (Luke 1:55).

r.h: The Lord himself will give you a sign
set: The year is about 735 BC. Rezin king of Aram (Damascus) and Pekah king of Israel (the northern kingdom) have marched against Jerusalem, wanting to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria. “The heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (7:2). Isaiah went to meet the young king and told him not to fear: “If you do not stand firm in faith, you shall not stand at all” (7:9).

Ahaz had other plans. He would soon send silver and gold to the king of Assyria and ask for his help (2 Kings 16:7–8), making Judah a vassal. When Isaiah offers him a sign from God, he refuses, hiding behind pious words.
str: vv. 10–11: God offers Ahaz a sign, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven.
v. 12: Ahaz refuses: I will not put the Lord to the test.
v. 13: Isaiah’s rebuke to the house of David: you weary my God.
v. 14: the Lord himself will give the sign: the young woman will bear a son, Immanuel.
vv. 15–16: before the child can choose good from evil, the lands of the two kings will be deserted.
kw: A visible pledge of God’s word. God offers it to strengthen faith, not to satisfy curiosity.

A young woman of marriageable age. The Greek translation made in Egypt before Christ, the Septuagint, rendered it parthenos, “virgin”, and Matthew quotes it in that form (Matthew 1:23). See the question below.
“God with us”. Isaiah repeats the name in 8:8 and 8:10. Matthew begins his Gospel with Immanuel (1:23) and ends it with Jesus’ promise, “I am with you always” (28:20).
vv: Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven.
God is generous: he lets Ahaz choose any sign at all. Sheol is the world of the dead; heaven the highest place.
But Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.
The words sound devout (Deuteronomy 6:16), but they hide a refusal to trust. Ahaz has already decided to rely on Assyria.
Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary mortals, that you weary my God also?
Isaiah now addresses not Ahaz alone but the whole royal house, the line to which God had promised a lasting throne (2 Samuel 7:16).
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.

When the king refuses, God gives the sign anyway. Many scholars think the first meaning was a child soon to be born in the royal house, perhaps Hezekiah, as a pledge that God had not abandoned David’s line. The Church, following Matthew, sees the full meaning in the virgin birth of Jesus, who is God with us in person.
He shall eat curds and honey by the time he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good.
Curds and honey may mean simple food in a land laid waste, or the food of plenty. Either way, within a few years the threat from the two kings will be gone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church sees in the virginal conception of Jesus the fulfilment of the divine promise given through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (CCC 497). The Second Vatican Council names Isaiah 7:14 among the Old Testament texts that, read in the light of later revelation, bring the figure of the Mother of the Redeemer into ever clearer light (Lumen Gentium 55). St Justin Martyr discussed this verse at length with the Jewish teacher Trypho, and St Irenaeus defended the reading “virgin” against those who preferred “young woman” (in substance, Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 66–67; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.21).

r.h: Chosen to be holy and blameless
set: The Letter to the Ephesians opens, after the greeting, with one of the longest sentences in the New Testament: in Greek, verses 3 to 14 are a single sentence of praise. It takes the form of a Jewish blessing, “Blessed be God”, like the prayers that begin “Blessed are you, Lord”. It praises the Father for his plan, carried out in the Son and sealed by the Holy Spirit.

The letter presents itself as written by Paul from prison (3:1). Many scholars think it was written after his death by a disciple who gathered up his teaching; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way, the Church receives it as inspired Scripture.
str: v. 2: greeting: grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
v. 3: blessed be God, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing.
v. 4: he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
vv. 5–6: he destined us for adoption as his children, to the praise of his glorious grace in the Beloved.
vv. 7–8: in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, the riches of grace lavished on us.
kw: The word that opens Jewish blessings. God has blessed us (eulogēsas); we bless him in return. Praise is the right response to grace.
Literally “without blemish”, the word used for sacrificial animals offered to God without defect. Here it describes the holiness God wants for his people (5:27).
A rare verb, “to fill with grace”. Its only other use in the New Testament is the angel’s greeting to Mary: kecharitōmenē, “favoured one”, full of grace (Luke 1:28).
vv: who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places
Every gift comes “in Christ”, a phrase that runs through this whole passage like a refrain.
just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Before anything existed, God had us in mind. Holiness is not our invention but his first purpose for us, and it is lived “in love”.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ
Adoption was a well-known legal act in the Roman world, giving the adopted child full rights as heir. In Christ we become sons and daughters of God.
to the praise of his glorious grace that he freely bestowed on us in the Beloved.
“The Beloved” recalls the Father’s voice at the Baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:11). All grace reaches us through the beloved Son.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses
Redemption means a ransom that releases captives. The price is Christ’s own blood, the blood that flowed from his side.
ch: The Catechism applies these very verses to Mary: the Father blessed Mary more than any other created person “in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” and chose her “in Christ before the foundation of the world, to be holy and blameless before him in love” (CCC 492). It teaches, with Blessed Pius IX’s definition of 1854, that Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception, by a singular grace and in view of the merits of Jesus Christ (CCC 491). She too is redeemed, but in a more exalted way, by the blood of her Son (CCC 492; Lumen Gentium 53). What God did fully in her at the start, he wants to do in all of us by the end.

r.h: His mother treasured all these things in her heart
set: This is the only story in the Gospels from the years between Jesus’ infancy and his public ministry. The Law asked every Israelite man to go up to the sanctuary for the three great feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16), and devout families went to Jerusalem at least for Passover. Pilgrims from Galilee travelled in large groups of relatives and neighbours, about three or four days’ journey each way.

Jesus is twelve, close to the age at which a Jewish boy took on the duties of the Law. Luke has already told us that Mary treasured and pondered what happened at the birth (2:19); now he ends the infancy stories with the same note.
str: vv. 41–42: the yearly Passover pilgrimage; Jesus is twelve.
vv. 43–45: Jesus stays behind; his parents travel a day, search among relatives, return to Jerusalem.
vv. 46–47: after three days they find him in the Temple among the teachers; all are amazed.
vv. 48–50: Mary’s question and Jesus’ answer about his Father; they do not understand.
v. 51: he goes down to Nazareth and is obedient to them; his mother treasures all these things in her heart.
kw: A strong word for pain and anguish. Luke uses it again of the elders of Ephesus weeping at Paul’s farewell (Acts 20:38). Mary’s anxiety is the sorrow of love, not of sin. Simeon had foretold that a sword would pierce her soul (2:35).
Literally “in the things of my Father”. It can mean “in my Father’s house” (NRSV) or “about my Father’s affairs”, as the POC renders it. Both are true: Jesus belongs wholly to his Father.

To keep carefully, to hold on to. In 2:19 Luke used a related verb (synetērei), adding that she pondered these things. Mary does not throw away what she cannot yet understand; she keeps it until its meaning is revealed.
vv: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
Many have seen in the three days a foreshadowing of the three days between the cross and the Resurrection, when Jesus was again lost to those who loved him and found again.
Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.
Mary speaks first, as a mother would. She calls Joseph “your father”: he is truly the father who raises and protects Jesus, as the Church honours him.
Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?
These are Jesus’ first words in Luke’s Gospel. Mary said “your father”; Jesus speaks of “my Father”. The word “must” will return in his Passion: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22).
But they did not understand what he said to them.
Luke is honest: even Mary and Joseph did not grasp everything at once. Faith is a journey.
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
The Son of God lives in obedience in an ordinary home for many years. Mary’s heart becomes the place where the mysteries of her Son are kept and slowly understood.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the finding in the Temple is the only event that breaks the silence of the Gospels about the hidden years of Jesus. Mary and Joseph did not understand his words, but they accepted them in faith, and Mary “kept all these things in her heart” during the years Jesus remained hidden in an ordinary life (CCC 534). Jesus’ obedience to his mother and legal father fulfils the fourth commandment perfectly (CCC 532). The Second Vatican Council says that Mary advanced in her pilgrimage of faith and faithfully kept her union with her Son even to the cross (Lumen Gentium 58). Pope St Paul VI, at Nazareth in 1964, spoke of the lessons of silence, family life and work taught by this hidden home.

qa: Does Isaiah 7:14 say “virgin” or “young woman”?

The Hebrew word ‘almâ means a young woman of marriageable age; the usual Hebrew word for virgin is another one. But the Greek translation made by Jewish scholars before Christ, the Septuagint, rendered it parthenos, virgin, and Matthew quotes this form to show its fulfilment in Mary (Matthew 1:23). The Church does not rest the virgin birth on one word of Isaiah, but on the testimony of Matthew and Luke, and reads the prophecy in its light: the sign promised to David’s house is fulfilled beyond all expectation when the Son of God is born of a virgin (CCC 497).
If Mary’s heart was immaculate, why did she not understand Jesus’ words?

Freedom from sin is not the same as knowing everything. Mary was full of grace, but she still lived by faith, not by sight. Luke shows her searching, asking, not understanding at once, and keeping what she did not grasp until God made it clear. The Council says that she advanced in her pilgrimage of faith (Lumen Gentium 58). That makes her close to us: a pure heart can still be a searching heart.
What does devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary mean?

It honours Mary’s inner life: her love for God and her Son, her faith, her sorrow and her care for us, all of it untouched by sin and wholly turned to God. St John Eudes in the seventeenth century promoted the liturgical honour of the Hearts of Jesus and Mary. After the apparitions at Fatima in 1917, Pope Pius XII consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart in 1942 and extended the feast to the whole Latin Church in 1944. True devotion always leads to the Heart of her Son, as Mary’s own words at Cana lead to him: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
rite: Mar Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit honoured by all the Syriac Churches, praised Mary’s purity in words the Church has often recalled: Christ and his Mother alone are beautiful in every way, for in him there is no blemish and in his Mother no stain (in substance, Nisibene Hymns 27). In the Season of the Apostles we remember that Mary was with the apostles in prayer before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). In many Syro-Malabar homes the family gathers each evening for the rosary; on this feast it is a fitting way to entrust our families to her heart, which kept the word of God and pondered it.
study: Sarah received a new name and a mission when all hope seemed gone. Where in my life do I need to trust that nothing is impossible with God?
Ahaz refused a sign because he had already decided to rely on his own plans. Where am I tempted to trust my own strategies rather than God?
Ephesians says God chose us to be holy and blameless in love. How does Mary help me believe that holiness is God’s plan for me too?
Mary did not understand at once but kept everything in her heart. What event in my life do I need to keep and ponder before God rather than judge too quickly?

lead: This Sunday’s readings ask what kind of people God’s people should be. Moses charges the judges of Israel to hear the small and the great alike, because judgment belongs to God. Isaiah, continuing where last Sunday’s reading left off, tells Jerusalem that God cannot bear worship offered by hands full of blood: wash yourselves, learn to do good, defend the orphan and the widow, and though your sins are like scarlet they shall be like snow. Paul makes himself a slave to all to win them for Christ, and trains like an athlete for an imperishable wreath. And in Luke, Jesus asks the most demanding thing of all: love your enemies, be merciful as your Father is merciful.

The thread that joins them is the character of God himself. He shows no partiality; he wants justice more than sacrifices; he spares nothing to save; he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked. In the Season of the Apostles the Church hears that those sent in Christ’s name must reflect the face of the Father.

r.h: Hear the small and the great alike
set: Moses is giving his first great speech in the plains of Moab, retelling the journey from Horeb. Last Sunday we heard God’s command to leave the mountain. Before telling of the departure, Moses recalls how he shared the burden of leadership: the people had grown so numerous that he could not bear them alone, so he took wise and experienced men from each tribe and set them as leaders and judges (1:9–15). The story of this appointment, made on the advice of his father-in-law Jethro, is told in Exodus 18:13–26.

Today’s verses are Moses’ charge to those judges. In a small community where everyone knew everyone, and where the powerful could easily press the weak, these words set out the basic principles of fair judgment.
str: v. 16: hear the cases fairly and judge rightly between brothers, and between an Israelite and a resident alien.
v. 17a: no partiality: hear the small and the great alike; do not fear anyone, for the judgment is God’s.
v. 17b: cases too hard for you, bring to me.
v. 18: Moses gave the people all the commands they were to keep.
kw: Literally “judge with righteousness”. Ṣedeq is the right order God wants among his people, not only correct procedure but what is truly just.
A foreigner living among Israel without land or family protection. The Law repeatedly commands care for the stranger, “for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

Literally “do not recognise faces”: do not let the face of the person, rich or poor, powerful or weak, decide the case. The New Testament uses the same idea when it says God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11).
vv: Give the members of your community a fair hearing, and judge rightly between one person and another, whether citizen or resident alien.
The stranger is given the same hearing as the citizen. Justice that protects only one’s own is not God’s justice.
You must not be partial in judging: hear out the small and the great alike
The small are named first. In practice it is the poor whose voice is easily ignored.
you shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s.
A judge acts in God’s name, not in the name of the powerful. This gives courage, and also humility: the judge too will be judged.
Any case that is too hard for you, bring to me, and I will hear it.
Even those with authority must know their limits and seek help. Good leadership is shared and humble.
ch: The Catechism defines justice as the constant and firm will to give God and neighbour their due, and quotes the Law: “You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbour” (CCC 1807; Leviticus 19:15). The Letter of James warns Christians against showing partiality in the assembly itself, honouring the rich and dishonouring the poor (James 2:1–9). The Church’s social teaching asks all who hold authority to serve the common good and to give special care to the poor and the weak (CCC 1902–1903, 2448).

r.h: Wash yourselves; learn to do good
set: Isaiah’s first chapter is a kind of overture to the whole book. Last Sunday we heard its opening: a people wounded from head to foot, Jerusalem left like a hut in a field, saved from becoming like Sodom only because God kept a few survivors (1:1–9). Isaiah now takes up the name of Sodom and turns it into a sharp address to the leaders and people of Jerusalem.

The setting is the Temple, crowded with sacrifices and festivals. Isaiah himself had received his call in that Temple (6:1–8), so he is not attacking worship as such. He attacks worship cut off from justice: prayers lifted by hands stained with the blood of the oppressed.
str: v. 10: the summons: hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom, you people of Gomorrah.
vv. 11–15: God refuses sacrifices, offerings, festivals and even prayers from hands full of blood.
vv. 16–17: nine commands: wash, be clean, remove evil, cease to do evil, learn to do good, seek justice, rescue the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow.
vv. 18–20: the offer: let us argue it out; scarlet sins made white; the choice between obedience and rebellion.
kw: Usually translated “law”, but its first meaning is instruction, the guidance a parent or teacher gives. Isaiah calls the prophetic word “the teaching of our God”.
A term of the law court: let us settle the case, reason it out together. The POC renders it “let us be reconciled”, which is where God wants the case to end.
Right judgment in practice, especially for those who have no one to defend them. The orphan and the widow are the test of a society’s justice.
vv: Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!
A shocking address to the holy city. The Church hears it as spoken first to herself whenever her worship and her life part company.
What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord
God commanded sacrifices in the Law. What he rejects is the idea that they can replace a just life.
even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood.
Raised hands were the posture of prayer. The same hands have harmed the weak. God will not look at hands he sees doing evil.

Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your doings from before my eyes; cease to do evil, learn to do good; seek justice, rescue the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow.
The washing God wants is a changed life. “Learn” is important: doing good is a skill, practised and grown.
Come now, let us argue it out, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow
The court case ends in an offer of mercy. Scarlet and crimson were fast dyes that could not be washed out; God promises to do what no washing can.
ch: The Catechism teaches that outward sacrifice, to be genuine, must express spiritual sacrifice, and that the prophets often denounced sacrifices not from the heart or not joined to love of neighbour (CCC 2100). The Church has always heard in verse 18 the promise fulfilled in Baptism and in the sacrament of Penance, where God washes away sins we could never remove ourselves. St Justin Martyr quoted verses 16 to 20 when he explained Christian Baptism to the emperor, calling it the washing by which believers are made new (in substance, First Apology 61).

r.h: Run so as to win the imperishable wreath
set: Chapters 8 to 10 of the letter deal with food offered to idols, which some Corinthians ate without scruple, troubling the consciences of others. In chapter 9 Paul gives his own example: as an apostle he had rights, including the right to be supported by the community, but he gave them up so as not to hinder the Gospel (9:1–18).

In today’s verses he explains the principle behind his whole life: he adapts himself to everyone in order to win them for Christ. Then he turns to an image the Corinthians knew well. The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympic Games, were held every two years near Corinth; the winner received a wreath of pine or celery that soon withered.
str: v. 19: though bound to no one, Paul has made himself a slave to all.
vv. 20–22a: to Jews as a Jew, to those outside the law as one outside it, to the weak as weak.
vv. 22b–23: all things to all people, to save some; all for the sake of the Gospel.
vv. 24–25: in a race only one wins the prize; athletes train for a perishable wreath, we for an imperishable one.
vv. 26–27: Paul does not run aimlessly or box at the air; he disciplines his body so as not to be disqualified.
kw: Paul is not lawless. He is bound by the law of Christ, the law of love (Galatians 6:2). His flexibility is in customs, never in faith or morals.
The victor’s crown of leaves at the games. Paul contrasts it with the crown of eternal life (2 Timothy 4:8; James 1:12).
A boxing term, literally “to strike under the eye”. Paul uses it as a vivid picture of self-discipline, not of hatred for the body.
vv: For though I am free with respect to all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.
Paul’s freedom is used for service. This is the pattern of Christ, who took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7).
To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews.
Paul was himself a Jew and kept Jewish customs when it helped his mission (Acts 21:26). He did not regard the practices of his people with contempt.
I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.
Not changing the message, but changing the manner. A missionary learns the language, food and customs of those he serves.
Run in such a way that you may win it.
Not every runner wins at the games, but in God’s race all who run faithfully can receive the prize. The point is to run in earnest.
Athletes exercise self-control in all things; they do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one.
If athletes discipline themselves for a few leaves, how much more should Christians for eternal life?
I punish my body and enslave it, so that after proclaiming to others I myself should not be disqualified.
Even the great apostle does not presume on his salvation. Preaching to others does not excuse the preacher from his own conversion.
ch: The Church has taken Paul’s “all things to all people” as a charter for inculturation: the Gospel must take flesh in each people’s culture while remaining whole and unchanged (Redemptoris Missio 52–54). The Catechism teaches that the way of perfection passes by way of the cross, that there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle, and that spiritual progress involves ascesis and mortification (CCC 2015). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, explains that Paul became all things not by changing his faith but by stooping to each person’s weakness out of love, as Christ did for us (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians).

r.h: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful
set: Luke’s Sermon on the Plain (6:17–49) is shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount, but shares much of it. Jesus has come down from the mountain where he chose the Twelve (6:12–16) and stands on a level place with a great crowd. He has just spoken four blessings for the poor, the hungry, those who weep and those who are hated, and four woes for the rich, the full, those who laugh and those who are praised (6:20–26).
Now he turns to “you that listen”. The love he commands is not a feeling but a decision to do good, even to those who do harm.
str: vv. 27–28: love your enemies, do good, bless, pray.
vv. 29–30: the cheek, the coat, giving and not demanding back.
v. 31: the golden rule.
vv. 32–34: three questions: what credit is it to love, do good and lend only to those who return it?
vv. 35–36: love, do good, lend expecting nothing; you will be children of the Most High; be merciful as your Father is merciful.
kw: Agapē is love that wills the good of the other. Jesus does not ask us to feel affection for those who hurt us, but to want and do their good.
The word usually means grace or favour. “What charis is that to you?” asks what is gracious, or God-like, about loving only those who love us.
Compassionate, moved with pity. Where Matthew says “Be perfect” (5:48), Luke says “Be merciful”: the perfection of the Father is his mercy.
vv: But I say to you that listen, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you
Four commands climb from inner attitude to action: love, do good, bless, pray. Prayer for an enemy is where love often has to begin.
bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
Jesus lived this on the cross: “Father, forgive them” (23:34), and Stephen followed him (Acts 7:60).
If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also
A blow on the cheek was above all an insult. Jesus asks his disciples not to answer insult with insult, breaking the chain of revenge (see the question below).
Do to others as you would have them do to you.
Many teachers taught a form of this rule. Jesus puts it in its most active form and sets it within love of enemies.
But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. Your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked.
The reason is God himself. Children resemble their Father; God sends his kindness even on those who do not thank him.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
This verse sums up the whole passage. Mercy is not one virtue among others; it is the family likeness of God’s children.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ died out of love for us while we were still enemies, and that the Lord asks us to love as he does, even our enemies (CCC 1825). It explains that “be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” cannot be kept by imitating God from outside, but only by a vital participation in his love, and that Christian prayer extends to the forgiveness of enemies, transfiguring the disciple into the likeness of the Master (CCC 2842–2844). The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings, begins its way of life with these words: bless those who curse you, pray for your enemies, love those who hate you (in substance, Didache 1). Pope Francis took “Merciful like the Father” from this verse as the motto of the Jubilee of Mercy (Misericordiae Vultus 13–14).

qa: When Jesus says “offer the other also”, does it mean we must accept abuse and never defend ourselves or others?

No. Jesus forbids revenge and the answering of insult with insult, not the protection of life and justice. When he was struck before the high priest, he asked, “If I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). The Church teaches that legitimate defence is allowed, and is even a grave duty for those responsible for others (CCC 2263–2265). A person suffering abuse is not asked by the Gospel to remain in danger. Forgiveness heals the heart; it does not require us to call evil good or to leave the weak unprotected.
In Isaiah, does God reject worship and sacrifice?

No. The same God commanded the sacrifices in the Law, and Isaiah received his call in the Temple (6:1–8). What God rejects is worship used as a cover for injustice. The prophets join the two together, as Jesus does when he tells us to be reconciled with our brother before offering our gift at the altar (Matthew 5:23–24). Our worship, above all the Eucharist, is meant to make our lives just and merciful.
Was Paul being two-faced when he became “all things to all people”?

No. Paul never changed the Gospel; he firmly resisted even Peter when he thought the truth of the Gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11–14). What he changed was his manner: customs, food, ways of speaking, so that nothing unnecessary would stand between people and Christ. Love made him flexible in small things so as to be faithful in great ones.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar Holy Qurbana the Peace is exchanged before the Anaphora begins, as we prepare to offer the gifts. Jesus’ command to love our enemies gives that gesture its full weight: we cannot share the peace of Christ with those near us while refusing to forgive. This Sunday we pray especially for Christians who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who have wronged them, that both may come to know the mercy of the Father.

Paul’s “all things to all people” also describes the long history of our Church. The St Thomas Christians kept the apostolic faith while living fully within the culture of Kerala; Fr Placid Podipara described them as Indian in culture, Christian in faith and Oriental in worship (in substance). In the Season of the Apostles we give thanks for that gift and pray for our missionaries who learn new languages and ways so that others may meet Christ.
study: Moses told the judges to hear the small and the great alike. Whose voice in my family, parish or workplace is easily ignored, and how can I make sure it is heard?
Isaiah says “learn to do good”. What is one good act I could practise this week until it becomes a habit?
Paul trained like an athlete for an imperishable wreath. What discipline in prayer, fasting or self-control would help me run better?
Jesus asks us to pray for those who abuse us. Who is the person I find hardest to pray for, and will I name them before God today?

lead: Both readings are about the comfort of God reaching people who suffer. Paul blesses “the God of all consolation”, who comforts him in every trouble so that he can pass that comfort on to others. In Mark, a woman who has suffered for twelve years reaches out in faith, touches the cloak of Jesus and is healed, and then hears him call her “Daughter”. In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns that the consolation of Christ is meant to flow on: the one who has been comforted becomes a comforter.

r.h: The God of all consolation
set: Second Corinthians was written after a painful time between Paul and the community at Corinth: a hurtful visit, a severe letter written “with many tears” (2:4), and news of a terrible affliction he had suffered in the province of Asia (1:8). Instead of the usual thanksgiving after the greeting, Paul begins with a blessing of God, in the Jewish form “Blessed be God…”. The word “consolation” and its verb occur ten times in these five verses.
str: v. 3: the blessing: God is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.
v. 4: God comforts us so that we may comfort others with the same comfort.
v. 5: as Christ’s sufferings overflow to us, so does consolation through Christ.
vv. 6–7: Paul’s sufferings and comfort are for the Corinthians; they share both, and his hope for them is firm.
kw: From the verb “to call to one’s side”. It is the comfort of someone who stands beside us, not only kind words. The same root gives Paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit (John 14:16).
Literally “pressure, crushing”. Paul uses it for real hardship: danger, opposition, despair (1:8). God does not always remove the pressure; he comforts within it.
Paul does not say his sufferings are like Christ’s; he says Christ’s sufferings overflow into his life. The apostle lives the life of his Lord, the Cross included.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation,
“Father of mercies” is a Jewish way of praying, still heard in synagogue prayer. Paul joins it to the name of Jesus: the merciful God is known as the Father of our Lord.
who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction
Comfort is never a private possession. What God gives us in our trouble becomes the gift we can hand to another.
For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.
Two overflowings, and the second matches the first. Those who share the Cross are not left without the comfort of the Risen Lord.
ch: Pope St John Paul II, in his letter on human suffering Salvifici Doloris (1984), dwells on Paul’s words about sharing the sufferings of Christ: human suffering, joined to Christ, is drawn into the work of redemption and becomes a source of strength for others (in substance, Salvifici Doloris 20–24). The Catechism teaches the same about the sick: by grace, suffering can be united to the saving Passion of Christ (CCC 1521). The Church’s works of mercy, among them to comfort the afflicted, are the shape of this reading in daily life (CCC 2447).

r.h: Daughter, your faith has made you well
set: Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue whose little daughter is dying (5:21–24). A large crowd presses around him. Mark sets one story inside another: the healing of the woman is told in the middle of the raising of Jairus’ daughter. Both concern a “daughter”, and the number twelve joins them: the woman has suffered for twelve years, and the girl is twelve years old (5:42).

Under the Law of Moses a woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean, and so was anything she touched (Leviticus 15:25–27). This was a matter of worship, not of guilt, but for twelve years it would have kept her apart from the Temple and from much of ordinary life.
str: vv. 25–26: twelve years of suffering, doctors, poverty, and no cure.
vv. 27–28: she has heard of Jesus; she comes from behind and touches his cloak.
v. 29: at once the bleeding stops, and she knows she is healed.
vv. 30–32: Jesus knows that power has gone out from him and looks for the one who touched him.
vv. 33–34: she tells the whole truth; he calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace.
kw: The power of God at work in Jesus. Mark says it “had gone forth from him”: the healing is not magic in the cloak but the living power of the Lord.
has made you well, has saved you
The Greek verb sōzō means both to heal and to save. The woman is healed in her body, and she is also given salvation and peace.
