In the Gospels this woman is the one individual Jesus addresses as “daughter” (Matthew and Luke tell the same healing). A woman who came hidden and alone is given a family name in public.
vv: She had heard about Jesus, and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,
She comes from behind, perhaps afraid that her uncleanness would be noticed. Her faith is humble and hidden, but it is real.
Immediately aware that power had gone forth from him, Jesus turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?”
Jesus does not ask because he must find a culprit. He wants to meet her. A healing received in secret is to become a face-to-face encounter.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.”
“Go in peace” is a Hebrew blessing; the priest Eli sent Hannah away with the same words (1 Samuel 1:17). Her body was already healed; now her shame is healed too, and she is restored before everyone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the sacraments are “powers that come forth” from the Body of Christ, which is ever-living and life-giving (CCC 1116), using the words of this story. What the woman received by touching his cloak, the Church receives in the sacraments. St Augustine, preaching on this miracle, contrasts the crowd that pressed on Jesus with the woman who touched him: the crowd presses, faith touches (in substance). Many crowd around Christ; few reach out to him in faith.

qa: Was the woman wrong to touch Jesus when the Law said she was unclean?

Jesus never blames her. The Law of uncleanness was about fitness for worship, not about sin. In Jesus the movement is reversed: her uncleanness does not pass to him; his holiness and healing pass to her. That is why he calls her forward, not to shame her, but so that everyone may see that she is clean and a daughter of God.
study: Paul says God comforts us so that we may comfort others. Whom has God comforted through me, and to whom could I pass on his comfort this week?
The woman came from behind, then stood before Jesus and told him the whole truth. What hidden need could I bring to him openly in prayer?

lead: On the feast of St Mariam Thresia the four readings trace the road of a life given wholly to God. Abram hears “Go from your country” and goes, not knowing the way. Sirach warns the one who comes to serve the Lord to be ready for testing, for gold is tried in fire. Paul says the secret of such a life: “it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.” And in Matthew the King reveals where that life is lived: in the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner, “you did it to me.” Call, testing, union with Christ, and service of the least: that is the shape of every holy life, and it is the shape of the life of the saint of Puthenchira.

r.h: Go to the land that I will show you
set: After the story of Babel, where people tried to make a name for themselves (11:4), Genesis narrows to one family. Terah had set out from Ur of the Chaldeans with his son Abram, Sarai his wife and his grandson Lot, and settled at Haran in the north (11:31). There the Lord speaks to Abram. This is the turning point of Genesis: from the scattering of the nations the story moves to the man through whom all the nations will be blessed.
Sarai is barren (11:30), and Abram is seventy-five years old. Everything in the promise of a great nation is humanly impossible. That is the point: the future will be God’s gift.
str: v. 1: the command: go from country, kindred and father’s house, to a land God will show.
vv. 2–3: the promises: a great nation, blessing, a great name, a blessing to others, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
v. 4: the response: Abram went, as the Lord had told him.
kw: A doubled Hebrew form, literally “go for yourself”. The same rare form returns when God tells Abraham to go to the land of Moriah with Isaac (22:2). Abraham’s life with God begins and reaches its height with the same call to set out.
The word and its verb occur five times in verses 2–3. After the curses of Genesis 3–11, blessing begins again, and it is meant to spread: “you will be a blessing.”
Not only Israel. From the first call, God’s plan for Abram has all humanity in view.
vv: Now the Lord said to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
The three circles grow narrower and dearer: land, clan, family home. God does not name the land. Abram must go first and be shown later.
I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.
At Babel people wanted to make a name for themselves (11:4). Here God gives the name. Greatness is received, not seized.
and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Paul reads this as the Gospel announced beforehand: the nations would be blessed through faith, in Abraham’s offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16).
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him; and Lot went with him.
No words from Abram, only obedience. His answer is his journey.
ch: The Catechism calls Abraham the model of the obedience of faith: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance” (Hebrews 11:8; CCC 144–145). It teaches that with Abraham God began to gather scattered humanity, and that the people descended from him would be the root onto which the Gentiles would be grafted (CCC 59–60). The Roman Canon names him “our father in faith”, and the Church honours him as father of all who believe (CCC 146).

r.h: Gold is tested in the fire
set: The Book of Sirach was written in Hebrew in Jerusalem about 180 BC by a teacher named Jesus son of Sirach, and translated into Greek in Egypt by his grandson after 132 BC, as the grandson tells in his prologue. It is one of the books the Catholic Church receives as Scripture (CCC 120) and was used so much in teaching new Christians that it was long called Ecclesiasticus, “the church book”.
Chapter 1 praised wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Chapter 2 turns to the cost: anyone who sets out to serve God must expect trials, and must cling to him in them.
str: v. 1: the warning: if you come to serve the Lord, prepare for testing.
vv. 2–3: set your heart right, be steadfast, cling to him.
v. 4: accept what comes, and be patient in humiliation.
v. 5: the image: gold in the fire, the acceptable in the furnace of humiliation.
v. 6: trust, walk straight, hope in him.
kw: The usual address of a wise teacher to his pupil (as in Proverbs). Testing is spoken of within a relationship of love, as a father speaks to a son.
The same Greek word as in the Lord’s Prayer, “do not bring us to the time of trial” (Matthew 6:13). Here it means the trials that prove and purify faith.
Being brought low: loss, shame, failure. Sirach says this low place can be a furnace where the soul is refined.
vv: My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing.
An honest beginning. God’s service is not a guarantee of an easy life; it is a guarantee of his company.
Cling to him and do not depart, so that your last days may be prosperous.
“Cling” is the word of a bond that holds, like the bond of husband and wife (Genesis 2:24 in Greek uses a related verb).
For gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable, in the furnace of humiliation.
The same image appears in Wisdom 3:6 and 1 Peter 1:7. Fire does not destroy gold; it makes it pure.
Trust in him, and he will help you; make your ways straight, and hope in him.
Three verbs, trust, walk straight, hope: the whole programme of the tested believer.
ch: The Church reads Sirach as a teacher of the moral life and of perseverance. The Catechism teaches that hope keeps us from discouragement and sustains us in times of abandonment (CCC 1818). The saints often spoke of trials as God’s refining fire. The image of gold in the furnace is taken up in the New Testament, where faith tested by fire is more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7).

r.h: Christ lives in me
set: Paul has just told how he opposed Peter at Antioch when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers (2:11–14). He goes on to state the heart of his Gospel: we are made righteous not by works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ (2:16). These three verses are his personal testimony, among the most intimate words he ever wrote.
str: v. 19a: through the Law I died to the Law, to live for God.
vv. 19b–20a: crucified with Christ; no longer I, but Christ living in me.
v. 20b: my life now is faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me.
v. 21: I do not set aside the grace of God; if righteousness came through the Law, Christ died for nothing.
kw: A Greek perfect tense: something done once that still stands. In baptism the believer is joined to the death of Christ (Romans 6:3–6), and lives from that moment on.
Not mere imitation of Christ from outside, but his life within. The “I” is not destroyed; it is healed and filled.
God’s gift, given without our deserving. To seek righteousness by our own efforts alone would be to treat the Cross as unnecessary.
vv: For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
The Law itself, by pointing to Christ and by showing sin, led Paul to die to it as a way of being made righteous. He does not despise the Law; he says it has done its work.
it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
The great sentence of Christian mysticism. The saints have read it as the goal of every life of prayer: that Christ may live his life again in us.
I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
The Greek can also be read “by the faith of the Son of God”, that is, his faithfulness; the NRSV notes this. Either way the life rests on him. And Paul says “me”: the love of the Cross is personal.
ch: The Catechism quotes these words to teach that Jesus knew and loved each one of us during his life, his agony and his Passion, and gave himself up for each one: “The Son of God… loved me and gave himself for me” (CCC 478). It also teaches that justification is the work of God’s grace, received in faith and baptism, and that it does not exclude but brings forth our cooperation in love (CCC 1987–1993). St John Chrysostom, commenting on this verse, notes that Paul makes the love of Christ for all the world his own, as if Christ had died for him alone (in substance, Commentary on Galatians).

r.h: You did it to me
set: This is the last of Jesus’ teachings in Matthew before the Passion (26:1–2). After the parables of the bridesmaids and the talents, Jesus describes the judgment itself. The Son of Man comes as King and Shepherd, and all the nations are gathered before him.

In the land of Israel sheep and goats often grazed together in one flock and were separated at evening. The scene is homely and solemn at once. Today’s reading gives the blessed side of the judgment (25:31–40); the Gospel continues with those on the left (25:41–46).
str: vv. 31–33: the coming of the Son of Man in glory; all nations gathered; sheep and goats separated.
vv. 34–36: the King’s welcome: inherit the kingdom, for I was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, in prison.
vv. 37–39: the surprise of the righteous: when did we see you?
v. 40: the answer: just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.
kw: Jesus’ favourite title for himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a human being” (literally “like a son of man”) receives everlasting dominion over all peoples.
The smallest, the lowest. Jesus calls them “members of my family”, literally “my brothers”. He takes the place of the person no one notices.
An inheritance is given because one is a child, not earned as wages. The kingdom “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” is the Father’s gift to his children.
vv: When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
The one who will judge is the one who was judged and crucified. The Judge is the Saviour.
for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,
Six needs, and none is unusual. Holiness here is made of ordinary acts of mercy.
Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food
The righteous did not know they were serving Christ. Their love was simple and unself-conscious.
just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.
Christ identifies himself with the poor. Love of neighbour is not something next to love of Christ; in the least, it is love of Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus identifies himself with the poor of every kind and makes active love toward them the condition for entering his kingdom (CCC 544), and that the Eucharist commits us to the poor: to receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren (CCC 1397). It also reminds us that we will be judged on our love (CCC 1022, quoting St John of the Cross). St Teresa of Calcutta summed up her life’s work with this verse, counting its words on her fingers: “you did it to me.”

qa: Does Matthew 25 mean that only good works matter, and faith is not important?

No. The righteous are called “blessed by my Father”: their life comes from God’s grace. Faith in Christ and love for the least belong together, as root and fruit. By grace our works of love have real worth before God (CCC 2008–2011), and faith that does not act in love is not living faith (Galatians 5:6). Matthew 25 shows what living faith looks like.
Why is Sirach in the Catholic Bible but not in some other Bibles?

Sirach belongs to the books found in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Church. The Church accepted it as inspired from early times; the Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), and later the Councils of Florence and Trent, list it among the sacred books (CCC 120). The Reformers placed it among the Apocrypha. Catholics and Orthodox read it as the word of God.
Who was St Mariam Thresia?

Mariam Thresia Chiramel Mankidiyan was born in 1876 at Puthenchira, in the present Thrissur district of Kerala. She gave her life to prayer, penance and the service of families, the sick and the dying, visiting homes and nursing those whom others avoided. In 1914 she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family. She died on 8 June 1926, was beatified by Pope St John Paul II in 2000 and canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019.
rite: St Mariam Thresia is a daughter of our own Syro-Malabar Church. Like Abram she left the security she knew to follow a call that others did not understand; like the gold in Sirach she passed through long trials, both inner darkness and misunderstanding; and like Paul she longed for Christ to live in her. Her life is the Gospel of today lived out in Kerala villages: she went to the homes of the poor and the sick, cared for the dying, and saw the family as the place where Christ is served.

The Congregation of the Holy Family, which she founded, continues this work. On her feast, families can pray together for those in their parish who are sick, lonely or in need, and choose one act of the six named by the King to do this week, as a family.
study: Abram went without knowing where. What is God asking me to leave or begin, even before I see the whole road?
Sirach says gold is tested in fire. Looking back, how has a trial purified my faith?
Paul says, “it is Christ who lives in me.” In which part of my day do I most need to let Christ live and act instead of my own self?
St Mariam Thresia served Christ in families and the sick. Which of the six works in Matthew 25 can my family do together this week?

lead: On the feast of Mar Aprem, deacon, teacher and poet of our Syriac tradition, the readings speak of God’s word received, kept and handed on. In Deuteronomy, Moses sets before Israel the covenant: the Lord will be their God, and they will be his treasured people, holy to him. Sirach praises Moses himself, the meek and faithful man to whom God gave “the law of life and knowledge” so that he might teach it. Paul tells what the new covenant gives: peace with God, hope that does not disappoint, and the love of God poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. And in Matthew, Jesus tells his disciples that they are salt and light, and that he has come not to abolish the Law and the prophets but to fulfil them. A teacher of the Church like Mar Aprem stands in this line: he received the word, let it fill his heart, and made it shine for others.

r.h: A people holy to the Lord
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses’ farewell speeches on the plains of Moab, before Israel crosses the Jordan. Its long central section of laws (chapters 12–26) ends with these verses. They are like the signing of a covenant: what God has said and what the people have promised are summed up in two solemn declarations.
The word “today” is repeated. Deuteronomy speaks to every generation as if it stood at the Jordan on that day, hearing the covenant for the first time.
str: v. 16: this very day: keep these laws with all your heart and soul.
v. 17: today you have declared that the Lord is your God and that you will walk in his ways.
vv. 18–19: today the Lord has declared that you are his treasured people, to be set high in praise, fame and honour, and holy to him.
kw: you have obtained agreement, you have declared
A rare form of the verb “to say”, found only here and in verse 18. Literally “you have caused (the Lord) to say”. Each partner in the covenant leads the other to speak a binding word.

A word for a king’s private treasure. God used it at Sinai: “you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples” (Exodus 19:5). Israel is precious to God, not because it is great, but because he loves it (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).
Holy means set apart for God. Israel’s holiness is first God’s choice, and then a way of life that answers it.
vv: This very day the Lord your God is commanding you to observe these statutes and ordinances; so observe them diligently with all your heart and with all your soul.
“With all your heart and with all your soul” echoes the Shema (6:5). The commandments are to be kept from within, not only outwardly.
Today you have obtained the Lord’s agreement: to be your God; and for you to walk in his ways
The covenant is a bond of two parties. God binds himself to be Israel’s God; Israel binds itself to walk with him.
Today the Lord has obtained your agreement: to be his treasured people, as he promised you
“As he promised” points back to the promises to Abraham. The covenant at Moab fulfils what God had sworn to the fathers.
and for you to be a people holy to the Lord your God, as he promised.
Israel is lifted high not for its own glory but so that the nations may see the holiness of its God.
ch: The Church reads Israel’s covenant with reverence: the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121), and the people of Israel remain the people to whom God first spoke (CCC 839, quoting the Roman Missal). The New Testament applies the language of this passage to the Church, called in Christ “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people” (1 Peter 2:9; CCC 803). The Church does not take Israel’s place; through Christ the Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree (Romans 11:17–18).

r.h: Moses, whose memory is blessed
set: Chapters 44 to 50 of Sirach are a hymn in praise of the ancestors of Israel: “Let us now sing the praises of famous men” (44:1). Ben Sira walks through the history of Israel from Enoch and Noah to the high priest Simon, his own contemporary. These verses are given to Moses, after the patriarchs and before Aaron, whose praise is much longer (45:6–22).
str: v. 1: Moses, raised from Jacob’s descendants, beloved by God and people, whose memory is blessed.
v. 2: God made him glorious, like the holy ones, and great before his enemies.
v. 3: signs done at his word; glory before kings; commandments for his people; a vision of God’s glory.
v. 4: chosen for his faithfulness and meekness.
v. 5: God’s voice, the dark cloud, the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob and Israel.
kw: Gentleness that does not insist on itself. Numbers 12:3 says that Moses was very humble, more than anyone on earth. Jesus will say, “Blessed are the meek” (Matthew 5:5), and “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).
The thick darkness into which Moses entered on Sinai, where God was (Exodus 20:21). The Fathers saw in it a sign that God is greater than all our ideas of him.
the law of life and knowledge
The Law is not a burden but a gift that gives life and understanding (compare Deuteronomy 30:15–20). It was given to Moses so that he might teach it.
vv: Moses, whose memory is blessed.
In Jewish custom one still adds “of blessed memory” to the name of a revered person who has died. Sirach gives Moses this honour.
He gave him commandments for his people, and revealed to him his glory.
On Sinai Moses asked, “Show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18), and was allowed to see God’s back, not his face.
For his faithfulness and meekness he consecrated him, choosing him out of all humankind.
God chooses the faithful and gentle. Moses’ authority came from God, not from force.
and gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, so that he might teach Jacob the covenant, and Israel his decrees.
“Face to face” as with a friend (Exodus 33:11). The goal of revelation is teaching: what Moses received, he handed on.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God revealed himself to Moses as the God of the fathers and as “I AM”, and that through Moses he gave Israel the Law as a preparation for the Gospel (CCC 204–205, 1961–1964). Moses is the great intercessor of the Old Testament, and his prayer foreshadows the prayer of Christ (CCC 2574–2577). St Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, reads Moses’ entry into the dark cloud as an image of the soul that comes ever closer to God, who is beyond understanding (in substance).

r.h: Hope does not disappoint
set: In the first four chapters of Romans Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles, need God’s mercy, and that God makes sinners righteous through faith in Christ, as he credited faith to Abraham (chapter 4). Now he begins to describe the new life of those who have been justified. Chapter 5 begins with peace and ends with grace overflowing where sin had abounded (5:20).
str: v. 1: justified by faith, we have peace with God through Christ.
v. 2: through him we have access to grace, and we boast in hope of God’s glory.
vv. 3–4: we boast even in sufferings: suffering, endurance, character, hope.
v. 5: hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
kw: Not only a calm feeling but a restored relationship: enemies have become friends (5:10). It is the Hebrew shalom, wholeness given by God.
The word for being brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ the door to God’s throne is open (Ephesians 2:18).
A perfect tense: poured once and still overflowing. It echoes the prophecy of the Spirit poured out (Joel 2:28) and Pentecost (Acts 2:33).
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Some ancient manuscripts read “let us have peace”. The difference in Greek is one vowel. Either way, peace is a gift received in Christ and then lived.
And not only that, but we also boast in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance,
Paul does not praise pain for its own sake. He sees what God makes of it in a believer: a chain that leads to hope.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
“God’s love” here is God’s love for us, given as a gift to live in us. Christian hope rests not on our feelings but on this love already given.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 5 to teach that love is God’s first gift, which contains all the others, and that this love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (CCC 733). It teaches that hope keeps us from discouragement and sustains us in times of abandonment (CCC 1817–1818), and that justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ and is granted through Baptism (CCC 1992). St Augustine often returned to verse 5: the love of God is poured out not from ourselves but by the Holy Spirit (in substance, On the Spirit and the Letter).

r.h: Salt, light and the fulfilled Law
set: Jesus has just spoken the Beatitudes on the mountain (5:1–12). Now he tells the disciples what they are in the world, and how his teaching stands toward the Law of Moses. Like Moses on Sinai, Jesus teaches from a mountain, but he speaks with his own authority.
Verses 17–20 introduce the rest of chapter 5, where Jesus takes six commandments and leads them to their full depth: “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you…”.
str: v. 13: you are the salt of the earth; salt that loses its taste is thrown out.
vv. 14–16: you are the light of the world; let your light shine so that others glorify the Father.
vv. 17–19: I have come to fulfil the Law and the prophets; not one letter will pass away.
v. 20: your righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees.
kw: The verb literally means “to become foolish”. In the Bible, wisdom is the salt of life; a disciple without it is like tasteless salt.
To fill full, to bring to completion. Jesus does not cancel the Law; he brings it to its goal, in his teaching and in his own life and death.
one letter, one stroke of a letter
The iota (Hebrew yod) is the smallest letter; the “stroke” is the small mark that tells one Hebrew letter from another.
vv: “You are the salt of the earth; but if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored?
Salt preserves, gives taste, and was used with sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13). Jesus does not say “try to be salt”; he says “you are”. The task follows from what grace has made us.
“You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.
Jesus calls himself the light of the world (John 8:12). The disciples shine with light that is his.
let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.
The aim is not our praise but the Father’s glory. Good works shown in humility point beyond themselves.
I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
Jesus honours the Law and the prophets as God’s word. Everything in them points to him and finds its meaning in him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus did not abolish the Law of Sinai but fulfilled it with such perfection that he revealed its ultimate meaning (CCC 577–582, quoting this passage), and that the New Law is the perfection of the Old (CCC 1965–1968). The Second Vatican Council teaches that lay people are to make Christ known to others above all by the witness of a life shining with faith, hope and charity (Lumen Gentium 31). On verse 20, the Church explains that “the scribes and Pharisees” here stand for a righteousness measured by outward observance; Jesus asks for a righteousness of the heart, and many Pharisees too sought that (CCC 579).

qa: Who was Mar Aprem?

St Ephrem the Syrian, Mar Aprem, was born about 306 at Nisibis in Mesopotamia and served there as a deacon and teacher. When Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363, he moved to Edessa, where he taught until his death in 373. He wrote biblical commentaries and hundreds of hymns, often sung by choirs he trained. He is called “the Harp of the Spirit”, and Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920.
Did Jesus abolish the Law of Moses?

No. He says plainly, “I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.” The moral law of the Ten Commandments remains and is deepened by his teaching (CCC 2052–2068). The ritual and ceremonial laws prepared for Christ and find their fulfilment in him, as the Church teaches from the Letter to the Hebrews and the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). The Law is not set aside; it is brought to its goal.
Paul says we are justified by faith. Then why does Jesus speak of commandments and good works?

Both are true together. We are made righteous by God’s grace, received in faith and Baptism; we do not earn the first grace (CCC 1996–2003). That grace then lives and acts in us, and the commandments are the shape of the new life. Jesus asks for a righteousness greater than outward observance: the love poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5).
rite: Mar Aprem is a teacher of our own Syriac tradition. His hymns, written in Syriac, have shaped the prayer of the Syriac Churches, East and West, and some of the poetry of our liturgical prayer goes back to him or to his school. He taught theology through poetry: he loved to say that God has clothed himself in our words and our names so that we might come to him, and he warned against prying into God with proud questions instead of praising him (in substance, Hymns on Faith).

Like Moses in Sirach, he received the word and handed it on as a teacher. Like the salt and light of the Gospel, he gave his life in service: according to an old account, at the end of his life he organised help for the sick and hungry during a famine in Edessa. On his feast our deacons, catechists and choirs can see in him a model: Scripture loved, prayed, sung and lived.
study: Deuteronomy says “today” again and again. How can I hear God’s word in the Qurbana today as if it were spoken for the first time to me?
Moses was chosen for faithfulness and meekness. Where do I need more gentleness in the way I teach or correct others?
Paul says hope does not disappoint because God’s love has been poured into our hearts. What helps me to remember that love when I suffer?
Mar Aprem made Scripture into song. Which verse from today’s readings could I learn by heart and pray this week?

lead: Both readings are about the one God whose love reaches beyond every boundary. Paul tells the Corinthians that knowledge puffs up but love builds up, and gives them one of the earliest Christian confessions: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. In Mark, a Gentile mother from the region of Tyre asks Jesus to heal her daughter, and her humble, quick-witted faith wins the healing. The one Lord is Lord of all, and humble love opens the way to him.

r.h: One God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ
set: The Corinthians had written to Paul with questions (7:1), and here he turns to a practical one: may Christians eat meat that had been offered to idols? In a Greek city much of the meat sold in the market came from temple sacrifices, and meals with friends were often held in temple dining halls. Some Corinthians said, “We know that idols are nothing, so we may eat anything.” Paul agrees with the truth they know, but he corrects the pride with which they hold it. Chapters 8 to 10 treat the question; today’s verses lay the foundation.
str: vv. 1–3: knowledge puffs up, love builds up; whoever loves God is known by him.
v. 4: no idol really exists; there is no God but one.
v. 5: there are so-called gods and lords.
v. 6: the confession: one God, the Father, from whom are all things; one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.
kw: The Corinthians prized spiritual knowledge. Paul does not despise it, but knowledge without love makes a person proud and careless of others.
Literally “build a house”. Love builds the community like a house; Paul uses the word often in these chapters (8:10; 10:23; 14:4).

Paul takes the Shema, “The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and unfolds it: “God” is said of the Father, “Lord” of Jesus Christ. Jesus is placed within the confession of the one God of Israel.
vv: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
A short sentence that judges much clever religion. Truth must be spoken and held in love (see 13:2).
but anyone who loves God is known by him.
Paul turns the question around. What matters most is not what we know about God but that God knows us, and to be known by God is to be loved by him.
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

Little more than twenty years after the Resurrection, Paul speaks of Jesus as the one through whom all things were made, the work of God alone. This verse is a seed of the Creed: “one Lord Jesus Christ… through him all things were made.”
ch: The Catechism quotes the Second Council of Constantinople, which draws on this verse: “one God and Father from whom all things are, one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things are, and one Holy Spirit in whom all things are” (CCC 258). The whole Trinity works as one in creation and salvation, each Person according to what is proper to him. On the question that follows, the Catechism quotes Paul’s warning about wounding a brother’s weak conscience, by which one sins against Christ (CCC 1789, citing 8:12): love for the neighbour’s conscience must guide how we use our freedom.

r.h: Even the dogs under the table
set: Jesus has just taught that what makes a person unclean comes from the heart, not from food (7:14–23). Now he goes into Gentile territory, the region of Tyre on the Phoenician coast, north of Galilee. He wants to stay hidden, perhaps to rest with his disciples. There a Gentile woman comes to him. Mark calls her a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth: a woman of another people and religion.

The story is told after a meal of five thousand where twelve baskets of bread were left over (6:43) and before the feeding of four thousand in a Gentile area (8:1–9). Bread runs through these chapters.
str: v. 24: Jesus goes to Tyre and wants no one to know.
vv. 25–26: a Gentile woman falls at his feet and begs him to deliver her daughter.
v. 27: the hard answer: let the children be fed first.
v. 28: her reply: even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.
vv. 29–30: for that word her daughter is delivered; she goes home and finds the child well.
kw: Mark gives both her language and culture (Greek) and her birth (Phoenician of Syria). She is wholly outside Israel.
The diminutive suggests house dogs, not street dogs. Jesus’ words still sound hard. Many commentators see him testing and drawing out her faith; she takes up his own image and turns it into a plea.
“Let the children be fed first.” The word leaves the door open: Israel first, then the nations. Paul says the same: the Gospel is “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
vv: Let the children be fed first, for it is not fair to take the children’s food and throw it to the dogs.
Jesus’ mission was first to Israel, God’s children by covenant. His word is not a refusal of the woman but a statement of order in God’s plan.
But she answered him, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
She is the only person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus. She does not deny Israel’s place; she asks only for a crumb, sure that a crumb of his power is enough.
So she went home, found the child lying on the bed, and the demon gone.
Jesus heals from a distance, without seeing the child. The mother believed his word and went home; she found it true.
ch: The Church sees in this woman a model of humble and persevering prayer. St Augustine, preaching on Matthew’s account of the same woman, praises her humility: she did not take offence at being compared to a dog, but accepted it and so was raised up (in substance, Sermon 77). The story also shows the Gospel going out to all peoples, as the Lord willed: the crumbs from Israel’s table become the bread of the nations, and the Church is sent to all (CCC 849).

qa: Was Jesus being harsh or prejudiced toward the woman?

Jesus’ words do sound hard, and the Gospel does not soften them. But the whole story shows his purpose: he does heal her daughter, and he praises her answer. He tests her faith and lets it shine. He came first to Israel, as God had planned, and through Israel to all nations. The woman understood that, and believed that there was enough for her too.
study: Paul says knowledge puffs up but love builds up. When I share what I know about the faith, does it build others up?
The Syrophoenician mother would not give up. For whom am I praying with that kind of humble persistence?

lead: On the feast of Mar Barnabas Shleeha the readings follow an apostle’s life from praise to mission to suffering. The song from Chronicles calls God’s people to make known his deeds among the nations. In Acts, Barnabas is sent to Antioch, rejoices at the grace of God he finds there, fetches Saul from Tarsus, and in that city the disciples are first called Christians. In Galatians, Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and the pillars of the Church give them the right hand of fellowship, asking only that they remember the poor. And in Matthew, Jesus sends his apostles like sheep among wolves, promising the Spirit of the Father to speak through them. Barnabas, the “son of encouragement”, shows what an apostle looks like: generous, joyful, quick to see God’s grace in others, and faithful under trial.

r.h: Make known his deeds among the peoples
set: The Books of Chronicles retell Israel’s history with special care for worship. In chapter 15 David brings the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem with music and joy. In chapter 16 the ark is set in its tent, offerings are made, and David appoints Levites to give thanks and praise. On that day a psalm of thanksgiving is sung (16:8–36).

The psalm is made of parts of three psalms found in the Psalter: verses 8–22 match Psalm 105:1–15, verses 23–33 match Psalm 96, and verses 34–36 come from Psalm 106. Today’s verses are its opening call to praise.
str: v. 8: give thanks, call on his name, make known his deeds among the peoples.
vv. 9–10: sing, tell his wonderful works, glory in his holy name.
vv. 11–12: seek the Lord and his presence; remember his works and judgments.
kw: From a root that means both to thank and to confess. To give thanks is to proclaim publicly what God has done.
God’s acts in history: the call of Abraham, the Exodus, the gift of the land. Israel’s praise tells a story.
Literally “seek his face”. With the ark now in Jerusalem, Israel can come before God in worship; the call is to seek him “continually”.
vv: O give thanks to the Lord, call on his name, make known his deeds among the peoples.
Praise that stays inside Israel is not enough; God’s deeds are to be told to the nations. The verse is a seed of mission.
Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice.
Joy is the mark of those who seek God. Barnabas, too, “rejoiced” when he saw God’s grace (Acts 11:23).
Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his presence continually.
Not a single act but a lifelong search. Even those who have found God keep seeking him.
Remember the wonderful works he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he uttered,
Remembering is the root of praise. In the Holy Qurbana the Church remembers the greatest of God’s works, the death and Resurrection of Christ.
ch: The Church prays these words also in the Psalter, as Psalm 105. The Catechism teaches that praise is the form of prayer that recognises most directly that God is God, giving him glory for his own sake (CCC 2639), and that the Psalms, sung by Christ and the Church, remain the great school of prayer (CCC 2585–2589). The call to “make known his deeds among the peoples” is fulfilled when the apostles proclaim the Gospel to all nations.

r.h: A good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith
set: After the martyrdom of Stephen, believers scattered by persecution went as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch (11:19). At Antioch, the great city of Syria on the river Orontes, some men from Cyprus and Cyrene began to proclaim the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well, not only to Jews (11:20). The church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas to see what is happening.

Barnabas has appeared before. His name was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus; the apostles called him Barnabas, “son of encouragement”, and he sold a field and laid the money at their feet (4:36–37). When the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of the newly converted Saul, it was Barnabas who brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (9:27).
str: v. 21: the hand of the Lord is with them; many believe and turn to the Lord.
v. 22: Jerusalem sends Barnabas to Antioch.
vv. 23–24: he sees the grace of God, rejoices, encourages all to remain faithful; he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.
vv. 25–26: he fetches Saul from Tarsus; a year of teaching; the disciples first called Christians at Antioch.
kw: The verb of Barnabas’ own name, “son of encouragement” (paraklēsis). He does exactly what his name says.
Luke rarely calls anyone “good”. Barnabas’ goodness shows in his joy at others’ success and his generosity in bringing Saul to share the work.
A Latin-style ending added to Christos: “those who belong to Christ”. The name was probably given by outsiders, who saw that these people were always speaking of Christ.
vv: News of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
The mother church keeps communion with the new community. Barnabas, a Greek-speaking Jew from Cyprus, was well suited to a mixed church.
When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast devotion;
He did not come to inspect suspiciously but to recognise God’s work. To see grace in others and rejoice is itself a grace.
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.
The same was said of Stephen (6:5). Holiness, not cleverness, made Barnabas fruitful.
Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul,
Barnabas does not keep the work for himself. He goes looking for the gifted man others had forgotten, and the history of the Church changes.
ch: The Church honours Barnabas as an apostle, a title Luke himself gives him (Acts 14:14), though he was not one of the Twelve. With Paul he was set apart by the Holy Spirit and sent on the first missionary journey (13:2–3). Pope Benedict XVI, in his Wednesday catechesis on Barnabas, Silas and Apollos (2007), described Barnabas as a man of encouragement and reconciliation who believed in Paul when others doubted, and who later gave a second chance to John Mark (in substance; see Acts 15:36–39). Ancient tradition, not Scripture, says he died a martyr in Cyprus.

r.h: The right hand of fellowship
set: Paul is defending the Gospel he preached to the Galatians. Some teachers were insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. Paul shows that his Gospel came from Christ by revelation (1:12) and that the leaders in Jerusalem recognised it.

He tells of a visit to Jerusalem “after fourteen years”, with Barnabas and Titus, a Gentile believer. Many scholars think this is the meeting described in Acts 15, often called the Council of Jerusalem; others connect it with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30. Either way, the outcome is the same: the Gentiles need not be circumcised, and the apostles are united.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul goes up with Barnabas and Titus, by revelation, and lays his Gospel before the leaders.
vv. 3–5: Titus is not compelled to be circumcised; Paul did not yield to false believers.
v. 6: the leaders added nothing to his Gospel.
vv. 7–9: they recognise that Paul is sent to the Gentiles as Peter to the circumcised; James, Cephas and John give the right hand of fellowship.
v. 10: only one request: remember the poor.
kw: Paul sets his Gospel before the leaders for their judgment. He is sure of his call, yet he seeks communion with those who were apostles before him.
James, Cephas (Peter) and John are called pillars of the Church, as of a temple. The image recalls that the Church is God’s house, built on the apostles (Ephesians 2:20).
A handshake of agreement and partnership. Koinōnia is communion: one faith, one Church, different fields of mission.
vv: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.
Barnabas stands beside Paul at this decisive moment. The fourteen years are counted either from Paul’s conversion or from his first visit to Jerusalem (1:18); scholars differ.
in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain.
Paul’s Gospel did not depend on human approval, but its fruit depended on communion. A Gospel cut off from the Church would be running in vain.
and when James and Cephas and John, who were acknowledged pillars, recognized the grace that had been given to me, they gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship
The pillars recognise “grace”, not merely ability. Unity in the Church is the recognition of God’s gifts in one another.
They asked only one thing, that we remember the poor, which was actually what I was eager to do.
Care for the poor is the one condition added to the Gospel. Paul later organised a great collection for the poor of Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ built his Church on the apostles, with Peter at their head, and that their communion continues in the bishops with the successor of Peter (CCC 880–881). Peter’s place among the apostles was given him by Christ (Matthew 16:18), and Paul here seeks communion with him. The Second Vatican Council points to the Church’s mission to the nations as born at Pentecost and carried on by the apostles in communion (Ad Gentes 4–5). The one request, to remember the poor, is still the mark of every true mission (CCC 2443–2444).

r.h: Sheep in the midst of wolves
set: Matthew 10 is Jesus’ great instruction to the Twelve as he sends them out (10:1–5). The first part concerns their mission in Galilee. From verse 16 the horizon widens: Jesus speaks of councils and governors, kings and Gentiles, persecution and family division. These words look ahead to the whole mission of the Church after Easter.

Jesus speaks of being flogged “in their synagogues”. In the first decades, disputes between the followers of Jesus and other Jews were disputes within the one people of Israel; the apostles themselves were Jews. These words are about the cost of witness, never a reason to blame the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4).
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves; wise as serpents, innocent as doves.
vv. 17–18: councils, synagogues, governors and kings: a testimony.
vv. 19–20: do not worry what to say; the Spirit of your Father will speak in you.
vv. 21–22: division in families; hated because of my name; the one who endures to the end will be saved.
kw: Practical, clear-sighted good sense. Disciples are not to be naïve about danger.
Literally “unmixed”, pure, without hidden motives. Wisdom without innocence becomes cunning; innocence without wisdom becomes foolishness.
The word from which “martyr” comes. To stand before rulers for Christ’s sake is itself to bear witness to him.
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
“I am sending you”: the mission begins in Christ. The sheep are not left alone; the Shepherd sends them and goes with them.
When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time;
Not a reason to neglect preparation, but a promise for the hour of trial.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
The Spirit who came at Pentecost speaks in witnesses. Stephen, “full of the Holy Spirit”, is the first example (Acts 7:55).
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Perseverance is a grace to be asked for daily. The end is not defeat but salvation.
ch: The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of the faith, bearing witness to Christ who died and rose, and that the Church has carefully kept the records of those who went to the end to witness to their faith (CCC 2473–2474). It teaches that all Christians are called to bear witness, and that the Holy Spirit is the principal agent of the Church’s mission (CCC 852). St John Chrysostom, preaching on these verses, notes the wonder that Christ sends sheep among wolves and yet the sheep overcome the wolves, so long as they remain sheep (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 33).

qa: Barnabas was not one of the Twelve. Why is he called an apostle?

“Apostle” means one who is sent. Luke calls Paul and Barnabas apostles (Acts 14:14) because they were sent by the Holy Spirit and the church of Antioch on mission (Acts 13:2–3). The Twelve have a unique place as the foundation of the Church, with Peter at their head; Barnabas and Paul are apostles in the wider sense, honoured by the Church with the same title.
Who first called the disciples “Christians”?

Acts says only that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch (11:26). The form of the word suggests it was coined by outsiders, perhaps as a nickname. Believers came to wear it with honour: “if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace” (1 Peter 4:16).
Did Paul refuse the authority of Peter and the other apostles?

No. Paul insists that his Gospel came from Christ, but he goes up to Jerusalem to lay it before Peter, James and John, and he values their recognition. The Church teaches that Peter’s authority comes from Christ (Matthew 16:18; CCC 881), and Paul’s visit shows that the Gospel is lived in communion with Peter and the apostles.
rite: The Syro-Malabar calendar keeps the feast of Mar Barnabas Shleeha in the Season of the Apostles, the season that remembers the Church’s first mission. Antioch, where Barnabas taught and where the disciples were first called Christians, became one of the great centres of early Christianity in Syria, and the starting point of the mission to the nations (Acts 13:1–3). Our Church, the Church of the Mar Thoma Nasranis, belongs to that wider Syriac family of Churches.

Barnabas teaches every parish the ministry of encouragement. He saw grace in a new community, believed in Saul when others feared him, and gave John Mark a second chance. On his feast, a family or parish group might ask: whom can we encourage this week, and whose gifts have we overlooked?
study: The psalm says, “make known his deeds among the peoples.” What has God done in my life that I could tell someone this week?
Barnabas “saw the grace of God” and rejoiced. Whose goodness have I been slow to notice or to praise?
The pillars asked Paul and Barnabas only to remember the poor. How does my parish or family remember the poor in a regular way?
Jesus promises that the Spirit of the Father will speak in his witnesses. When have I needed courage to speak of Christ, and how can I prepare by prayer?

lead: Both readings show how Christ spreads through the world. Paul says that God leads the apostles in Christ’s triumphal procession and through them spreads everywhere “the fragrance that comes from knowing him”. In Mark, Jesus, moved with pity, touches a leper and makes him clean, and the healed man cannot stop telling the news, until people come to Jesus from every quarter. The touch of Christ, received with faith, becomes a fragrance that cannot be hidden.

r.h: The aroma of Christ
set: Paul has been explaining why he changed his travel plans and wrote a painful letter instead of visiting Corinth (1:15–2:4). He had sent Titus to Corinth and waited anxiously for news. At Troas, on the coast of Asia, a door opened for the Gospel, yet he was so restless about Titus and the Corinthians that he moved on to Macedonia (2:12–13). The story of his meeting with Titus resumes only at 7:5.
In between, from 2:14, Paul breaks into thanksgiving and begins a long reflection on the apostolic ministry. Even his anxieties and changes of plan are part of God’s victory.
str: vv. 12–13: an open door at Troas, but no rest without Titus; on to Macedonia.
v. 14: thanks be to God, who leads us in triumph in Christ and spreads the fragrance of knowing him.
vv. 15–16a: we are the aroma of Christ: to some a fragrance from death to death, to others from life to life.
vv. 16b–17: who is sufficient? We are not peddlers of God’s word; we speak in sincerity, sent from God.
kw: In a Roman triumph a victorious general led his army and his captives through the city, while incense was burned along the way. Paul pictures himself in Christ’s procession, a captive of Christ’s love who now shares his victory.
Euōdia is the “pleasing odour” of sacrifices in the Greek Old Testament (Genesis 8:21). Paul’s life, offered with Christ, rises to God like the fragrance of an offering (compare Ephesians 5:2).
Used of small traders who watered down wine to sell it. Paul will not water down the Gospel for gain or popularity.
vv: When I came to Troas to proclaim the good news of Christ, a door was opened for me in the Lord;
An “open door” is Paul’s image for an opportunity for the Gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9). Even so, love for the Corinthians weighed more on him than a successful mission.
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him.
The victory is Christ’s, not Paul’s. A fragrance spreads silently and reaches where words cannot.
For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing;
The aroma is offered first “to God”. A Christian life is worship before it is a message.
but in Christ we speak as persons of sincerity, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence.
Three marks of a true minister: sincerity, being sent by God, and living before God’s face.
ch: The Church has long linked this passage with the anointing of Christians. St Cyril of Jerusalem, explaining the anointing with chrism to the newly baptised, tells them that they have become a fragrance of Christ (in substance, Mystagogical Catecheses 3). The Catechism teaches that the chrism of Confirmation gives the baptised a share in the mission of Christ and the fullness of the Holy Spirit, so that their lives may give off “the aroma of Christ” (CCC 1294, quoting 2:15). Verse 17 is also a lasting warning to all who preach: the word of God must never be sold or diluted.

r.h: I do choose. Be made clean!
set: This is the last healing in Mark’s first chapter. Jesus has been preaching and healing throughout Galilee (1:39). Under the Law, a person with a skin disease called “leprosy” (a broader term than modern leprosy) was unclean and had to live apart, crying out “Unclean, unclean” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Only a priest could declare someone clean again, with the offerings described in Leviticus 14.
The leper breaks the distance by coming to Jesus. Jesus breaks it further by touching him.
str: v. 40: the leper kneels and begs: if you choose, you can make me clean.
v. 41: Jesus, moved with pity, stretches out his hand, touches him, and says: I do choose; be made clean.
v. 42: the leprosy leaves him at once.
vv. 43–44: Jesus sends him to the priest, as Moses commanded, as a testimony to them, and tells him to say nothing.
v. 45: he spreads the news; Jesus can no longer enter a town openly; people come from everywhere.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. It is a gut-wrenching compassion. Some ancient manuscripts, among them Codex Bezae, read “moved with anger” instead. Most editions keep “pity”; if “anger” is original, it is anger at the disease and the suffering it caused.
The leper doubts not Jesus’ power but his willingness. Jesus answers with the same word: “I do choose.” His will is to heal.
Not only cured but restored: able to return to worship, family and village. Jesus heals the body and the isolation.
vv: A leper came to him begging him, and kneeling he said to him, “If you choose, you can make me clean.”
A perfect prayer: humble, trusting, leaving everything to the Lord’s will.
Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him

Under the Law, touching a leper made one unclean. Jesus’ touch reverses the flow: his holiness passes to the leper. The touch comes before the word, and it was perhaps the first touch the man had felt in years.
go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.
Jesus respects the Law of Moses and the priests. The healed man’s return to the community must be recognised in the proper way.
But he went out and began to proclaim it freely, and to spread the word
Mark uses for the healed man the words he uses for preaching: “proclaim” and “the word”. A healed sinner becomes a herald, even if, here, against the Lord’s command.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a sign that God has visited his people, and that he often uses physical signs such as the laying on of hands; the sick try to touch him, and in the sacraments Christ continues to touch us to heal us (CCC 1503–1504). St John Chrysostom, commenting on the parallel account in Matthew, notes that Jesus touched the leper to show that he is not under the Law but above it, and that for the clean nothing is unclean (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 25). The Church has always seen in the healing of lepers a sign of the forgiveness of sins: in the sacrament of Penance Christ still says, “I do choose. Be made clean!”

qa: Why did Jesus tell the man to say nothing?

Mark often shows Jesus asking for silence about his miracles. He did not want to be followed only as a wonder-worker, or misunderstood as a political Messiah, before his Passion revealed what kind of Messiah he is (Mark 8:29–31). Here the result proves the wisdom of the command: crowds made it impossible for him to enter towns openly.
study: Paul says Christians are the aroma of Christ. What fragrance does my daily life leave in my home and workplace?
The leper prayed, “If you choose, you can make me clean.” What do I need to bring to Christ with that humble trust, perhaps in the sacrament of Reconciliation?

lead: This Sunday’s four readings are about trust. In Deuteronomy, Moses recalls the day at Kadesh when Israel would not trust the God who had carried them through the wilderness, and then, when it was too late, rushed into battle on their own strength. In Isaiah, Jerusalem, once the faithful city, has turned to bribes and forgotten the orphan and the widow; God promises to purify her like silver in the furnace until she is called faithful again. Paul tells the Corinthians to pursue love and to seek the gifts that build up the whole Church, not only the speaker. And in Luke, Jesus tells his little flock not to worry about food and clothing, but to seek the Kingdom and to keep their treasure where no thief comes near. Fear made Israel turn back, and greed made Jerusalem unfaithful; trust in the Father frees us to love and to give. In the Season of the Apostles the Church hears again the Lord’s word to his small community: “Do not be afraid, little flock.”

r.h: You would not trust the Lord
set: Moses is giving his first great speech in the plains of Moab, retelling the forty years of the journey. Here he comes to the saddest moment: Kadesh-barnea, on the southern edge of the promised land, about two years after the Exodus. The full story is told in Numbers 13–14. Spies went up into the land; they brought back its fruit, but most of them also brought fear: the people were strong and the cities walled. The people refused to go up.

Just before today’s verses Moses said: “in spite of this, you have no trust in the Lord your God” (1:32), the God who had carried them “just as one carries a child” (1:31). Today’s reading tells what followed: the oath that this generation would not enter the land, the exceptions of Caleb and Joshua, and the people’s second mistake, a battle God had not commanded. In Numbers the reason Moses may not enter is his own failure at Meribah (Numbers 20:12); here he speaks of the Lord being angry with him “on your account” (1:37). The two books look at the same sad story from different sides: the leader shares the fate of his people.
str: v. 33: the God who went before them in fire and cloud, whom they would not trust.
vv. 34–36: the oath: this evil generation shall not see the good land, except Caleb.
vv. 37–38: Moses too shall not enter; Joshua shall lead Israel in.
v. 39: the little ones they feared for will enter and possess it.
vv. 40–43: the people repent too late, go up against God’s word, and are warned in vain.
vv. 44–46: defeat by the Amorites; weeping that is not heard; the long stay at Kadesh.
kw: The verb behind “you have no trust” in verse 32 comes from the root of “amen”: to lean on something firm. Israel’s sin at Kadesh was not first a broken rule but a refusal to lean on God.
Literally “he filled after the Lord”: Caleb followed God fully, all the way. The same Hebrew phrase is used of Caleb and Joshua in Numbers 32:12.

Translated “presumptuously went up” in verse 43. The word suggests something boiling over: pride that will not wait for God. Unbelief and presumption look like opposites, but both put our own judgment in the place of God’s word.
vv: who goes before you on the way to seek out a place for you to camp, in fire by night, and in the cloud by day
God had been their guide and scout every day. The fire and the cloud (Exodus 13:21) were there before their eyes, and still they would not trust.
except Caleb son of Jephunneh. He shall see it
One man’s faithfulness stands out against a whole generation’s fear. Caleb had said, “Let us go up at once” (Numbers 13:30).
your children, who today do not yet know right from wrong, they shall enter there
The people had said their children would be taken as booty (Numbers 14:3). God turns their fear around: the very children they used as an excuse will receive the gift.
We have sinned against the Lord! We are ready to go up and fight
The confession is right, but what follows is not. They wanted to undo their sin by their own strength, against God’s new command. True repentance obeys God now; it does not try to rewrite yesterday.
Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you
Victory was never in their weapons but in God’s presence among them. Without him the same mountain that was given becomes a defeat.
chased you as bees do
The Hebrew word for bees is dĕbôrîm, from which the name Deborah comes. The picture is of a swarm that will not let its victims go.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews reads this story as a warning for Christians: the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, so “let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest” (Hebrews 3:16–4:11). The Catechism teaches that faith is first a personal adherence of the whole person to God who reveals himself (CCC 150), and it names presumption as a sin against hope: hoping to be saved by one’s own powers, or expecting God’s gifts without conversion (CCC 2092). Kadesh shows both dangers in one day: first fear that will not trust, then pride that will not obey.

r.h: The faithful city
set: This passage continues the opening chapter of Isaiah, in which God brings a case against his people. After the call to wash and make themselves clean (1:16–20), the prophet turns to Jerusalem itself. Isaiah preached there in the eighth century before Christ; he knew its court, its judges and its Temple well.

The passage opens with a lament, the word “How” that begins a funeral song (as in Lamentations 1:1). The city that was once full of justice now has rulers who take bribes and neglect the orphan and the widow. Yet the lament turns into a promise: God will purify the city as a smith purifies silver, and it will again be called “the faithful city”. The closing verses (29–31) speak of oaks and gardens, probably places where idols were worshipped.
str: vv. 21–23: the lament: the faithful city has become unfaithful; silver turned to dross; rulers who love bribes.
vv. 24–26: God’s judgment as refining: he will smelt away the dross and restore judges as at the first.
vv. 27–28: Zion redeemed by justice; rebels and those who forsake the Lord will perish.
vv. 29–31: shame for the sacred oaks and gardens; the strong become like tinder and burn.
kw: The phrase opens the passage (v. 21) and closes the promise (v. 26). Between the two, God works to give back to Jerusalem the name she lost. The word comes from the same root as “amen”: firm, reliable.

A pair the prophets often join. Justice is right judgment, especially for the weak; righteousness is the right order of life that God wants. Isaiah measures the city’s faith by how it treats the orphan and the widow.
The waste that separates from silver when it is melted. God’s judgment here is not to destroy the silver but to remove what spoils it.
vv: How the faithful city has become a whore!

The prophets often describe idolatry and injustice as unfaithfulness in marriage, because God’s covenant with his people is like a marriage (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3). The harsh word expresses the pain of a betrayed love.
Everyone loves a bribe and runs after gifts. They do not defend the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them.
For Isaiah, worship and justice cannot be separated. A city can be full of sacrifices (1:11) and still be unfaithful if the weakest have no one to defend them.
I will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy.
God’s hand is “turned against” the city, but in order to cleanse it. His anger serves his love.
Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city.
Judgment is not God’s last word. He restores what was lost, “as at the first”.
Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness.
Redemption and repentance go together. The Hebrew word for “those who repent” literally means “those who turn back”.
ch: The Church hears in this passage both a warning and a hope. The warning is that faith is shown in justice for the poor. The Catechism quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life (CCC 2446). The hope is that God purifies rather than abandons. Holy Scripture often speaks of God testing his people like silver and gold in the fire (Malachi 3:3; 1 Peter 1:7); the Church sees here the patient work of grace, which cleanses a heart and a community until they are faithful again.

r.h: Pursue love, build up the Church
set: Paul has just written his great hymn to love (chapter 13). Now he applies it to a problem at Corinth. Some members prized the gift of speaking in tongues, a prayer in the Spirit that others could not understand, and seem to have used it in the assemblies as a sign of being more spiritual. Paul does not forbid the gift (14:5, 39), but he sets a test for every gift: does it build up the Church?
By “prophecy” Paul does not mean chiefly foretelling the future. He means speaking God’s word in a way others can understand, so that they are strengthened, encouraged and consoled (14:3).
str: v. 1: pursue love; strive for the spiritual gifts, especially prophecy.
vv. 2–5: tongues speak to God and build up the speaker; prophecy speaks to people and builds up the Church.
v. 6: what use is Paul to them unless he brings revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching?
vv. 7–9: three pictures: flute, harp and bugle must give clear notes.
vv. 10–12: a sound without meaning makes us foreigners; seek gifts that build up the Church.
kw: The verb means to run after, to chase. Love is not only a feeling to wait for but a goal to pursue with effort. Every other gift is measured by it.

In this chapter, prayer or speech in the Spirit that the hearers do not understand without an interpreter. At Pentecost the apostles were understood by people of many languages (Acts 2:6–11); at Corinth an interpreter was needed (14:13, 27).
Literally “house-building”. The word comes again and again in this chapter (vv. 3, 4, 5, 12, 26). The Church is God’s house, and every gift is a tool for building it.
vv: Pursue love and strive for the spiritual gifts, and especially that you may prophesy.
The verse joins chapter 13 to chapter 14. Gifts are good, and Paul tells them to strive for them; but love is the path on which the gifts must walk.
those who prophesy speak to other people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
A good description of every true word in the Church: it builds, it encourages, it consoles. Preachers, catechists and parents can test their words by these three.
If they do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is being played?
Paul uses music to make his point. A beautiful instrument that plays no clear tune helps no one.
since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church.
Paul does not cool their eagerness; he turns it in the right direction, from the self to the community.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Holy Spirit gives special gifts to the faithful of every rank, which are to be received with thanksgiving, and that judgment about their genuineness and right use belongs to those who preside in the Church (Lumen Gentium 12). The Catechism adds that charity is the true measure of all charisms (CCC 800), and that charisms are for the good of the Church (CCC 799–801). St Augustine explained that at Pentecost the gift of tongues was a sign that the Church would speak in the languages of all nations (in substance, Homilies on 1 John 6).

r.h: Do not worry, little flock
set: Jesus is on his journey to Jerusalem, teaching his disciples along the way. Just before this passage, a man asked him to settle a quarrel about an inheritance, and Jesus told the parable of the rich fool who built bigger barns and died that same night (12:13–21). Now he turns to his disciples: the opposite of greed is not careless poverty but trust in the Father.

Matthew gives much of this teaching in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:25–34). Luke has some features of his own: he speaks of ravens rather than “birds of the air”, and he adds the tender words to the “little flock” and the command to sell possessions and give alms.
str: vv. 22–23: do not worry about food and clothing; life is more than these.
vv. 24–26: consider the ravens; worry cannot add an hour to life.
vv. 27–28: consider the lilies; God clothes the grass, how much more you.
vv. 29–31: do not strive like the nations; your Father knows; strive for his Kingdom.
v. 32: do not be afraid, little flock; the Father is pleased to give you the Kingdom.
vv. 33–34: sell, give alms, keep treasure in heaven; where your treasure is, your heart is.
kw: Anxious care that divides the heart and pulls it in many directions. Jesus does not forbid work or planning; he forbids the worry that forgets the Father. Martha is “worried and distracted by many things” in the same Gospel (10:41).
A tender name. The disciples were few and weak, as Israel was called God’s flock (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34). Their smallness is no reason for fear, because the Kingdom is the Father’s gift.
Both the treasure and the place where it is kept. Jesus moves the disciples’ storehouse from earth to heaven, and the heart follows it.
vv: Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them.
Ravens were counted among the unclean birds (Leviticus 11:15), yet God feeds even them (Psalm 147:9). The rich fool built barns; the ravens have none, and they live by God’s care.
And can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?
The Greek can mean a cubit added to one’s height or a short measure added to one’s age; the NRSV takes it of time. The point is the same: worry adds nothing.
even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.
Solomon was remembered as the richest and most splendid of Israel’s kings (1 Kings 10). A wild flower, given its beauty by God, outshines him.
Instead, strive for his kingdom, and these things will be given to you as well.
Jesus does not say that food and clothing do not matter. He puts them in their place: they come “as well”, when God comes first.
“Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
The Kingdom is not earned by anxious effort; it is given by a Father who delights to give. That is why the disciples can afford to give, too.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
A simple test of the heart: where do my thoughts go when my mind wanders? What would I find hardest to lose?
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of our heavenly Father, who takes care of his children’s smallest needs, and it quotes this teaching of the Lord (CCC 305). It also teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). Trust is not laziness: the Church teaches that God gives his creatures the dignity of acting and cooperating in his plan (CCC 306–307). Pope Francis notes that Jesus invited people to be attentive to the beauty of the world, and pointed to the lilies and the birds as signs of the Father’s care (Laudato Si’ 96–97).

qa: Does Jesus forbid us to work, save or plan for the future?

No. Paul himself worked with his hands and told the Thessalonians that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). What Jesus forbids is worry that takes the place of trust, and greed that makes possessions our treasure. The disciple works and plans as a child of the Father, and shares with the poor.
In Deuteronomy, the people repent and weep, and the Lord does not listen. Does God refuse forgiveness?

No. In Numbers the Lord says, “I do forgive, just as you have asked” (Numbers 14:20). What God refused was the people’s plan to go up and fight against his new command. Forgiveness takes away guilt, but some consequences of sin may remain; the people had to learn trust again in the wilderness. God’s “no” protected them from a battle they could not win without him.
Does the gift of tongues still exist in the Church?

The Church teaches that the Holy Spirit continues to give charisms, ordinary and extraordinary, for the good of the Church, and that they are to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church’s pastors (Lumen Gentium 12; CCC 799–801). Paul’s rule still holds: every gift is measured by love and by whether it builds up the Church.
rite: In the Season of the Apostles our Church remembers that the Gospel came to India through Mar Thoma Shleeha, and that for many centuries the St Thomas Christians lived as a small community among many neighbours. “Do not be afraid, little flock” has been their story: they trusted the Father, kept the faith and handed it on in their families. Today the Syro-Malabar Church has eparchies in India and across the world, but it remains a little flock that lives by the same trust.

Paul’s concern that prayer in the assembly be understood speaks to us too. Our Holy Qurbana was for centuries prayed in Syriac, and today it is prayed in Malayalam and in many other languages, so that all may understand and answer “Amen”. Isaiah’s words about the orphan and the widow remind every parish and family that the Qurbana we celebrate must be lived in justice and care for the weak.
study: At Kadesh Israel first would not trust God, and then would not wait for him. Which is my more common temptation: fear or presumption?
Isaiah measures a city’s faith by how it treats the orphan and the widow. Who are the orphans and widows in my parish today, and who defends their cause?
Paul says every gift must build up the Church. How do I use my gifts: to be seen, or to build up others?
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” What would I find hardest to give away, and what does that tell me about my heart?

lead: Both readings speak of trouble that does not have the last word. Paul tells the Corinthians how he was crushed in Asia until he despaired of life, and learned to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. In John, on the night before his Passion, Jesus warns his disciples that they will be scattered and will face persecution, and then gives them his peace: “take courage; I have conquered the world!” An apostle is not someone spared from trouble, but someone who has found that Christ is stronger.

r.h: God who raises the dead
set: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5), after a painful time in his relations with the Corinthians. He opens it by blessing “the God of all consolation” (1:3), who consoles us in every affliction so that we can console others. Now he tells them what he has just been through.

Asia here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Türkiye, with its capital at Ephesus, where Paul worked for a long time. He does not say what happened. Some connect it with the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41) or with the “wild animals” he fought there (1 Corinthians 15:32); others think of a grave illness. We do not know. What Paul wants them to know is not the details but what God did.
str: v. 8: the affliction in Asia: crushed beyond strength, despairing of life.
v. 9: the sentence of death, so that we would rely on God who raises the dead.
v. 10: he rescued us, he will rescue us, on him we have set our hope.
v. 11: the Corinthians’ prayers help, so that many will give thanks.
kw: Literally pressure, crushing, as grapes are pressed. It is the same word Jesus uses in today’s Gospel: “In the world you face persecution” (John 16:33). The apostle’s life is lived under this pressure, and God’s consolation meets him there.
The word apokrima means an official answer or verdict. Paul felt as if the verdict of death had already been given. That verdict became a lesson in trust.
vv: we were so utterly, unbearably crushed that we despaired of life itself.
Paul does not pretend to be stronger than he was. He speaks openly of despair. Holiness is not the absence of fear but faith that holds on through it.
so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
A prayer of Israel, still said daily, praises God “who gives life to the dead”. Paul has learned it in his own body: the God who raised Jesus is the one to lean on when every human hope fails.
as you also join in helping us by your prayers, so that many will give thanks on our behalf
The great apostle asks for the prayers of a troubled community. Prayer joins Christians together, and the answer to many prayers becomes the thanksgiving of many.
ch: The Church sees in this passage the meaning of Christian suffering: it can teach us to rely on God and unite us to Christ’s death and Resurrection. The Catechism teaches that intercession, asking on behalf of another, is a prayer that conforms us to the prayer of Jesus, and that the first Christian communities lived this fellowship intensely, as Paul gave them a share in his ministry through their prayers (CCC 2634–2636).

r.h: I have conquered the world
set: These are the last words of Jesus’ long farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–16), just before his great prayer to the Father (chapter 17). He has spoken of going away, of the coming of the Spirit, and of sorrow turned into joy like a mother’s after childbirth (16:21). Now he sums up: he came from the Father and is going back to the Father.
The disciples think they understand at last. Jesus gently shows them that their faith will soon be tested: within hours they will run away. Yet he speaks these words so that they may have peace.
