str: vv. 25–28: no longer in figures: the Father himself loves you; I came from the Father and go to the Father.
vv. 29–30: the disciples: now you speak plainly; we believe you came from God.
vv. 31–32: “Do you now believe?” You will be scattered; yet I am not alone.
v. 33: peace in me; persecution in the world; take courage, I have conquered the world.
kw: A saying with a hidden meaning, a riddle or image, like the good shepherd (10:6) or the woman in labour (16:21). The “hour” when Jesus speaks plainly is the hour of his death and Resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit who leads into all truth (16:13).
Speech that is frank and without fear. After Pentecost the apostles speak about Jesus with the same parrēsia, boldness (Acts 4:13, 29, 31).

The perfect tense: a victory already won whose effect remains. Jesus says it before the cross, as if the battle were over. The same verb appears again in 1 John 5:4: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.”
vv: for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
Jesus does not need to persuade an unwilling Father. The Father’s love comes first and meets the disciples who love his Son.
you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.
Mark recalls the prophecy “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). Jesus knows they will fail, and he still loves them and promises peace.
In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!
Jesus does not promise a life without trouble. He promises himself: peace “in me”, and a victory that is already his.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the time of his Passover Jesus teaches us to pray to the Father “in his name”, and that faith in the Son introduces the disciples into the knowledge of the Father (CCC 2614). The Church has always read “I have conquered the world” as the source of the martyrs’ courage. Pope St John Paul II began his ministry in 1978 with the words “Do not be afraid! Open wide the doors for Christ”, a call that comes from the same confidence in the Risen Lord.

qa: Jesus says, “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.” Does Jesus not intercede for us?

He does. Scripture says that Christ always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). In this verse Jesus means that the Father does not need to be won over: “the Father himself loves you.” When we pray in Jesus’ name, we are not standing outside, asking him to persuade God; we pray united with the Son, as children loved by the Father.
study: Paul learned to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. When did a difficult time teach me to trust God more?
Jesus says, “In the world you face persecution. But take courage.” Whom do I know who needs to hear this today, and how can I bring them Christ’s peace?

lead: Both readings ask where we look for life. The Colossians were tempted to find holiness in a list of human rules, “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”, but Paul reminds them that they have died and risen with Christ. John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask Jesus whether he is the one to come, and Jesus answers by pointing to his works: the blind see and the poor hear good news. In both readings, the answer is a person: Christ himself, who gives new life and does not disappoint those who take no offense at him.

r.h: If with Christ you died
set: The letter is addressed to the church at Colossae, a small town in the Lycus valley in what is now Türkiye, founded by Paul’s co-worker Epaphras (1:7). The Church receives it as Paul’s letter; many scholars think it may have been written in Paul’s name by a disciple, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way it is the inspired word of God.

Some teachers at Colossae were pressing a “philosophy” (2:8) with rules about food and drink, festivals and sabbaths (2:16), and the worship of angels and visions (2:18). We do not know exactly who they were; many scholars think they mixed Jewish observances with other religious ideas of the region. Paul has just reminded the Colossians that in baptism they were buried with Christ and raised with him (2:12). Why then should they live as if they were still under such powers?
str: v. 20: if you died with Christ to the elemental spirits, why submit to regulations?
v. 21: the regulations: do not handle, taste, touch.
v. 22: they concern perishable things and are human commands.
v. 23: they look wise and severe, but they do not overcome self-indulgence.
kw: The word stoicheia means basic elements, like the letters of the alphabet or the elements of nature. Paul may mean the basic principles of a worldly religion, or the spiritual powers people thought ruled the world. Either way, Christ is above them all (2:10, 15).
From dogma, a decree. Paul is not speaking against the Church’s teaching, but against rules imposed as if they could give what only Christ gives.
Literally “self-chosen worship”. The word is not found in Greek writing before this letter. It describes religion that we design for ourselves, in place of the worship that comes from Christ.
vv: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the universe, why do you live as if you still belonged to the world?
Baptism is a real death and a real new birth. The Christian lives from that new life, not from fear of the world’s powers.
they are simply human commands and teachings.
Paul echoes Isaiah 29:13, the verse Jesus quoted when he warned against putting human tradition in the place of God’s commandment (Mark 7:7).
These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-imposed piety, humility, and severe treatment of the body, but they are of no value in checking self-indulgence.
Harshness to the body without a changed heart does not make a person holy. The cure for disordered desire is life in Christ, which Paul goes on to describe: “seek the things that are above” (3:1).
ch: Paul’s words do not condemn fasting and self-denial, which Christ himself practised and which the Church has always kept. They condemn rules that take the place of Christ. The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ call to penance aims first not at outward works, sackcloth and ashes, fasting and mortification, but at the conversion of the heart; without this, such penances remain sterile and false, yet interior conversion urges expression in visible signs and works of penance (CCC 1430). It names fasting, prayer and almsgiving as the chief forms of this penance (CCC 1434).

r.h: Are you the one who is to come?
set: Jesus has just finished his instructions to the Twelve as he sent them out on mission (chapter 10). Matthew now turns to the question of who Jesus is, beginning with John the Baptist. John had been arrested by Herod Antipas (4:12; 14:3–4). The Jewish historian Josephus says he was held in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.

John had preached a coming one who would bring fire and judgment, with the axe at the root of the trees (3:10–12). Jesus, instead, was healing the sick and eating with sinners. From prison John sends his disciples with a direct question.
str: v. 1: Jesus finishes instructing the Twelve and goes on to teach and preach.
vv. 2–3: John in prison hears of Christ’s works and sends his question.
vv. 4–5: Jesus’ answer: what you hear and see, in the words of Isaiah.
v. 6: blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.
kw: the one who is to come

A title for the one God would send at the end. John used it when he said, “one who is more powerful than I is coming after me” (3:11). Psalm 118:26 blesses “the one who comes in the name of the Lord”.
Literally “the works of the Christ”. Matthew calls them the Messiah’s works before John asks. Jesus’ works answer the question better than any title.
From skandalon, the stick of a trap or a stone that trips. Jesus may not match what people expect of the Messiah; blessed is the one who does not stumble over him.
vv: Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?
An honest question from a great prophet. God is not offended by honest questions brought to Jesus.
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.

Jesus answers with the words of Isaiah about the age of salvation (Isaiah 35:5–6; 26:19; 61:1). Notice that the list ends not with the greatest miracle, the raising of the dead, but with the poor hearing good news.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.
A beatitude for those who trust Jesus even when he does not do what they expected. It is spoken for John, and for us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus accompanies his words with mighty works and signs, which show that the Kingdom is present in him and attest that he is the promised Messiah (CCC 547). It adds that his signs did not abolish all evils here below; he came to deliver people from the greatest slavery, sin (CCC 549). Jesus’ answer to John also shows the Church’s way: the Gospel is proclaimed by works of mercy as well as words, and the poor are its first hearers.

qa: Did John the Baptist doubt that Jesus was the Messiah?

The Gospel does not say. Some Fathers, among them St John Chrysostom, held that John asked for the sake of his disciples, so that they would go to Jesus and see for themselves (in substance, Homilies on Matthew). Many modern interpreters think John himself was puzzled, because Jesus was not bringing the fiery judgment he had preached. Either way, Jesus answers with kindness, and immediately afterwards praises John as more than a prophet (11:9–11).
study: Paul warns against religion that we design for ourselves. Are there practices in my life that I keep for show or out of fear, rather than out of love for Christ?
Jesus says, “Blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.” When has God acted in my life differently from what I expected, and how did I respond?

lead: Both readings tell the story of salvation in a few strokes. Paul sets two men side by side: Adam, through whose disobedience sin and death entered the world, and Christ, through whose obedience grace and life overflow for all. In Mark, Jesus tells of a vineyard owner who sends servant after servant and at last his beloved son, whom the tenants kill; yet the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. Where human refusal is great, God’s faithfulness is greater: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”

r.h: Where sin increased, grace abounded
set: In the first chapters of Romans Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles, need God’s saving justice, and that it is given through faith in Christ (3:21–26). In the first verses of chapter 5 he spoke of peace with God and of God’s love poured into our hearts. Now he looks at the whole of human history through two figures, Adam and Christ.

The passage is one of the most important in Scripture for the Church’s teaching on original sin. Paul’s sentences are long and sometimes broken off (v. 12 begins a comparison that is completed only in v. 18), because he is reaching for something greater than words: the abundance of grace.
str: v. 12: through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and death spread to all.
vv. 13–14: sin and death reigned even before the law; Adam is a type of the one to come.
vv. 15–17: the gift is not like the trespass: “much more” the grace of the one man Jesus Christ.
vv. 18–19: one man’s trespass, condemnation for all; one man’s obedience, justification and life for all.
vv. 20–21: the law came in; where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.
kw: In verse 12 the NRSV reads “because all have sinned”. The old Latin translation read “in whom (in Adam) all have sinned”, and St Augustine built on it. Modern scholars mostly read “because”, but the Church’s teaching does not depend on one phrase: the whole passage teaches that all are affected by Adam’s sin and all need Christ (vv. 18–19).
A pattern or imprint, like the mark a seal leaves. Adam is a “type of the one who was to come”: as one man’s act affected all, so does Christ’s, but in the opposite direction and far more.
Paul uses a strengthened verb: grace did not only match sin, it overflowed beyond it. This is the heart of the passage.
vv: just as sin came into the world through one man, and death came through sin, and so death spread to all because all have sinned
Paul speaks of death not only as the end of the body but as separation from God. Sin is not only each person’s own fault; it is a power that entered the world and spread.
Adam, who is a type of the one who was to come.
From the beginning God’s plan pointed to Christ. The first man already foreshadows the new Adam (1 Corinthians 15:22, 45).
For just as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.
“The many” in Hebrew style means all, as verse 18 says. Christ’s obedience, “to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), undoes Adam’s disobedience.
but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more
This is no excuse to sin, as Paul says at once (6:1–2). It is the reason no sinner need despair.
ch: The Council of Trent, in its decree on original sin, appealed to this passage (Session 5, 1546). The Catechism teaches that all are implicated in Adam’s sin, as St Paul affirms (CCC 402), and that original sin is a sin “contracted” and not “committed”: a state, not a personal act (CCC 404). It also recalls the words of St Leo the Great: Christ’s inexpressible grace gave us blessings better than those the demon’s envy had taken away (CCC 412). The Church’s teaching on original sin is never without the Good News: it is the reverse side of the truth that Jesus is the Saviour of all (CCC 389).

r.h: The stone the builders rejected
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem and cleansed the Temple. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders have asked him by what authority he acts (11:27–33). He answers with this parable, and they understand that it is spoken against them (12:12).

The opening words echo Isaiah’s song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), where the vineyard is the house of Israel and God is the owner who planted it with care. In Jesus’ parable, the vineyard is still God’s and still good; the problem is with the tenants entrusted with it. Vineyards were often owned by people who lived far away and let them to tenants for a share of the harvest.
str: v. 1: the vineyard planted with care and let to tenants.
vv. 2–5: servant after servant sent for the fruit, beaten, insulted, killed.
vv. 6–8: last of all the beloved son; killed and thrown out of the vineyard.
v. 9: the owner will come and give the vineyard to others.
vv. 10–11: Psalm 118: the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.
v. 12: the leaders understand, and want to arrest him, but fear the crowd.
kw: The same word the Father’s voice used at Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration: “my Son, the Beloved” (1:11; 9:7). Jesus tells his own story: he is not one more servant but the only Son.
The tenants think that by killing the heir they can take the inheritance. Sin always imagines that God’s gifts can be seized by getting rid of God.

Literally “head of the corner”: the main stone that holds two walls together, or the top stone of an arch. The early Church used this psalm verse again and again of the Risen Christ (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7).
vv: A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the wine press, and built a watchtower
Every detail shows the owner’s care. God has given his people everything they need to bear fruit.
He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
The owner’s hope seems almost foolish. It is the foolishness of God’s love, which sends the Son even knowing what will happen.
He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.

The vineyard is not destroyed; its care is given to new tenants. Many interpreters see here the leadership of God’s people entrusted to the Twelve and to those who follow them. That is a warning to every Church leader in every age.
‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone
Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23, sung at the great feasts. The parable ends not with the death of the son but with his vindication: a hint of the Resurrection.
ch: The Catechism, describing the images of the Church, says that the Church is God’s vineyard and cultivated field, and that the true vine is Christ (CCC 755); it adds that the Lord compared himself to the stone rejected by the builders which became the cornerstone (CCC 756). The Church reads this parable as addressed first to herself and her pastors. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ’s Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; see CCC 597).

qa: Does this parable mean that God rejected the Jewish people?

No. Mark says that the leaders understood the parable was told against them, and that they feared the crowd (12:12): the people are not the target. The vineyard itself is not condemned; it remains God’s. St Paul, a Jew who loved his people, insists that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The Church teaches that the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4).
study: Paul says that “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.” Where in my life or my family do I most need to believe this?
The owner sent servant after servant and finally his beloved son. What fruit is God asking of the “vineyard” entrusted to me: my family, my work, my parish?

lead: Both readings speak of a life that only God can give. Second Peter says that God’s divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, so that we may become participants of the divine nature, and calls us to make every effort to let faith grow into love. In John, many disciples find Jesus’ teaching on the bread of life too hard, and Jesus answers: “It is the spirit that gives life.” God gives the gift, and his Spirit makes it fruitful in us; our part is to receive it and let it grow.

r.h: Participants of the divine nature
set: Second Peter presents itself as the testament of the apostle Peter, written near the end of his life (1:14). The Church receives it as part of the New Testament. Its authorship was questioned already in the early centuries, and many scholars today think it was written by a disciple in Peter’s name, handing on his teaching to a later generation; others defend Peter’s authorship. Its message is the same either way: hold fast to the faith received from the apostles.

The letter warns against false teachers who mocked the hope of Christ’s coming and lived carelessly (chapters 2–3). Today’s verses come first, as the positive foundation: God has given everything, so Christians must grow in a life that shows it.
str: v. 3: God’s divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness.
v. 4: through his promises we escape corruption and share the divine nature.
vv. 5–7: a ladder of virtues: faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection, love.
vv. 8–9: these keep us fruitful; without them we are short-sighted and forget the cleansing of our sins.
kw: One of the boldest phrases in the New Testament. It does not mean that we stop being creatures, but that by grace we truly share God’s own life, as children share their father’s life. The Fathers of the East and West built their teaching on our divinisation on this verse.

In Greek cities a chorēgos paid the costs of a chorus for a festival, generously. The verb came to mean to supply richly. God has supplied everything; the Christian, in turn, is to “supply” virtue upon virtue.
Excellence. The same word is used of God’s own “glory and goodness” in verse 3 and of the Christian’s goodness in verse 5. The virtue we grow in is a reflection of his.
vv: His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness
The letter begins with gift, not with demand. Everything that follows is a response to what God has already given.
so that through them you may escape from the corruption that is in the world because of lust, and may become participants of the divine nature.
Two movements: escape from corruption and sharing in God’s life. Salvation is not only being forgiven but being drawn into God’s own life.
you must make every effort to support your faith with goodness
Grace does not make us passive. Because God has given everything, we make every effort. Faith comes first, and love comes last in the list (v. 7), as its crown.
For anyone who lacks these things is short-sighted and blind, and is forgetful of the cleansing of past sins.
A Christian who stops growing has forgotten his baptism. Remembering how much we have been forgiven makes us eager to grow.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it explains why the Word became flesh: to make us “partakers of the divine nature”; it adds St Athanasius’ famous words, that the Son of God became man so that we might become God (CCC 460). It teaches that Baptism makes the newly baptized a partaker of the divine nature (CCC 1265), and that grace is a participation in the life of God (CCC 1997). The virtues listed here are not our own achievement apart from God: they grow by grace, with our cooperation.

r.h: The words I have spoken are spirit and life
set: Jesus has just finished his discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum, in which he said that he is the bread of life and that his flesh is true food and his blood true drink (6:55). Now the scene changes: not the crowd but many of his own disciples find the teaching too hard.
Jesus does not take back what he said. Instead he points them higher: to his ascension, and to the Spirit who gives life. Only in the Spirit can his words be received.
str: v. 60: many disciples: this teaching is difficult; who can accept it?
v. 61: Jesus knows they are complaining: does this offend you?
v. 62: what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?
v. 63: the spirit gives life; the flesh is useless; my words are spirit and life.
kw: Literally hard, rough, harsh. The disciples do not say the teaching is unclear; they say it is hard to accept. The problem is not understanding but believing.

The same family of words is used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8 in the Greek) and the same verb of the crowd earlier in this chapter (6:41). The disciples repeat the old murmuring over the manna.
The Spirit is the giver of life, as the Creed says. The flesh of Jesus gives life because it is filled with the Spirit; human nature on its own cannot.
vv: This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?
The Greek can also mean “who can listen to him?” Some teachings of Christ are hard not because they are unclear but because they ask for faith.
Does this offend you?
Jesus names their stumbling openly. He does not soften the teaching to keep followers.
Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?
If they stumble at his words about his flesh, what will they say when that same flesh ascends to the Father? The bread of life is the body of the One who came down from heaven and will return there.
It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.
Jesus is not denying what he just said about eating his flesh. “The flesh” here means human nature left to itself, our merely human way of understanding. His words are received only by the Spirit.
ch: St Augustine explained that the disciples understood Jesus’ words in a fleshly way, as if he meant flesh cut up like meat in a market; but he gives his flesh in a way that is spiritual and life-giving (in substance, Tractates on John 27). The Catechism quotes St Thomas Aquinas: that the true Body and Blood of Christ are present in this sacrament cannot be apprehended by the senses, but only by faith (CCC 1381). In every Eucharistic prayer the Church calls upon the Holy Spirit, because it is the Spirit who gives life.

qa: Jesus says, “the flesh is useless.” Does this mean the Eucharist is only a symbol?

No. A few verses earlier he says, “my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink” (6:55). In verse 63 he does not say “my flesh is useless” but “the flesh”, meaning human nature without the Spirit and a merely human way of judging. The Church has always read these verses together: Christ’s flesh, filled with the Spirit and risen, truly gives life, and it is received in faith.
study: Second Peter says God has given us “everything needed for life and godliness”. Which virtue in the list do I most need to “supply” this week?
When a teaching of Christ or his Church is hard for me, do I complain, walk away, or ask the Spirit to help me receive it?

lead: Both readings ask how Christians live in a world where good and evil grow side by side. First Peter tells believers who suffer for doing right not to be afraid, but to honour Christ in their hearts and to give a reason for their hope with gentleness, because Christ the righteous suffered for the unrighteous. In Matthew, Jesus explains why the master lets the weeds grow with the wheat until the harvest: judgment belongs to God at the end, and now is the time of patience. The Christian answer to evil is not fear or force, but hope, gentleness and trust in the Lord of the harvest.

r.h: A reason for your hope
set: First Peter is written to Christians scattered through five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, whom it calls “exiles” (1:1). Most were not facing a state persecution yet, but they were slandered and pushed aside by their neighbours because they no longer joined in the old ways of life (4:3–4). The letter teaches them how to live as Christ’s people in such a world: with good conduct, without fear, and with hope.

Today’s verses take up words from Isaiah 8:12–13, where the prophet is told not to fear what the people fear but to regard the Lord of hosts as holy. Peter applies them to Christ: in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord.
str: v. 14: blessed if you suffer for what is right; do not fear their threats.
v. 15: sanctify Christ as Lord; always be ready to give a reason for your hope.
v. 16: with gentleness and reverence and a clear conscience.
v. 17: better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
v. 18: Christ suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.
kw: A reasoned answer, as in a court. From this word comes “apologetics”. Every Christian, not only scholars, is to be ready to explain why he or she hopes.
The manner matters as much as the message. Gentleness toward the questioner, and reverence (literally “fear”) before God. A true answer given with contempt is not a Christian witness.
Christ’s suffering is not repeated; it is complete and sufficient. Hebrews uses the same word (Hebrews 9:26–28). The Eucharist does not add to it but makes that one sacrifice present.
vv: But even if you do suffer for doing what is right, you are blessed.
An echo of Jesus’ beatitude: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10).
but in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be ready to make your defense to anyone who demands from you an accounting for the hope that is in you
Notice the order: first Christ honoured in the heart, then the answer on the lips. Peter speaks of “the hope that is in you”: people notice hope, and ask about it.
yet do it with gentleness and reverence.
The best defense of the faith is a life that matches it, so that those who speak evil are put to shame by good conduct.
For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring you to God.

Here is the reason for all the rest. Christ’s innocent suffering brought us to God; our suffering for good, joined to his, becomes a share in his work. “Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit” speaks of his death and Resurrection; the next verse goes on to his proclamation to “the spirits in prison”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the disciple of Christ must not only keep the faith and live by it, but also profess it, confidently bear witness to it and spread it (CCC 1816). The Church connects the verses that follow this reading (3:18–19) with Christ’s descent to the dead (CCC 632). Today many Christians in many lands suffer for their faith; the Church prays for them, and also for those who wrong them, as Christ prayed for those who crucified him.

r.h: Let both grow together until the harvest
set: Matthew 13 gathers seven parables of the Kingdom. After the sower (13:1–23), Jesus tells this parable to the crowds; later, in the house, he explains it to his disciples (vv. 36–43). Between the two parts come the mustard seed and the yeast (vv. 31–35), which today’s reading leaves out.

The “weeds” were very likely darnel, a grass that grows in wheat fields and looks much like wheat until the ears appear. Its grains can make people ill, so farmers separated them carefully at harvest. Pulling darnel out early would tear up the wheat, whose roots were tangled with it.
str: vv. 24–26: good seed sown; an enemy sows weeds at night; both appear together.
vv. 27–28: the servants’ question: where did the weeds come from? An enemy has done this.
vv. 29–30: do not gather them now; let both grow until the harvest.
v. 36: the disciples ask for the meaning.
vv. 37–39: the sower is the Son of Man, the field the world, the enemy the devil, the harvest the end of the age.
vv. 40–43: the judgment at the end; the righteous will shine like the sun.
kw: Probably darnel, a weed that looks like wheat while it grows. The resemblance is the point: in this world it is not always easy to tell good from evil, and we are not the final judges.
“Let both of them grow together.” The same Greek verb also means to forgive. The master’s patience gives time for growth and, in human terms, time for conversion.
A phrase found in Matthew alone among the Gospels (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20). The final separation belongs to that day and to God’s angels, not to the servants now.
vv: but while everybody was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and then went away.
Evil in the world does not come from God, who sowed only good seed. It has an enemy behind it, working secretly.
No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them.
The master cares more about saving the wheat than about destroying the weeds quickly. Impatient zeal can do great harm to the good.
the field is the world
Jesus says the field is the world. The parable is about God’s patience with the whole human family, and about how his people live within it.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
An echo of Daniel 12:3: the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky. The end of the story is not burning but glory for those who belong to the Father.
ch: St Augustine used this parable against the Donatists, who wanted a Church made only of the pure: in this age the Church is a mixed field, and the final separation belongs to the Lord (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, embracing sinners in her bosom, is at once holy and always in need of purification (Lumen Gentium 8; CCC 827). The Catechism also quotes verses 41–42 among Jesus’ solemn warnings about hell, which are a call to responsibility and conversion (CCC 1034, 1036).

qa: If the weeds must be left until the harvest, should the Church never correct sin?

The parable forbids us to take God’s place as final judge, and to try to root out evil people by force. It does not forbid correction. Jesus himself teaches how to correct a brother or sister (Matthew 18:15–17), and the Church calls sinners to conversion through the sacrament of Reconciliation. In the parable “the field is the world”; the patience of the master is the patience God shows to every sinner, ourselves first.
study: Peter says, “Always be ready to make your defense… for the hope that is in you.” If someone asked me today why I hope, what would I say?
The master tells his servants, “Let both of them grow together.” Where am I tempted to judge or uproot others, when God is asking me to be patient and to grow as wheat?

lead: Both readings look beneath the surface. Paul asks how a holy commandment could become an occasion of death, and answers that the fault lies not in the law but in sin, which uses even good things against us. In Mark, Jesus looks past the long robes and the large gifts to a poor widow whose two small coins are worth more than all the rest. God judges the heart, and he gives the grace that the law alone could not give. Today the Church also remembers Sts Gervasius and Protasius, early martyrs of Milan whose relics St Ambrose discovered in 386.

r.h: The law is holy
set: Paul has just said that Christians have died to the law through the body of Christ (7:4–6). A reader might conclude that the law itself was bad. Paul rejects this at once. He speaks in the first person, “I”, but most interpreters, ancient and modern, hear more than his private story: the story of Adam, who received one command and was deceived, and the story of everyone who meets God’s law while still under the power of sin.
str: v. 7: the question, “That the law is sin?” and the answer: by no means; the law made sin known, as the command “You shall not covet” made coveting known.
vv. 8–11: sin seized its opportunity in the commandment, deceived and killed.
vv. 12–13: the conclusion: the law is holy, just and good; sin is shown to be what it is.
kw: The word of the tenth commandment in the Greek Old Testament (Exodus 20:17). Paul chooses the one commandment that touches the heart rather than the hand: no outward act is needed to break it.
Literally a starting point or base of operations, used of an army’s base. Sin is pictured as an enemy that turns the commandment into its base of attack.
The same verb Paul uses for the serpent deceiving Eve (2 Corinthians 11:3). The echo of Genesis 3 is deliberate: a good command, a lie, and death.
vv: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”
The law is like a light switched on in a dark room: it does not create the dirt, it shows it.
For sin, seizing an opportunity in the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
Sin is almost a person here, a power that lies and kills. Paul does not blame God’s gift but the enemy who abuses it.
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.
This verse settles the matter. Whatever Paul says against relying on the law, he never says the law is evil.
ch: The Catechism, quoting this verse, teaches that according to Christian tradition the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect: like a tutor it shows what must be done, but does not of itself give the strength, the grace of the Spirit, to do it (CCC 1963). The Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel (CCC 1964). What the law could not do, Christ does, as Paul will say in Romans 8:3–4. St Augustine, writing on Paul’s teaching, says the law was given so that grace might be sought, and grace so that the law might be fulfilled (in substance, On the Spirit and the Letter).

r.h: Two small coins
set: These are the last scenes of Jesus’ teaching in the Temple before his words about its destruction (13:1–2). He has been questioned by priests, Pharisees, Sadducees and a scribe. A scribe has just been told he is not far from the kingdom (12:34), so Jesus is not condemning every scribe, but a way of using religion for honour and gain.

According to the Mishnah, there were thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for offerings in the Temple court, probably in the Court of the Women, where both men and women could go. Anyone could see how much a person gave.
str: vv. 38–40: a warning against religious display and greed.
vv. 41–42: Jesus sits and watches the giving; a poor widow puts in two small coins.
vv. 43–44: Jesus calls his disciples and teaches them how God counts.
kw: The lepton was the smallest coin in use. Mark explains for readers in the Roman world that two of them make a quadrans (NRSV “a penny”), the smallest Roman coin.
all she had to live on
Literally “her whole life”. The widow gives not a part but everything. A few days later Jesus will give his whole life.
vv: They devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers.
Widows were among those the Law of Moses told Israel to protect (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 24:17). Jesus warns against any who would exploit them while appearing devout.
He sat down opposite the treasury, and watched the crowd putting money into the treasury.
Jesus watches. He sees what no one else sees, and he sees the heart.
For all of them have contributed out of their abundance; but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.
God does not measure the size of the gift but what it costs and the love behind it.
ch: The Catechism sets this widow before every disciple: Jesus asks us to prefer him to everything and everyone, and gives as an example the poor widow of Jerusalem who gave out of her poverty all that she had to live on (CCC 2544). St Cyprian of Carthage holds her up to the wealthy who come to the Lord’s table empty-handed: a poor widow gave two coins, and the rich should be ashamed to give nothing (in substance, On Works and Almsgiving 15).

qa: Does Jesus praise the widow, or lament that she was made to give her last coins?

Some modern readers hear the scene as a lament, because Jesus has just condemned those who devour widows’ houses. The words of Jesus, though, are words of praise: she “has put in more than all” the others. The Church has always read it so (CCC 2544). Both truths stand: God treasures the gift of the poor, and those who lead God’s people must never exploit them.
study: The command “You shall not covet” showed Paul what was in his heart. Which commandment shows me most clearly where I need God’s grace?
The widow gave “all she had to live on”. What would it mean for me to give God not my spare things but something of myself?

lead: This Sunday’s readings are about a word that gives life and a time that must not be wasted. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells Israel that the Lord’s statutes are their wisdom before the nations, and that no nation has a God so near. Isaiah sees the nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord to learn his ways, beating their swords into plowshares. Paul teaches the Corinthians how to use their Christian liberty: seek the good of the other, and do everything for the glory of God. And in Luke, Jesus urges his hearers to read the signs of their own time, to settle accounts while they are still on the way, and to repent.

The thread is this: God has come near and spoken. His word is not a burden but life, wisdom and peace, first for Israel and through Israel for all peoples. The right answer is to turn to him now, while there is time, and to live in a way that builds up others and gives him glory. In the Season of the Apostles the Church hears how that word went out from Zion to the ends of the earth, and to us.

r.h: A God so near
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses’ last words to Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from the promised land. Chapters 1–3 have recalled the journey from Horeb. Now, in chapter 4, Moses turns from history to exhortation: “So now, Israel, give heed.” A new generation is about to enter the land, and Moses wants them to know that their life there depends on listening to the Lord.

The reference to the Baal of Peor recalls Numbers 25: at Shittim, on these same plains, many Israelites joined in the worship of the Baal of Peor, and a plague followed. Those who held fast to the Lord survived. Moses uses this recent memory as a lesson: faithfulness is life.
str: vv. 1–2: the call to hear and keep the statutes, adding nothing and taking nothing away.
vv. 3–4: the lesson of the Baal of Peor: those who held fast to the Lord are alive.
vv. 5–6: keeping the law is Israel’s wisdom in the sight of the nations.
vv. 7–8: two questions of wonder: what nation has a God so near, and what nation has such just laws?
kw: The same verb that opens the great prayer of Israel, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4). In the Bible, to hear is to obey: listening that does not change life is not yet hearing.

A pair that runs through Deuteronomy. The first word comes from a root meaning to engrave, things fixed by God; the second means judgments, decisions about what is just. Together they name the whole of the Lord’s teaching.
The verb used when a man “clings” to his wife (Genesis 2:24). Israel’s faithfulness to the Lord is pictured as the bond of love in marriage.
vv: So now, Israel, give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live
The purpose of the law is life. God does not command in order to burden but in order that his people may live.
You must neither add anything to what I command you nor take away anything from it
The word belongs to God, not to us. The same warning closes the Bible (Revelation 22:18–19).
while those of you who held fast to the Lord your God are all alive today.
Moses speaks to people who remember. Faith rests on what God has done in their own lifetime.
For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?
Israel’s greatness is not its size or its army but the nearness of its God. Christians hear this verse fulfilled beyond measure in the Word made flesh, who “lived among us” (John 1:14).
ch: The Church receives the Law given to Israel as God’s gift and as a true revelation. The Catechism teaches that the commandments take their full meaning within the covenant: they express what it means to belong to God (CCC 2062). Jesus did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17), and he summed it up in the love of God and neighbour, quoting Deuteronomy itself (Matthew 22:37). Moses’ question, “What other great nation has a god so near?”, has been read by Christians as a promise kept in the Incarnation and in the Eucharist, where God is nearer still.

r.h: All the nations shall stream to it
set: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem in the second half of the eighth century before Christ, in the days of kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). His first chapter is a harsh indictment of Judah’s sins. Then, suddenly, comes this vision of hope: not Jerusalem as it is, but as God will make it.

An almost identical oracle appears in Micah 4:1–3. Scholars do not agree whether one prophet borrowed from the other or both used an older text. Either way, the Church received it twice in her Scriptures, as if to underline its importance.
str: v. 1: a new title: the word Isaiah “saw”.
v. 2: the mountain of the Lord’s house raised above all mountains; the nations stream to it.
v. 3: the peoples invite one another to go up and learn; instruction goes out from Zion.
v. 4: the Lord judges between nations; swords become plowshares; war is no longer learned.
v. 5: the call to Israel: walk now in the light of the Lord.
kw: Literally “at the end of the days”. Not simply some later time, but the time when God brings his plan to its goal. The New Testament says that in Christ these last days have begun (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17).
The verb from which the Hebrew word for river comes. The picture is strange on purpose: rivers flow down, but here the nations flow up the mountain, drawn by God.
Usually rendered “law”, but its root sense is teaching or direction. What goes out from Zion is God’s teaching for the way of life, and the nations come wanting to learn it.
vv: In days to come the mountain of the Lord’s house shall be established as the highest of the mountains
Zion was not a high mountain. Its height is the honour God gives it, because his presence dwells there.
that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.
The nations do not come to conquer Jerusalem but to be taught. Peace begins with learning God’s ways.
they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks
Weapons are not merely laid down; they are reforged into tools that feed people. The iron is the same; its purpose changes.
O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord!
The vision ends with an appeal to Israel now. The future peace is to be lived in advance by God’s own people.
ch: The Fathers saw this prophecy beginning to be fulfilled when the Gospel went out from Jerusalem. St Justin Martyr, quoting the words about the law going forth from Zion (“out of Zion shall go forth instruction”), tells the Roman emperor that twelve men went out from Jerusalem into the world, unlearned and unable to speak well, and by the power of God proclaimed Christ to every race (in substance, First Apology 39). The Second Vatican Council quotes the words about swords and plowshares in its teaching on peace, and calls Christians to work for a peace that is the fruit of justice and love (Gaudium et Spes 78).

r.h: Do everything for the glory of God
set: Since chapter 8 Paul has been answering a practical question from Corinth: may Christians eat meat that has been offered to idols? In a Greek city much of the meat sold in the market (Greek makellon) came from animals sacrificed in temples, and invitations to meals with pagan friends were part of ordinary life.

Paul has already forbidden taking part in meals in idol temples (10:14–22): one cannot share the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. Now he deals with the ordinary market and the private home, and gives a principle that reaches far beyond food.
str: vv. 23–24: the Corinthian slogan corrected: not everything builds up; seek the other’s good.
vv. 25–26: market meat may be eaten, for the earth is the Lord’s.
vv. 27–29a: at a host’s table eat without scruple, unless someone points out that the food was sacrificed; then abstain for his conscience.
vv. 29b–30: Paul defends his liberty and his thanksgiving.
v. 31: the rule for all of life: do everything for the glory of God.
kw: A building word. For Paul the measure of an action is not only whether it is allowed but whether it builds up the community, the temple of God (3:16).
The inner judgment about right and wrong. Paul respects the conscience of the weaker brother even when it is mistaken about the facts, because to make him act against it would harm him.
The word from which “Eucharist” comes. Paul gives thanks over his food, as Jews blessed God at meals and as Jesus gave thanks at the Last Supper (11:24).
vv: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are beneficial.
Paul seems to quote a slogan used at Corinth (as in 6:12) and corrects it. Liberty is real, but it is for love.
Do not seek your own advantage, but that of the other.
This is the heart of Paul’s ethic, learned from Christ, who did not please himself (Romans 15:3).
for “the earth and its fullness are the Lord’s.”
Paul quotes Psalm 24:1. Later Jewish teachers used the same verse to teach that every food should be received with a blessing; Paul uses it to show that no food is unclean in itself.
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
Nothing is too ordinary to be offered to God. A meal, a day’s work, a conversation can all give him glory.
ch: The Church teaches that a person must always obey the certain judgment of conscience, and also has the duty to form it well (CCC 1790, 1783). Paul adds that charity respects the conscience of others: we should not lead a brother to act against his conscience (CCC 1789, which cites this letter). The motto of St Ignatius of Loyola and the Society of Jesus, Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God, echoes the words “do everything for the glory of God”.

r.h: Unless you repent
set: Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem (9:51), teaching the crowds about readiness for the coming of the Son of Man (12:35–48). Just before this reading he rebuked the crowds for being able to read the weather but not “the present time” (12:56). These verses continue that warning.

Luke alone records the two events in 13:1–5. Nothing else is known of Galileans killed by Pilate while offering sacrifice, but the Jewish historian Josephus tells of other harsh acts by Pilate, so the report fits his character. The tower of Siloam stood near the pool of Siloam, in the south of Jerusalem; its fall is also known only from Luke.
str: 12:57: judge for yourselves what is right.
12:58–59: a parable from the courts: settle with your accuser on the way, before it is too late.
13:1: news of the Galileans killed by Pilate.
13:2–3: were they worse sinners? No; but unless you repent, you will all perish.
13:4–5: the eighteen killed at Siloam: the same question and the same answer.
kw: In 12:56 Jesus speaks of “the present time”: not clock time but the decisive moment of God’s visit. The crowds can read the sky but not the hour of salvation standing before them.
Literally to change one’s mind, to turn round. In the Gospels it means a turning of the whole person back to God, not only sorrow for a single act.
The smallest coin, the same as the widow’s two coins in Mark 12:42. Nothing will be left unpaid.
vv: Thus, when you go with your accuser before a magistrate, on the way make an effort to settle the case
The road to the court is the time of grace. We are all on that road; the moment to be reconciled with God and neighbour is now.
Do you think that because these Galileans suffered in this way they were worse sinners than all other Galileans?
Many people then, as now, assumed that disaster proves guilt. Jesus rejects that assumption, as the Book of Job had done.
No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.
Jesus turns a question about others into a question about us. The tragedy is a call, not a verdict on the victims.
Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them
The first case was a crime by a ruler, the second an accident. Whether evil comes from human hands or from chance, the lesson is the same.
ch: The Church does not teach that every suffering is a punishment for the sufferer’s own sins. Jesus says the same of the man born blind (John 9:3), and St John Paul II, reflecting on Job, wrote that not all suffering is a consequence of a fault (in substance, Salvifici Doloris 11). What Jesus asks is conversion. The Catechism explains that his call to conversion is first of all a call to interior conversion, a radical reorientation of the whole life, a return to God with all our heart (CCC 1430–1431). The parable that follows in Luke, the barren fig tree given one more year (13:6–9), shows that God’s patience gives us time to turn.

qa: When a disaster strikes, should we say it is God’s punishment?

Jesus forbids us to conclude that those who suffer are worse sinners than others (Luke 13:2–4). God permits evil only to draw good from it, in ways we may not see in this life (CCC 312–314). The right response to tragedy is compassion for the victims, prayer, and our own conversion, not judgment of others.
Paul says we may eat meat sold in the market. Do Christians still have rules about food?

Paul teaches that no food is unclean in itself, since the earth is the Lord’s (10:26; see Mark 7:19). The Church’s days of fasting and abstinence are not about clean and unclean food. They are acts of penance and love, willingly embraced in union with Christ, and each Church sets its own discipline (CCC 1438, 2043). Syro-Malabar Catholics follow the fasts and abstinences laid down by their own Church.
Does “You must neither add anything to what I command you nor take away anything from it” mean the Church may not develop doctrine?

Moses forbids changing God’s word to suit ourselves. The Church does not add new revelation; she guards the deposit she received and, with the help of the Holy Spirit, comes to understand it more deeply (Dei Verbum 8, 10). Development of doctrine is growth in understanding, not a change of the word.
rite: In the Season of the Apostles our Church celebrates the Church’s mission: the word going out from Zion, as Isaiah saw, carried by the apostles to the nations and by Mar Thoma Shleeha to India. Isaiah’s picture of the nations coming to learn God’s ways is fulfilled every time a catechism class meets in a parish or a family reads Scripture together at evening prayer. Every Holy Qurbana proclaims the word and then gives us the One who is nearer to us than Moses could have imagined.

Paul’s words “do everything for the glory of God” fit the Syro-Malabar home well: the blessing before meals, the evening family prayer, and the work of farmers, teachers and nurses offered to God. Our Church’s rich tradition of fasting is lived not to make some foods unclean but to turn the heart to God.
study: Moses asks what other great nation has a god so near to it. Where have I experienced God’s nearness this week?
Isaiah sees swords turned into plowshares. Is there a “sword” in my words or relationships that God is asking me to reforge into something that builds up?
Paul says, “Do not seek your own advantage, but that of the other.” Where in my family or parish could I give up a right for someone else’s good?
Jesus says, “unless you repent”. What turning is he asking of me now, while I am still on the way?

lead: Paul ends his long reflection on Israel and the nations not with an argument but with a cry of praise: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Jesus, in Matthew, speaks of the heart as a treasure from which words come out, good or evil. When the heart is filled with God’s mercy, the mouth speaks praise. Today the Church also remembers St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591), the young Jesuit who died after nursing the plague-stricken in Rome.

r.h: How unsearchable are his ways
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul’s anguished reflection on why most of his own people, Israel, had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah. He insists that God has not rejected his people (11:1), that the Gentiles are a wild olive branch grafted onto Israel’s tree (11:17–24), and that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26). These verses are his conclusion: a summary of God’s plan of mercy and a hymn of praise.
str: vv. 30–31: the pattern of mercy: Gentiles once disobedient, now shown mercy; Israel now disobedient, so that they too may receive mercy.
v. 32: God has shut up all in disobedience, so as to have mercy on all.
vv. 33–35: the doxology: the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, with words from Isaiah and Job.
kw: Used of fish caught together in a net (Luke 5:6). All, Jews and Gentiles, are enclosed together under disobedience, so that no one is saved except by mercy.
Literally “that cannot be tracked”, like footprints that cannot be followed. God’s ways are not irrational; they are beyond our tracing.
vv: For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.
This is not a statement that God causes sin. It says that the whole human race stands in need of mercy, and that God’s purpose in permitting disobedience is mercy.
O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
Paul has thought hard about God’s plan for three chapters. When he reaches the end of thinking, he does not despair; he worships.
“Or who has given a gift to him, to receive a gift in return?”
Paul draws on Job 41:11. No one can put God in debt. Everything is grace.
ch: The Church reads Romans 9–11 with deep respect for the Jewish people. The Second Vatican Council, drawing on this letter, teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, for God does not take back his gifts or his call, and that the Church awaits the day when all peoples will call on the Lord with one voice (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism links the full inclusion of Israel with the glorious coming of Christ (CCC 674). Before such a mystery, Paul shows us the right posture: not speculation about others, but praise of God’s mercy, which we ourselves have received.

r.h: The tree is known by its fruit
set: Jesus has healed a blind and mute man, and some Pharisees have said that he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons (12:22–24). Jesus answers that a kingdom divided cannot stand, and warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (12:25–32). These verses close his answer: what people say reveals what is in their hearts.
str: v. 33: the tree and its fruit.
vv. 34–35: the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart; good and evil treasure.
vv. 36–37: every careless word will be accounted for on the day of judgment.
kw: The heart is pictured as a storeroom. What is laid up there comes out in speech and action, as Jesus also says of treasure in heaven (6:21).
Literally an “idle” or “workless” word (argos, from a- “not” and ergon “work”): talk that does no good. Jesus warns that even such words reveal the heart and will be judged.
vv: for the tree is known by its fruit.
Jesus’ works of healing are good fruit; to call them the work of Satan is to refuse to see. The same test applies to us: our deeds show who we are.
For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
“You brood of vipers!” recalls the name John the Baptist gave to those who came without repentance (3:7). Jesus is not condemning a whole people but a hardness of heart that resists God’s work.
for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
Words are not small things. They can build up or destroy, heal or wound.
ch: The Letter of James echoes this teaching: the tongue is a small member, yet it can set a whole forest ablaze; from the same mouth come blessing and cursing (James 3:5–10). The Church sees in the guarding of speech a work of charity and truth: the Catechism warns against rash judgment, detraction and calumny, which destroy the reputation of others (CCC 2477–2479). The Rule of St Benedict devotes a chapter to restraint of speech, recalling that in much speaking one does not escape sin (in substance, Rule 6, quoting Proverbs 10:19).

rite: St Aloysius Gonzaga was born to a noble family in northern Italy and gave up his inheritance to join the Society of Jesus. While a student in Rome he cared for the sick during an epidemic, caught the disease and died at twenty-three. The Church honours him as a patron of young people. His life fits today’s Gospel: a good tree, known by its fruit.
study: Paul ends his hardest thinking with praise. When I cannot understand God’s ways, do I turn to worship or to complaint?
Jesus says the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. What do my words this past week reveal about what fills my heart?

lead: Two pairs of readings are given today. In the weekday readings Paul speaks of our earthly body as a tent and of the eternal house God has prepared, and Jesus says that a lamp is not lit to be hidden. For Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyred in England in 1535, Peter tells Christians not to be surprised at the fiery ordeal, and Jesus sends his disciples out like sheep among wolves. The two pairs meet in these martyrs: men who walked by faith and not by sight, and who would not hide their light even before a king.

r.h: A house not made with hands
set: Paul has been describing the hardships of his ministry: afflicted but not crushed, carrying in the body the death of Jesus (4:8–10). He has just said that our slight momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (4:17). Now he explains the ground of his hope: what awaits us beyond this mortal life.
str: v. 1: if this earthly tent is destroyed, we have an eternal building from God.
vv. 2–4: we groan, longing to be further clothed, so that the mortal may be swallowed up by life.
v. 5: God has given the Spirit as a guarantee.
vv. 6–7: so we are confident, walking by faith, not by sight.
kw: Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and knew how quickly a tent is taken down. The body in this life is a temporary dwelling, not our final home.
A business word for a first payment that guarantees the rest. The Holy Spirit given to us now is the pledge of the life to come (also 1:22; Ephesians 1:14).
vv: For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
Paul does not despise the body; he looks forward to its transformation. The Christian hope is not escape from the body but resurrection.
so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
Death is not the last word. Life swallows death, as Paul also says in 1 Corinthians 15:54.
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
A short sentence that describes the whole Christian life on earth.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of Christian death, quotes Paul’s desire to be away from the body and at home with the Lord (5:8; CCC 1005). The Church prays for the faithful departed with this hope: death is the end of our earthly pilgrimage, and for those who die in Christ it is the passage to the eternal house God has prepared.

r.h: The lamp on the lampstand
set: These sayings follow the parable of the sower and its explanation (4:1–20). Jesus has spoken of the word sown in different kinds of soil. Now he adds two short parables about light and measure: the word is meant to be revealed, and those who listen well will receive more.
str: vv. 21–23: the lamp is not put under a basket; what is hidden will be revealed.
vv. 24–25: the measure you give; to those who have, more will be given.
kw: A small clay oil lamp. The Greek of 4:21 says literally “Does the lamp come…?”, and many interpreters hear in it a hint of Christ himself, the light who has come into the world.
A grain measure of about nine litres. Putting it over a lamp would put the light out.
vv: Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?
The answer is obvious. The kingdom, now hidden like a seed, is meant to shine for all.
Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.
Here the measure is the measure of attention. The more generously we listen to the word, the more God gives.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the laity are called to make Christ known by the witness of their lives, shining with faith, hope and charity, like a light in the world (in substance, Lumen Gentium 31, 35). A faith kept entirely private, hidden under the basket, has forgotten what it is for.

r.h: If you suffer as a Christian
set: First Peter is addressed to Christians scattered through the provinces of Asia Minor (1:1), who were facing insults and hostility from their neighbours because of their faith. Tradition places its writing at Rome, which the letter calls “Babylon” (5:13), shortly before or during the persecution under Nero.
str: vv. 12–13: do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings.
vv. 14–16: blessed if insulted for the name of Christ; suffer as a Christian, not as a wrongdoer.
vv. 17–19: judgment begins with the household of God; entrust yourselves to the faithful Creator.
kw: Literally a burning, as in a smelter’s furnace where gold is refined (1:7). Suffering is pictured as a test that purifies.
The name occurs only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; here). It was probably first used by outsiders; Peter tells believers to bear it with honour.
vv: But rejoice insofar as you are sharing Christ’s sufferings
The Christian does not seek suffering, but when it comes for Christ’s sake, it is a sharing in his own Passion.
Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.
What the world counts shame, faith counts glory.
let those suffering in accordance with God’s will entrust themselves to a faithful Creator, while continuing to do good.
Two things: trust God, and keep doing good. Martyrs do not curse their persecutors.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith: the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473). The Church has carefully kept the records of those who gave their lives for Christ (CCC 2474).

r.h: Sheep among wolves
set: Jesus has chosen the Twelve and is sending them out on mission (10:1–15). In this part of his instructions he looks further ahead, to the persecutions his disciples will face before councils, governors and kings.
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves: wise as serpents, innocent as doves.
vv. 17–18: they will be handed over and brought before governors and kings as a testimony.
vv. 19–20: do not worry what to say; the Spirit of your Father will speak.
vv. 21–22: division in families; hated for my name; the one who endures will be saved.
kw: Prudent, shrewd in practical matters. The disciple is not naive; he uses good sense.
Literally “unmixed”, without any blend of guile. Prudence must never become cunning.
vv: so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.

St Thomas More used every legal means to avoid giving the king grounds to condemn him, and kept silent where he could; but he would not take an oath against his conscience. That is the serpent and the dove together.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
Many martyrs, simple people among them, have answered their judges with a wisdom that was not their own.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Endurance is not mere stubbornness. It is faithfulness kept to the end, by grace.
ch: The Church sees this promise fulfilled in the martyrs of every age. St John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, and St Thomas More, Lord Chancellor of England, refused the oath demanded by King Henry VIII, which implied rejecting the authority of the Pope, and would not accept the king as supreme head of the Church in England. Fisher was beheaded on 22 June 1535 and More on 6 July. They were canonised together in 1935, and in 2000 St John Paul II declared St Thomas More patron of statesmen and politicians.

rite: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More are saints of the whole Church, and their witness speaks to every Catholic in public life. In our own day many Christians in many lands suffer for their faith; we pray for them, and for those who wrong them, as the martyrs themselves prayed. Thomas More is said to have declared on the scaffold that he died the king’s good servant, but God’s first.
study: Paul says, “we walk by faith, not by sight.” Where in my life do I most need to walk by faith right now?
Thomas More was wise as a serpent and innocent as a dove. How can I be faithful to my conscience at work or in public life without being either naive or cunning?

lead: Paul tells the Corinthians that his boast is a clear conscience: he has dealt with them sincerely, by the grace of God and not by worldly cleverness. In Luke, a woman lights a lamp and sweeps her house until she finds one lost coin, and Jesus says there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents. An honest heart before God, and a God who searches for the lost: the two readings belong together.

r.h: The testimony of our conscience
set: Second Corinthians is the most personal of Paul’s letters. Relations with the church at Corinth had been strained: Paul had changed his travel plans (1:15–2:1), and some accused him of being unreliable, saying yes and no at the same time (1:17). Before answering the charge he appeals to his conscience and to their own knowledge of him.
str: v. 12: Paul’s boast: the testimony of his conscience; he has acted with sincerity by God’s grace.
vv. 13–14: he writes plainly; on the day of the Lord they will be each other’s boast.
v. 15: his first plan: to visit them twice, for a double favour.
kw: Paul uses the word family of boasting more in this letter than anywhere else. He refuses to boast in himself, but he may boast in what God’s grace has done (10:17).
Purity of motive, transparency. Paul has no hidden agenda; what he writes is what he means.
vv: Indeed, this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: we have behaved in the world with frankness and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God

Ancient manuscripts differ here: some read “frankness” (or simplicity), others “holiness”. NRSV follows the first; the Malayalam POC follows the second. Either way, Paul credits his good conduct to God’s grace, not to his own cleverness.
that on the day of the Lord Jesus we are your boast even as you are our boast.
Paul looks at the quarrel in the light of the last day. In the end, pastor and people will be each other’s joy before Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that conscience is a person’s most secret core and sanctuary, where he is alone with God, whose voice echoes in his depths (CCC 1776, quoting Gaudium et Spes 16). A good and pure conscience is enlightened by true faith (CCC 1794). Paul’s example shows that a clear conscience is not self-praise: it comes from living before God by grace.

r.h: The lost coin
set: Luke 15 begins with tax collectors and sinners coming near to listen to Jesus, and Pharisees and scribes grumbling that he welcomes sinners and eats with them (15:1–2). Jesus answers with three parables of the lost: a sheep, a coin and a son. This is the shortest of the three, and the only one with a woman at its centre.
str: v. 8: a woman loses one of ten silver coins, lights a lamp, sweeps and searches.
v. 9: she finds it and calls her friends to rejoice.
v. 10: so there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents.
kw: A Greek silver coin, worth roughly a day’s wage. Ten of them were a large sum for a poor household; some think they may have been her savings or part of her dowry.
The finder cannot rejoice alone; joy calls for companions. Heaven rejoices with God over every sinner found.
vv: does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?
A village house had few windows and a floor of beaten earth. Finding a small coin meant light, effort and patience. God searches for us with the same care.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
The coin does nothing to be found; the woman does everything. Repentance is our part, but it begins with God’s search.
ch: St Gregory the Great saw the woman as the Wisdom of God: the lamp is the light of Christ shining in the clay vessel of his humanity, and the house is swept as the conscience is stirred, until the lost image of God in man is found again (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 34). The Catechism turns to the third parable of this chapter, the prodigal son, to describe conversion and the Father’s joy at the return (CCC 1439).

qa: Why does Jesus use a woman in this parable?

Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Simeon and Anna, the man with the mustard seed and the woman with the yeast (13:18–21), the shepherd and the woman here. Jesus speaks to every listener from ordinary life. The searching shepherd and the searching woman both show how God seeks the lost.
study: Paul could appeal to the testimony of his conscience. Is there any matter in which my conscience is not at peace, and what step would bring it peace?
The woman lit a lamp and swept until she found the coin. Who is someone I could seek out this week with that kind of patience?

lead: Today the Church celebrates the birth of John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ. The four readings form a portrait of the prophet he would become. Nathan stands before King David and says, “You are the man!”: the courage that John would show before Herod (Mark 6:18). Jeremiah hears that God knew him before he was formed in the womb and consecrated him before he was born: the call that John received while still in Elizabeth’s womb (Luke 1:15, 41). Paul says that when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son: John stands at that threshold, the last of the prophets and the first to point to the Lamb. And in Luke, the neighbours ask, “What then will this child become?”

The key words are name, womb and time. God names John before his parents do; God forms and calls his prophets from the womb; and God chooses the time. John’s whole life will say what his name means: the Lord has shown favour.

r.h: You are the man!
set: Chapter 11 tells how King David, at the height of his power, took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and when she conceived, arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle against the Ammonites. The chapter ends: “the thing that David had done displeased the Lord” (11:27). Now the Lord sends the prophet Nathan.

Nathan had earlier brought David the promise of an everlasting dynasty (7:1–17). The same prophet who announced God’s blessing now announces God’s judgment. In Israel the king was not above God’s law, and the prophet was the voice that reminded him.
str: vv. 1–4: Nathan’s parable: the rich man, the poor man and his one ewe lamb.
vv. 5–6: David’s anger: the man deserves to die; he must restore fourfold.
v. 7a: “You are the man!”
vv. 7b–9: the Lord recalls his gifts to David and names his crimes.
v. 10: the sentence: the sword shall never depart from your house.
kw: A female lamb. Nathan says it was “like a daughter” to the poor man: the lamb stands for Uriah’s wife, cherished by her husband and taken by the king. The story leads David to judge the case before he knows it is his own.
Two words in Hebrew. The parable’s trap closes. David has pronounced sentence on himself.
The Lord says David “despised” his word (v. 9) and “despised” the Lord himself (v. 10). Sin against a neighbour is contempt for God.
vv: but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought.
Nathan’s details are tender on purpose: the lamb drank from the poor man’s cup and lay in his bosom “like a daughter”. The story wakes David’s pity before it wakes his conscience.
he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity.
David applies the law of Exodus 22:1, which required fourfold restitution for a stolen sheep. Zacchaeus will promise the same (Luke 19:8).
Nathan said to David, “You are the man!
A prophet’s courage in four words. Nathan risks his life, as John the Baptist would when he told Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18).
Why have you despised the word of the Lord, to do what is evil in his sight?
Adultery and murder are named plainly. God’s word does not excuse the powerful.
ch: The Catechism uses Nathan’s parable to teach about the tenth commandment: envy and greed can lead to the worst crimes, and Nathan’s story moved David to repentance (CCC 2538). Immediately after this reading David confesses, “I have sinned against the Lord” (12:13), and the Church’s tradition links Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance, with this moment. St Ambrose, writing to the Emperor Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390, urged him to repent as David had done when Nathan rebuked him; the emperor did public penance (in substance, Letter 51). The prophet’s duty to speak the truth to power continued in John the Baptist, and continues in the Church.

r.h: Before I formed you in the womb
set: Jeremiah was called in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (1:2), about 627 BC, and prophesied until after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. He came from a priestly family of Anathoth, a village a few kilometres north of Jerusalem (1:1). His ministry was one of the hardest in the Old Testament: he was mocked, beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern.

This reading gives his call (vv. 4–10) and the Lord’s promise of strength for the conflicts ahead (vv. 16–19). The verses between, two visions of an almond branch and a boiling pot (vv. 11–15), are omitted.
str: vv. 4–5: the Lord’s word: known, consecrated and appointed before birth.
vv. 6–8: Jeremiah’s objection, “I am only a boy”, and the Lord’s answer: go, speak, do not fear.
vv. 9–10: the Lord touches his mouth and gives him authority over nations.
vv. 16–19: judgment on idolatry; Jeremiah must stand firm, made a fortified city, iron pillar and bronze wall.
kw: More than information: to know someone personally, to choose and care for them. God’s knowledge of Jeremiah came before his body existed.
To set apart as holy for God. Jeremiah was dedicated to his mission before he could choose it.
A young man, not yet old enough to speak with authority among the elders. Jeremiah pleads his youth; God answers with his presence.
vv: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
Three verbs, all before birth. The verb “formed” is the potter’s word used of the forming of Adam (Genesis 2:7).
Then I said, “Ah, Lord God! Truly I do not know how to speak, for I am only a boy.”
Like Moses (Exodus 4:10), Jeremiah feels unequal to the task. God does not deny his weakness; he promises to be with him.
Now I have put my words in your mouth.
The prophet speaks not his own words but God’s. This is why John the Baptist could call himself only “the voice” (John 1:23).
to pluck up and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.
Four verbs of tearing down, two of building up. Judgment is never God’s last word; it clears the ground for planting.
They will fight against you; but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you.
The promise is not that there will be no fight, but that God will be with him in it.
ch: The Catechism quotes Jeremiah 1:5 in teaching that human life must be respected and protected from the moment of conception: God knows and loves each person from the womb (CCC 2270). The liturgy applies these words to John the Baptist, who was filled with the Holy Spirit even before his birth (Luke 1:15). The Catechism says that John was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, and that in him the Holy Spirit completes his speaking through the prophets (CCC 717, 719). Many Fathers held that John was sanctified before birth when he leapt for joy at Mary’s greeting (Luke 1:41, 44); this is why the Church keeps his birthday as a feast, as she does for Christ and for the Virgin Mary.

r.h: When the fullness of time had come
set: The Galatians, Gentile converts in central Asia Minor, were being urged by some teachers to accept circumcision and the observance of the Mosaic law in order to be full members of God’s people. Paul insists that they have already received everything through faith in Christ and the gift of the Spirit (3:1–5).

In 3:23–29 Paul compared the law to a paidagōgos, the household slave who supervised a child until he came of age. Here he develops the picture: an heir who is a minor is no better off than a slave, until the day his father sets.
str: vv. 1–2: the picture: an heir who is a minor lives under guardians until the date set by his father.
v. 3: so we were enslaved to the elemental spirits of the world.
vv. 4–5: when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem and adopt.
vv. 6–7: God sent the Spirit of his Son, crying “Abba! Father!”; so you are a child and an heir.
kw: Time pictured as a vessel filled up to the brim. The coming of Christ is not an accident of history but the moment God appointed.
the elemental spirits of the world
