The word means the basic elements of something, like letters of the alphabet or the elements of nature. Scholars debate whether Paul means the elementary principles of religion or the spiritual powers people thought ruled the world. Either way, it is a slavery from which Christ delivers us.
A legal term in the Roman world for taking someone as a son with full rights of inheritance. Through the Son we become children of God by grace.
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law
This is probably the earliest mention of Jesus’ mother in the New Testament, though she is not named. The Son was truly human, born as we are, and truly a Jew, living under the law of Moses.
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
God “sent his Son” (v. 4) and “sent the Spirit of his Son” (v. 6): the two sendings that make us children of the Father. Abba is the Aramaic word Jesus himself used in prayer (Mark 14:36).
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
Paul switches to “you” singular. Each believer is addressed personally: you are a child of God.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of Mary: God sent forth his Son, but to prepare a body for him he wanted the willing co-operation of a creature (CCC 488). It quotes verse 6 to show that the Holy Spirit, sent into our hearts, makes us cry “Abba! Father!” and so teaches us to pray as children (CCC 683, 742). John the Baptist stands at the edge of the fullness of time: the last prophet under the law, who sees the Son and points to him.

r.h: His name is John
set: Luke tells the births of John and Jesus side by side: two annunciations (1:5–25 and 1:26–38), the meeting of the two mothers (1:39–56), and two births (1:57–80 and 2:1–21). The pattern shows both the likeness and the difference: John is great, but Jesus is greater.

Zechariah, a priest, had been struck mute when he doubted the angel’s promise of a son in his old age (1:18–20). Elizabeth had been barren. The angel had said that the child was to be named John and that many would rejoice at his birth (1:13–14). Now that word is fulfilled.
str: vv. 57–58: Elizabeth gives birth; neighbours and relatives rejoice at the Lord’s mercy.
vv. 59–61: on the eighth day, at the circumcision, they want to name him Zechariah; Elizabeth says, “No; he is to be called John.”
vv. 62–63: Zechariah writes on a tablet: “His name is John.”
v. 64: his mouth is opened, and he praises God.
vv. 65–66: fear and wonder through the hill country: “What then will this child become?”
kw: The Hebrew name means “the Lord has been gracious” or “the Lord has shown favour”. The name itself announces the time of grace that is beginning.
The neighbours hear that the Lord “had shown his great mercy” to Elizabeth. Mercy is a key word of Luke’s first chapter, sung by Mary (1:50, 54) and by Zechariah (1:72, 78).
A small wooden tablet, often coated with wax, on which one wrote with a stylus. Zechariah cannot speak, so he writes.
vv: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
The angel’s promise is fulfilled: “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14). The Church still rejoices on this day.
But his mother said, “No; he is to be called John.”
Elizabeth already knows the name. Luke does not say how; perhaps Zechariah had written it for her, or perhaps the Spirit who filled her at the Visitation (1:41) had made it known.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And all of them were amazed.
Zechariah does not write ‘His name shall be John’, but “His name is John”. The name was given by God; he only obeys. His obedience opens his mouth.
Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue freed, and he began to speak, praising God.
His first words after months of silence are praise. The song he sings, the Benedictus, follows in 1:68–79.
All who heard them pondered them and said, “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
“The hand of the Lord” in the Old Testament is God’s power at work in his chosen ones. The question is answered in 1:76: “you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High.”
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord’s immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way: “prophet of the Most High”, he surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last (CCC 523). St Augustine notes that the Church celebrates the birthday of only two persons in this way, John and Christ (in substance, Sermons on the Nativity of John). He also saw a sign in the seasons: John’s birth is kept as the days begin to grow shorter, and Christ’s as they begin to grow longer, fulfilling John’s word, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

qa: Why does the Church celebrate John’s birth, when for other saints she keeps the day of their death?

For most saints the Church keeps the day of their death, their birth into heaven. John is an exception, with Christ and the Virgin Mary, because his birth itself was holy: he was filled with the Holy Spirit even before birth (Luke 1:15) and leapt for joy in the presence of the Lord (1:41, 44). The Church also remembers his martyrdom on another day.
Why is the feast on 24 June?

The angel told Mary that Elizabeth was in her sixth month (Luke 1:36). The Church therefore keeps John’s birth about six months before Christmas. The date comes from this reckoning, not from any record of the exact day.
Was John the Baptist Jesus’ cousin?

Luke calls Elizabeth Mary’s “relative” (1:36, Greek syngenis), a word for a kinswoman of any degree. So John and Jesus were related, but the Gospel does not say exactly how. ‘Cousin’ is a common way of putting it, but the text says only that they were kin.
rite: In the East Syriac tradition of our Church, John the Baptist has a special place in the season of Denha, when the Church celebrates the Lord’s Baptism in the Jordan and the revelation of the Holy Trinity; the first Friday of Denha is kept in his memory. Today, in the Season of the Apostles, his birth reminds us that every mission begins with God’s call, often long before we know it.

Syro-Malabar families give their children the names of saints at baptism, and many of our people bear the name of John. Like Elizabeth and Zechariah, Christian parents receive each child as God’s gift, knowing that the child’s life belongs first to him. The question of the neighbours is the question we ask at every baptism: “What then will this child become?”
study: Nathan risked his life to tell the king the truth. Is there a truth I need to hear about myself, or one I should lovingly speak to another?
God said to Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.” How does this change the way I see myself, and every unborn child?
Paul says that because we are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying “Abba! Father!” How can I pray more as a child of God this week?
Zechariah’s mouth was opened when he obeyed. Is there an act of obedience to God that I have been putting off?

lead: Both readings ask what a Christian owes to the state, and both answer by placing the state under God. Paul tells the Christians in Rome that every lawful authority has its place from God and serves the common good, so taxes and obedience are a matter of conscience. In Matthew, Jesus is asked a trap question about the Roman tax; he asks whose image is on the coin, and gives an answer that has guided the Church ever since: give the emperor what is his, and give God what is God’s. The coin bears Caesar’s image; the human person bears God’s.

r.h: There is no authority except from God
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, to a Church he had not yet visited. Nero was emperor, in the calm early years of his reign. The Christians of Rome were a small group with no power, some of them Jews who had been expelled under Claudius and had returned (Acts 18:2). The Roman historian Tacitus reports loud complaints in the city about indirect taxes around AD 58. Paul has just told his readers not to repay evil for evil and to leave vengeance to God (12:17–21). Now he speaks of the ruler who punishes wrongdoing as God’s servant for the common good.
str: vv. 1–2: every person should be subject; all authority comes from God; to resist it is to resist God’s order.
vv. 3–4: rulers exist to restrain evil and encourage good; the authority is “God’s servant for your good”.
v. 5: obey not only from fear of punishment but for the sake of conscience.
v. 6: this is also why you pay taxes.
kw: Literally “to place oneself under”, to accept one’s place in an order. It is not blind obedience to anything a ruler commands, but respect for the order that God wills for life in society.
Paul calls the civil authority by the same word he uses for ministers of the Gospel. The ruler is a servant, not a master, and he is accountable to God for the good of the people.
The inner judgment by which a person knows right and wrong before God. Paul grounds civic duty in conscience; the same conscience can also tell a Christian when a command must be refused (Acts 5:29).
vv: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities; for there is no authority except from God
Paul does not say that every ruler is good, but that authority as such belongs to God’s plan for human life together. Rulers receive their power in trust.
for it is God’s servant for your good.
Here is the measure of all authority: the good of those it serves. An authority that works against the good of its people departs from its own purpose.
Therefore one must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.
A Christian is an honest citizen even when no one is watching, because he obeys God.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches that every human community needs an authority, and that authority has its source in God (CCC 1897–1899). It adds that authority is exercised legitimately only when it seeks the common good by morally lawful means; if rulers enact unjust laws, these do not bind in conscience (CCC 1903). Citizens owe rulers respect, taxes and a share in the common good (CCC 2238–2240), and they are obliged in conscience not to follow civil commands that are contrary to the moral order, for “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (CCC 2242; Acts 5:29). Paul himself, who wrote these lines, was later put to death under the same emperor, faithful to Christ to the end.

r.h: Whose head is this?
set: Jesus is in the Temple in Jerusalem during his last days before the Passion. After three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14), they try to trap him. Two groups who were usually opposed join together: some disciples of the Pharisees, who resented Roman rule, and the Herodians, supporters of the house of Herod, who depended on Rome. The tax in question was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, a sore sign of foreign rule. If Jesus said “Pay it”, he could lose the people; if he said “Do not pay”, he could be reported to the governor as a rebel.
str: vv. 15–17: the plot and the flattering question: is it lawful to pay the tax to the emperor?
vv. 18–19: Jesus sees their malice and asks for the coin.
vv. 20–21: “Whose head is this?” “The emperor’s.” Give to the emperor and give to God.
v. 22: they are amazed and go away.
kw: From the Latin census: the tax counted per head. It had to be paid in Roman coin.

The silver denarius of Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. The word is the one used in the Greek Old Testament for man made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27).
Not simply “give” but “give back”, pay what is owed. The coin already belongs to Caesar; the person already belongs to God.
vv: Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and teach the way of God in accordance with truth
The flattery is meant to push him into a dangerous answer. Yet what they say is true, more true than they know.
Show me the coin used for the tax.
Jesus does not carry the coin himself; his questioners produce it, in the Temple. Their own pockets give the answer.
Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.
The two halves are not equal. Caesar may claim coins; God claims the whole person. The state has a real place, but it is not God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this saying when it teaches the duty of citizens and its limit: when the commands of civil authority are contrary to the moral order, the citizen must refuse, for one must give to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (CCC 2242). Tertullian drew out the meaning of the image: give the coin with Caesar’s image to Caesar, and give to God yourself, who bear God’s image (in substance, On Idolatry 15). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the political community and the Church are independent in their own fields, yet both serve the same human persons (Gaudium et Spes 76).

qa: Does Romans 13 mean Christians must obey any government, even a cruel one?

No. Paul describes what authority is for: to reward good and restrain evil. The Church teaches that laws contrary to the moral order do not bind in conscience, and that citizens must refuse commands that go against God’s law (CCC 1903, 2242). The apostles themselves told the council in Jerusalem, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29). Christians obey lawful authority out of conscience, and for the same reason they may not obey it in what is evil.
study: Paul calls the ruler “God’s servant for your good”. How can I pray for and support those who govern, and also help them serve the common good?
If the coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image, what does it mean that I bear God’s image? What in my life have I not yet given back to God?

lead: Both readings are about true and false teachers. Paul fears that the Corinthians, betrothed to Christ, will be led astray by smooth preachers who bring “another Jesus”. In John, Jesus teaches in the Temple, and the people wonder where his learning comes from; he answers that his teaching is not his own but the Father’s, and asks them to judge rightly, not by appearances. The test of a teacher is not eloquence or credentials but whether he seeks the glory of the One who sent him.

r.h: Betrothed to one husband
set: Chapters 10–13 of 2 Corinthians are Paul’s sharpest words to this Church. Since his last letter, preachers have arrived at Corinth who boast of their speaking skill and of letters of recommendation, and who look down on Paul as weak and unimpressive in person (10:10). Paul calls them, with irony, “super-apostles”. To defend the Gospel he must now speak about himself, which he calls a kind of foolishness.
str: v. 1: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness.
vv. 2–3: his divine jealousy: he has betrothed them to Christ and fears they will be seduced as Eve was.
v. 4: they accept another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel all too easily.
vv. 5–6: he is not inferior to the super-apostles; untrained in speech, but not in knowledge.
kw: The jealousy of God himself, who loves his people as a husband loves his bride and will not share them with idols (Hosea 2:19–20). Paul shares God’s own protective love for the Church.

In Jewish custom the betrothal was already binding; the bride was then led to the bridegroom’s house. Paul sees himself as the friend who arranged the betrothal and must present the bride faithful on the wedding day, the Lord’s coming.
Literally “the over-much apostles”. Paul mocks their self-importance. True apostleship is measured by faithfulness to Christ crucified, not by impressive speech.
vv: I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
The whole Church, and each soul, is the bride of Christ. Faithfulness to the Gospel is faithfulness in love.
as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
Error rarely comes as plain evil. Like the serpent, it comes with clever words and makes the truth seem small.
I may be untrained in speech, but not in knowledge
Paul may have lacked the polished style that the Greeks admired, but he did not lack the knowledge of Christ. The Gospel does not depend on rhetoric.
ch: The Catechism draws on this verse when it teaches that the Church is the bride of Christ: the Apostle speaks of the whole Church and of each of the faithful as a bride betrothed to Christ the Lord, to become one spirit with him (CCC 796). The Church has always heard in Paul’s fear a warning against changing the Gospel: there is not “another Jesus”, but the one handed on by the apostles. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, notes that Paul calls his concern jealousy because it burns with love for them, not for himself (in substance, Homilies on 2 Corinthians).

r.h: My teaching is not mine
set: Jesus has gone up to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 10), the joyful autumn harvest feast when people lived in shelters made of branches. Opinions about him are divided, and the authorities are seeking to kill him (7:1). In the middle of the feast he teaches openly in the Temple. The “one work” he speaks of is the healing of the man at the pool of Bethesda on a sabbath (5:1–18), which had first stirred the authorities against him.
str: vv. 14–15: Jesus teaches in the Temple; they wonder at his learning.
vv. 16–18: his teaching comes from the Father; whoever wants to do God’s will will recognize it.
vv. 19–20: none of you keeps the law; why seek to kill me? The crowd: “You have a demon!”
vv. 21–24: the argument from circumcision on the sabbath; judge with right judgment.
kw: Literally “letters”: the learning of one trained under a teacher of the Law. Jesus had not studied in a rabbinic school, yet he taught with authority.
Jesus does not claim a teaching of his own invention. As the Son he speaks what he has received from the Father (12:49).
Literally “according to the face”, by what is seen on the surface. Right judgment looks to the purpose of the Law and the heart of God.
vv: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.
This is not modesty but a statement of who he is. The Son’s teaching is the Father’s teaching, because the Son is one with the Father (10:30).
Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God
Knowing the truth about Christ is not only a matter of study. Those who set themselves to obey God come to recognize his voice.
If a man receives circumcision on the sabbath in order that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I healed a man’s whole body on the sabbath?

A boy is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3) even if it falls on a sabbath; later Jewish teachers also recorded this rule. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if one rite of the covenant may be done on the sabbath, how much more may a whole person be made well.
Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.
The words are for every age. We easily judge by outward signs; God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
ch: St Augustine asks how the teaching can be both “mine” and “not mine”, and answers that the Son is himself the Word of the Father: what is the Father’s teaching but the Word? He also takes verse 17 as a rule for faith: understanding is the reward of faith; do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe so that you may understand (in substance, Tractates on John 29). In John, “the Jews” in verse 15 means the Temple authorities and their circle in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as such; Jesus, his disciples and the crowd were all Jews, and the Church warns against any reading that blames the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

study: Paul fears that the Corinthians may accept “another Jesus”. What images of Jesus in today’s culture differ from the Jesus of the Gospel and the Church?
Jesus says, “Do not judge by appearances.” Whom have I judged by appearances this week, and how can I look again with right judgment?

lead: This Sunday’s four readings speak of hearing God and of a door. In Deuteronomy, Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb they heard the voice of God out of the fire, though they saw no form, and received the ten commandments to live by. In Isaiah, the prophet cries woe on those who heard the same law and ignored it: those who swallow up the land of the poor, who feast without regard for the Lord, who call evil good and good evil; yet the Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness. Paul, closing his first letter to Corinth, arranges a weekly collection for the poor of Jerusalem, speaks of a wide door opened for the Gospel, and sums up everything in one line: let all that you do be done in love. And in Luke, Jesus is asked whether only a few will be saved, and answers: strive to enter through the narrow door. The God who spoke at Horeb still speaks; to hear him is to enter by the narrow door of love and justice, and that door is open to people from east and west, north and south.

r.h: You heard the sound of words but saw no form
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses’ last words to Israel in the plains of Moab, before they cross the Jordan. In chapter 4 he ends his first great speech with an urgent call to keep the law. He takes the people back in memory to Horeb, the name Deuteronomy gives to Sinai, so that a new generation may stand there in spirit, as if they themselves had been present.

These verses lead straight into the warning that follows: since you saw no form on the day the Lord spoke to you, do not make an idol in the shape of any creature (4:15–19). Israel meets God first as a voice that speaks and commands, not as an image to be looked at.
str: v. 10: remember the day at Horeb: “Assemble the people for me,” so that they learn to fear me and teach their children.
v. 11: the mountain blazing to the heavens, wrapped in dark cloud.
v. 12: the Lord spoke out of the fire; you heard words but saw no form.
v. 13: he declared his covenant, the ten commandments, written on two tablets of stone.
v. 14: Moses is charged to teach the statutes for life in the land.
kw: The key word of the passage. God is known at Horeb by what he says. Faith begins in hearing: “Hear, O Israel” (6:4).
Any visible shape. Israel saw none, so no image could stand for the Lord. This is the ground of the prohibition of idols in the next verses.
The Hebrew name for the ten commandments (also 10:4). They are words spoken by God to his people, the terms of a covenant of love, before they are rules.
vv: Assemble the people for me, and I will let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me as long as they live on the earth, and may teach their children so
Revelation is given to an assembly, and it is meant to be handed on in the family. Parents are the first teachers of the faith.
Then the Lord spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of words but saw no form; there was only a voice.
The fire shows God’s holiness; the voice shows his nearness. He does not remain silent behind the cloud.
He declared to you his covenant, which he charged you to observe, that is, the ten commandments; and he wrote them on two stone tablets.
The covenant is not an idea but a way of life. God himself writes it, as later he will write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
ch: The Catechism quotes Deuteronomy 4 when it explains the commandment against idols: God revealed himself at Horeb without any form, so that his people would not make a carved image of him (CCC 2129). It then explains why Christians may venerate images: by becoming man, the Son of God has introduced a new economy of images, and the honour paid to an image passes to the one it represents (CCC 2131–2132, following the Second Council of Nicaea). The Letter to the Hebrews contrasts the blazing mountain of Sinai with Mount Zion, where we come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and warns: “See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking” (Hebrews 12:18–25).

r.h: The Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness
set: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ, a time of wealth for the powerful in Judah and of hardship for the poor. Just before this passage stands the Song of the Vineyard (5:1–7): God planted Israel like a choice vine and looked for justice, but found bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry. The woes that follow show what that “bloodshed” and “cry” looked like in daily life.

Each woe begins with the Hebrew hôy, the cry of mourning used at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30). The prophet laments those who are already walking toward death. In the land of Israel each family was meant to keep its inheritance, because the land belonged to God (Leviticus 25:23); when the rich bought up field after field, the poor lost not only property but their place in the covenant people.
str: vv. 8–10: first woe: on those who join house to house and field to field; the great houses will be empty, the fields barren.
vv. 11–12: second woe: on those who rise early for strong drink and feast with music, but do not regard the deeds of the Lord.
vv. 13–17: the consequence: exile for want of knowledge; Sheol opens its mouth; the proud are brought low, and the Lord is exalted by justice.
vv. 18–19: third woe: on those who drag sin like a cart and mock: let God hurry up and act.
v. 20: fourth woe: on those who call evil good and good evil.
kw: A cry of grief over the dead. These woes are not curses spoken in anger, but the prophet’s mourning over people who are destroying themselves.
The pair that runs through Isaiah: right dealing in the courts and faithful, upright relations in the community. Verse 16 says that God shows his holiness precisely in these.
Holiness in Isaiah is God’s utter otherness and majesty (6:3). But the Holy One is not distant from the poor; his holiness is seen when justice is done.
vv: Ah, you who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is room for no one but you

Greed ends in loneliness. Those who take everything are left “to live alone in the midst of the land.” The prophet Micah raises the same cry (Micah 2:2), and the story of Naboth’s vineyard shows it in action (1 Kings 21).
For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield a mere ephah.
A homer was ten ephahs (Ezekiel 45:11), so the harvest will be a tenth of the seed sown. The land taken by injustice will not feed its new owners.
whose feasts consist of lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine, but who do not regard the deeds of the Lord
Isaiah does not condemn music or celebration, but feasting that forgets God and the poor.
But the Lord of hosts is exalted by justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness.
The centre of the passage. God’s holiness is not shown by pomp but by setting things right.
Ah, you who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness
The last woe is the deepest: when a people changes the names of good and evil, conscience itself is darkened.
ch: The Church hears in Isaiah’s first woe her teaching on the universal destination of goods: the earth is entrusted to all humankind, and the right to private property does not abolish this original common destination (CCC 2402–2403). Pope St John Paul II quoted verse 20 in Evangelium Vitae (1995), warning that when conscience is darkened a society comes to call evil good and good evil, above all in matters of human life (in substance, Evangelium Vitae 24). St Basil the Great, preaching against greed, asked the rich man how he could call his own what he had received to share (in substance, Homily on “I will pull down my barns”).

r.h: Let all that you do be done in love
set: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, probably around AD 54–55. Now, at its close, he turns to practical matters: the collection for the poor Christians of Jerusalem, his travel plans, and the visits of Timothy and Apollos.

The collection was very dear to Paul. When Paul met the leaders of the Church in Jerusalem, they asked him to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10), and he gathered gifts from the Churches of Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia (2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–27). For him it was more than relief: it was a sign that Gentile and Jewish Christians are one Body, and that the Gentiles, who had received spiritual blessings from Jerusalem, now share with Jerusalem in return.
str: vv. 1–4: the collection for the saints: set aside something on the first day of every week; approved messengers will carry it to Jerusalem.
vv. 5–9: Paul’s plans: through Macedonia to Corinth; but first Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door has opened.
vv. 10–12: Timothy and Apollos: receive Timothy without fear; Apollos will come later.
vv. 13–14: closing charge: keep alert, stand firm, be courageous, be strong; let all be done in love.
kw: A word used in everyday Greek for a gathering of money. Paul also calls it koinōnia, sharing, and charis, grace (2 Corinthians 8:4, 6). Giving is a share in God’s own gift.
on the first day of the week
Sunday, the day of the Lord’s resurrection. This is among the earliest witnesses that Christians already marked that day, as when they met to break bread at Troas (Acts 20:7).
A door for the Gospel, an opportunity opened by God (also 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3). Paul sees both the open door and the many adversaries.
vv: On the first day of every week, each of you is to put aside and save whatever extra you earn
Giving is regular, personal and in proportion to what one has. It is joined to the Lord’s Day.
for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
Opportunity and opposition often come together. Paul does not wait for an easy road before walking through the door God opens.
Keep alert, stand firm in your faith, be courageous, be strong.
Four short commands, like a soldier’s orders. “Be courageous” translates a verb meaning “act like grown men”: a mature and steady faith.
Let all that you do be done in love.
One line sums up the whole letter, with its hymn of love in chapter 13. Collections, plans and courage are worth nothing without love (13:3).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Christian assembly on Sunday goes back to the beginnings of the apostolic age (CCC 2178), and it links Sunday with works of mercy and care for the poor (CCC 2186). St Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around AD 150, describes the Sunday Eucharist and adds that those who are well off give what they wish, and the gift is kept by the one who presides to help orphans, widows, the sick and prisoners (in substance, First Apology 67). Paul’s collection lives on wherever the faithful give for the poor of another Church.

r.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
set: Since 9:51 Jesus has been on his long journey to Jerusalem, where he will suffer. Luke reminds us of it here (v. 22). Along the way he teaches about the Kingdom, and just before this he has told the small parables of the mustard seed and the yeast (13:18–21): the Kingdom begins small and grows.
Someone now asks a question that people debated in that age: will only a few be saved? Jesus does not answer with a number. He turns the question from “how many?” to “what about you?”
str: vv. 22–23: on the way to Jerusalem; the question: will only a few be saved?
v. 24: strive to enter through the narrow door; many will try and not be able.
vv. 25–27: the owner shuts the door; those outside knock: “We ate and drank with you”; “I do not know where you come from.”
vv. 28–29: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets in the Kingdom; people come from east and west, north and south.
v. 30: the last will be first, and the first last.
kw: From the word for an athletic contest, the root of our word “agony”. Entering the Kingdom asks for effort and perseverance, not a casual wish.
Not a door that keeps people out, but one that is entered one by one, without the baggage of pride. Christ himself says, “I am the gate” (John 10:9).
The master of the house who gives the banquet. In the parables he stands for God, or for Christ, who will one day close the door.
vv: Someone asked him, “Lord, will only a few be saved?”
The question is about other people. Jesus will not satisfy curiosity; he speaks to the heart of the one asking.
Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
There is still time now; the door is open. But it will not stay open forever. Today is the day to enter.
We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.
Being near Jesus outwardly is not enough. Knowing about him, even sharing his table, must become a life of doing what he says.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.
The banquet of the nations foretold by the prophets (Isaiah 25:6) will be full. The narrow door leads to a very wide table.
Indeed, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.
No one can presume on his place. Grace overturns our rankings.
ch: The Catechism quotes the Lord’s words on the narrow way when it teaches about the final destiny of the human person: they are a call to responsibility and conversion, for each of us must use our freedom with a view to our eternal destiny (CCC 1036). It teaches too that God predestines no one to go to hell, and that the Church prays that no one should be lost (CCC 1037, 1058). The Kingdom, first announced to the children of Israel, is meant to welcome people of all nations (CCC 543). The Second Vatican Council teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ, but seek God sincerely and try to do his will known through conscience, may attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16). The warning in verses 26–27 is addressed to everyone who is close to the Lord outwardly; the Church reads it first as a word to herself.

qa: Will only a few be saved?

Jesus does not give a number, and the Church does not either. The Church teaches that God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), that Christ died for all, and that God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). At the same time, salvation is not automatic: we must freely accept God’s grace and persevere. Jesus’ answer is meant for each listener: do not count others; strive to enter yourself.
Since Israel saw no form at Horeb, are images in our churches wrong?

Deuteronomy forbids making an image to worship as God, because God is invisible. But in Christ the invisible God has become visible: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The Second Council of Nicaea (787) taught that Christians may honour images of Christ, Mary and the saints, because the honour passes to the person represented (CCC 2131–2132). We do not worship an image; we worship God alone.
Is Isaiah against owning houses and fields?

No. The law of Israel protected each family’s land as its inheritance, and the Church defends the right to private property (CCC 2403). Isaiah condemns greed that swallows up the land of others until the poor have no place. The Church teaches that property is held in stewardship, with care for the common good (CCC 2404).
rite: In the Season of the Apostles our Church remembers the apostles’ mission to the nations, and we recall that Mar Thoma Shleeha opened a wide door for the Gospel in our land. Paul’s Sunday collection for the poor of another Church lives on in the offerings of Syro-Malabar parishes and eparchies for missions in India and abroad, and for the poor among us.

In the Holy Qurbana we too stand before the Lord who speaks: the readings are proclaimed, and we hear his voice, as Israel did at Horeb. Then we are fed at the table where people come from east and west. The narrow door is entered by a life of love; Paul’s words, “Let all that you do be done in love,” are a good rule to take home from the altar.
study: At Horeb Israel heard God’s voice and was told to teach their children. How is God’s word handed on in my family?
Isaiah mourns over those who “call evil good and good evil”. Where do I see this in my own world, and where am I tempted to do it myself?
Paul asks for a gift set aside on the first day of every week. How do I join my Sunday with generosity to the poor?
Jesus answers the question “Will only a few be saved?” by saying “Strive to enter.” What would striving to enter the narrow door mean for me this week?

lead: The weekday readings speak of mercy and of signs. Paul asks the Corinthians to forgive a member who has hurt the community, so that he is not overwhelmed by sorrow and Satan gains nothing. In Matthew, Jesus refuses a sign on demand and points to the sign of Jonah: his own death and resurrection, and a call to repent. Today the Church also keeps the memory of St Irenaeus of Lyons, bishop, whose name means “peace”, and offers readings for him: the high priest who bears Israel’s names on his heart, the priest whose lips guard knowledge, the apostolic teaching handed on to Timothy, and the Spirit who reminds the Church of all that Jesus said. Irenaeus guarded that teaching against error and worked for peace in the Church.

r.h: Forgive and console him
set: Paul had made a painful visit to Corinth, during which someone seems to have wronged or openly defied him, and he then wrote a letter “with many tears” (2:4). The community responded and disciplined the offender. Now Paul says the punishment is enough. Older interpreters, among them several Fathers, thought this was the man of 1 Corinthians 5; many scholars today think rather of someone who opposed Paul during that visit. Either way, the point is the same: discipline must lead to healing.
str: vv. 5–6: the offender hurt the whole community; the punishment by the majority is enough.
vv. 7–8: now forgive and console him; reaffirm your love.
vv. 9–11: Paul forgives with them, before Christ, so that Satan may not take advantage.
kw: From charis, grace: to forgive is to give freely what is not deserved, as God has done for us in Christ.
The same root as Paraclete. The community must not only stop punishing; it must comfort and restore.
Literally “in the face of Christ”. The Latin Vulgate rendered it in persona Christi, words that later theology used for the priest who acts in the person of Christ.
vv: so now instead you should forgive and console him, so that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Correction that never ends can crush a person. The goal of discipline is to bring the sinner home.
So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.
Forgiveness is not only a decision in the heart; it must be shown in a public act of welcome.
And we do this so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
Satan can use a community’s harshness as easily as its laxity. An unforgiving Church plays into his hands.
ch: The Catechism teaches that reconciliation with the Church is inseparable from reconciliation with God: whomever the Church receives anew into her communion, God will welcome back into his (CCC 1445). This passage shows that pattern in the first generation: the community corrects, then forgives and restores, and the apostle forgives with it. The Church has always held that the purpose of penance is healing and return, not shame.

r.h: Something greater than Jonah
set: Jesus has healed a man who was blind and mute, and some have said he casts out demons by Beelzebul (12:22–24). Now some scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, some proof from heaven that will settle the question. Jesus has already given many signs; what they ask for is a sign that will force belief, on their terms.
str: v. 38: the request: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.”
vv. 39–40: no sign but the sign of Jonah: three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
vv. 41–42: the Ninevites and the queen of the South will rise in judgment; something greater is here.
kw: In the Gospels a sign points beyond itself to God’s action. Jesus refuses signs that are demanded to test him (16:1–4).
The word in the Greek Old Testament for the “large fish” of Jonah 1:17. The point is not the kind of animal but God’s rescue from death.
The Greek is neuter: “something more”. Not only a greater prophet or king is here, but the Kingdom itself, present in Jesus.
vv: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.
In Jewish reckoning part of a day could count as a day, so Friday afternoon to Sunday morning fits “three days”. The sign is the Resurrection.
because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
Pagan Nineveh repented at the word of a reluctant prophet. The warning is to every hearer who has the Gospel and does not turn.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him, but that they are not meant to satisfy curiosity or a desire for magic, and that in spite of his evident miracles some reject him (CCC 548). The Church has always read the sign of Jonah as the Lord’s burial and Resurrection (CCC 994 names the sign of Jonah among the Lord’s announcements of his Resurrection). “This generation” in Matthew is the generation that refuses to believe, in any age; it is not a judgment on the Jewish people, and the first to believe in the Risen Lord were themselves Jews (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: On his heart before the Lord
set: Exodus 28 describes the vestments of Aaron, the high priest. Over his heart he wore the breastpiece, set with twelve precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes (28:15–21). Inside it were kept the Urim and Thummim, sacred lots used to seek God’s decision.
str: v. 28: the breastpiece fastened to the ephod with a blue cord, so that it never comes loose.
v. 29: Aaron bears the names of Israel on his heart as a continual remembrance before the Lord.
v. 30: the Urim and Thummim on his heart: he bears the judgment of Israel before the Lord continually.
kw: A square pouch of woven cloth worn on the chest. It is called “of judgment” because through it God’s decision was sought for the people.
Sacred lots whose exact form is unknown. The words are often explained as “lights and perfections”. They showed that the priest does not decide by himself but seeks God’s will.
vv: So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart when he goes into the holy place, for a continual remembrance before the Lord.
The priest enters God’s presence carrying the people on his heart. A shepherd remembers his flock by name when he prays.
thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the Israelites on his heart before the Lord continually.
“Continually” is said twice. Intercession is not occasional; it is the shape of a priest’s life.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews sees all the priesthood of Aaron fulfilled in Christ, the high priest who “always lives to make intercession” for those who approach God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The Catechism teaches that everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured finds its fulfilment in Christ, the one mediator (CCC 1544). A bishop like Irenaeus shares in that priesthood and carries his people on his heart.

r.h: The lips of a priest should guard knowledge
set: Malachi preached after the return from exile, in the fifth century before Christ, when the Temple had been rebuilt but worship had grown careless. The priests offered blemished animals and taught falsely (1:6–14; 2:8). God reminds them of his covenant with Levi, the ancestor of the priestly tribe, as a picture of what a priest should be.
str: v. 4: the command is given so that the covenant with Levi may stand.
vv. 5–6: a covenant of life and peace; Levi revered God, taught truly and turned many from sin.
v. 7: the priest’s lips guard knowledge; he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.
kw: Here not the written Law alone but the teaching the priest gives the people. True instruction was “in his mouth”.
The same word as the prophet’s name, Malachi, “my messenger”. The priest who teaches truly speaks for God.
vv: True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in integrity and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity.
Teaching and life go together. Levi’s words could turn others because his own walk was upright.
For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.
The priest is a guardian of truth he did not invent. People have a right to sound teaching.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the first task of priests, as co-workers of the bishops, is to proclaim the Gospel of God to all (Presbyterorum Ordinis 4), and that bishops are authentic teachers of the faith (Lumen Gentium 25). Irenaeus lived this verse: he wrote to protect his people from teachings that twisted the Scriptures, setting out the faith received from the apostles.

r.h: Continue in what you have learned
set: The letter presents itself as Paul’s last testament to Timothy, written from prison as his death draws near (4:6). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul’s name, while others hold it is Paul’s own; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. Timothy had learned the faith from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (1:5) and from Paul himself.
str: v. 14: continue in what you have learned, knowing from whom you learned it.
v. 15: from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which lead to salvation through faith in Christ.
vv. 16–17: all scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training.
kw: Literally “God-breathed”. The Scriptures come from the breath, the Spirit, of God, while being truly written by human authors.
The word for the upbringing of a child. Scripture forms a person over a lifetime, not only in moments of study.
vv: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it
Faith is received from trustworthy people. Knowing from whom we learned is part of knowing that it is true.
All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness
At first “scripture” meant what we call the Old Testament. The Church, guided by the Spirit, recognized the apostolic writings with it as one Bible.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse in teaching that the books of Scripture, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, have God as their author, and teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wanted put into writing for our salvation (Dei Verbum 11; CCC 105–107). Irenaeus was a living example of verse 14: as a boy in Asia Minor he heard St Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, and he could say from whom he had learned (in substance, Eusebius, Church History 5.20).

r.h: He will teach you everything
set: At the Last Supper Jesus prepares his disciples for his departure. He promises the Advocate, gives them his peace, and tells them that his going to the Father is reason for joy. The hour of the Passion is near: “the ruler of this world is coming.”
str: v. 26: the Advocate, sent by the Father in my name, will teach you and remind you.
v. 27: my peace I give you, not as the world gives.
vv. 28–29: rejoice that I go to the Father; I tell you before it happens.
v. 30: the ruler of this world is coming; he has no power over me.
kw: One called to stand beside another, to defend, comfort and guide. The Spirit continues Jesus’ own presence with the disciples.
The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel but makes the Church remember and understand what Jesus said.
vv: But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.
Here is the root of the Church’s living Tradition: the Spirit keeps Jesus’ words alive and leads the Church into their depth.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.
The world’s peace depends on the absence of trouble. Christ’s peace remains even in the hour of the Cross.
If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.

The Church reads this in the light of the faith that the Son is equal to the Father. St Augustine explains it of the Son in the form of a servant he took for our sake (in substance, Tractates on John); other Fathers read it of the Father as the source from whom the Son is eternally begotten.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, recalls to the Church all that Christ said and guides her into all truth (CCC 243, 729). St Irenaeus wrote that where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God, and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church and every grace (in substance, Against Heresies 3.24.1). He also called the Son and the Spirit the “two hands” of the Father, by which God forms and saves the human person (in substance, Against Heresies 4, preface; 5.6.1).

qa: Who was St Irenaeus?

He was born in Asia Minor, probably around AD 130–140, and as a youth heard St Polycarp of Smyrna, a disciple of the apostle John. He became a priest at Lyons in Gaul, and after the bishop Pothinus died in the persecution of 177, he succeeded him. His great work, Against Heresies, defended the faith against the Gnostics by appealing to the Scriptures and to the teaching handed down by the bishops in succession from the apostles. When Pope Victor threatened to cut off the Churches of Asia over the date of Easter, Irenaeus urged peace, living up to his name (Eusebius, Church History 5.24). He died around AD 200; later tradition honours him as a martyr, though early sources are silent. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, with the title “Doctor of Unity”.
rite: Irenaeus came from the East and served in the West; he belongs to the whole Church. For Syro-Malabar Catholics, who treasure an apostolic faith received from Mar Thoma Shleeha and kept through the centuries, his teaching is close to home: the faith is known by its apostolic roots and kept in communion. His famous saying, that the glory of God is the human person fully alive (in substance, Against Heresies 4.20.7), is a fitting prayer for every family.
study: Paul asks the Corinthians to forgive and console a man who had hurt them. Is there someone in my family or parish whom I need to welcome back?
Irenaeus could say from whom he had learned the faith. Who handed the faith on to me, and to whom am I handing it on?

lead: On the feast of the two great apostles the readings show the risen life of Christ working through weak human servants. In 2 Kings, the prophet Elisha prays over the dead son of the Shunammite woman, and the child opens his eyes. In Acts, Peter kneels and prays beside the body of Tabitha at Joppa and says, “Tabitha, get up,” and she rises: the power that worked through the prophets and through Jesus now works through his apostle. Paul, defending his ministry, lists his labours, prisons, beatings and shipwrecks, and boasts only of his weakness. And in John, the risen Lord asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and entrusts him with his flock, foretelling the death by which Peter would glorify God. Peter the shepherd and Paul the missionary both gave their lives in Rome. The Church also gives the readings of the Seventh Tuesday of the Apostles, which fit the feast well: love as the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:7–10), and Jesus healing in Peter’s own house (Mark 1:29–34).

r.h: Take your son
set: Elisha succeeded Elijah as prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century before Christ. In Shunem, a village in the Jezreel valley, a wealthy woman had shown him hospitality and built a small upper room for him to stay in (4:8–10). She had no son, and her husband was old. Elisha promised her a son within the year.

The reading tells of the gift, the loss and the restoring of that child. The verses left out (22–31) tell how the mother rode to Elisha at Mount Carmel and would not leave him, and how Elisha’s servant Gehazi laid the prophet’s staff on the child without result. Elijah had raised a widow’s son in a similar way (1 Kings 17:17–24).
str: vv. 16–17: the promise of a son, and his birth “at that season”.
vv. 18–21: the boy falls ill in the harvest field and dies on his mother’s lap; she lays him on the prophet’s bed.
vv. 32–35: Elisha shuts the door, prays, and stretches himself on the child; the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes.
vv. 36–37: “Take your son.” The mother bows and takes him.
kw: The usual title of Elisha in these stories. It means one who belongs to God and speaks and acts with his power.
Elisha does not raise the child by his own power. He first shuts the door and prays to the Lord. Every miracle in the Bible is God’s work.
Seven is the number of fullness. The child’s sneezing seven times is a sign of breath fully returned: life is the gift of God’s breath (Genesis 2:7).
vv: She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God, closed the door on him, and left.
The mother says nothing to her husband of the death. She lays the child on the prophet’s bed, as if handing him back to the one through whom God gave him.
So he went in and closed the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.
Prayer comes first. Jesus too put the mourners outside before raising Jairus’ daughter (Mark 5:40), and Peter will do the same at Joppa.
putting his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands
The prophet gives himself wholly, body to body, to the dead child. Some Fathers saw here a picture of the Son of God who came down to our measure to give us life.
She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground; then she took her son and left.
Her faith is rewarded. The story ends in silent thanksgiving.
ch: Several Fathers read Elisha’s action as a figure of the Incarnation: the Word made himself small, stretching himself, as it were, over dead humanity to give it life. The Church sees in the prophets’ miracles a preparation for Christ, who raised the dead by his own word, and for the apostles, who would act in his name. The Catechism distinguishes such raisings, which brought people back to ordinary earthly life, from Christ’s own Resurrection to a glorious life that can no longer die (CCC 646). Elisha’s miracle points ahead; Christ fulfils it.

r.h: Tabitha, get up
set: After Saul’s conversion, the Church in Judea, Galilee and Samaria has peace (9:31). Peter is travelling among the communities, and at Lydda he has healed a paralysed man named Aeneas (9:32–35). Joppa, the port on the coast, the modern Jaffa beside Tel Aviv, was not far away. There a disciple named Tabitha has died.

Joppa is the town from which Jonah once fled from God’s call to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3). In the next chapter, Peter, staying at Joppa, will receive the vision that sends him to the Gentile Cornelius (10:5–23).
str: vv. 36–37: Tabitha, a disciple rich in good works, dies; her body is laid in the upper room.
vv. 38–39: two men bring Peter; the widows weep and show the clothes she made.
v. 40: Peter sends all out, kneels, prays, and says, “Tabitha, get up”; she opens her eyes and sits up.
vv. 41–42: he presents her alive; many believe in the Lord.
kw: The feminine form of “disciple”, used only here in the New Testament. Tabitha is honoured as a true follower of Christ.
Tabitha is Aramaic, Dorcas Greek; both mean gazelle. Luke gives both names, as Joppa was a city of two languages.
The verb of resurrection. Peter’s words, “Tabitha, get up”, echo Jesus’ words to Jairus’ daughter, “Talitha cum” (Mark 5:41), which differ by one letter in Aramaic.
vv: She was devoted to good works and acts of charity.
Literally “full of good works and almsgiving”. Her holiness was in her needle and her generosity.
All the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
The poor widows are her best witnesses. Each garment tells of her love. Charity is remembered long after we are gone.
Peter put all of them outside, and then he knelt down and prayed. He turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.”
Peter does exactly what he had seen Jesus do in Jairus’ house (Mark 5:40–41). But he first kneels and prays: the power is not his own, but Christ’s.
This became known throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
The miracle is not an end in itself. It leads people to faith in the Lord.
ch: The Church sees in Peter’s ministry the continuation of Christ’s own: Jesus gave the Twelve a share in his power to heal and to raise (Matthew 10:8), and in Acts they act in his name, never in their own (Acts 3:12, 16). The Catechism teaches that the apostles were sent to continue Christ’s own mission, acting in his name and by his power (CCC 858–859). Tabitha, whose good works speak for her, is honoured in East and West as a model of practical charity, and many parish women’s groups in various lands have been named “Dorcas societies” after her.

r.h: I will boast of my weakness
set: In chapters 10–13 Paul answers rival preachers at Corinth who boasted of their Jewish descent, their eloquence and their visions. Paul hates boasting, but to protect the Corinthians he plays the “fool” and boasts for a while (11:1, 16–21). Yet he turns the boasting upside down: instead of successes, he lists sufferings.

His list matches what Acts tells: stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), beating with rods at Philippi (Acts 16:22–23), the escape from Damascus (Acts 9:23–25). It also tells of much that Acts does not record, such as three shipwrecks, all before the famous shipwreck at Malta, which came later (Acts 27). The forty lashes minus one was a synagogue discipline (Deuteronomy 25:3 allows forty; one was held back so as not to exceed the limit). That Paul accepted it five times shows he still counted himself a member of the synagogue and kept returning to his own people.
str: vv. 21b–23a: Hebrews, Israelites, descendants of Abraham, ministers of Christ: so am I, and more.
vv. 23b–27: the catalogue of labours, imprisonments, beatings, dangers and hardships.
vv. 28–29: daily anxiety for all the Churches; weak with the weak.
vv. 30–33: I will boast of my weakness; God knows I do not lie; let down in a basket at Damascus.
kw: A word Paul uses more than anyone else in the New Testament. For him the only true boast is in the Lord (10:17) and in the cross (Galatians 6:14).
His heaviest burden is not the beatings but the daily care for all the Churches. A shepherd’s heart suffers with every member.
The key word of these chapters. Paul will hear the Lord say, “power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
vv: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
Paul never denies his Jewish identity. He remains proud to belong to the people of the covenant (Romans 9:3–5; 11:1).
Five times I have received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one.

These punishments were given by synagogue authorities in particular places, not by a whole people. Paul himself never blames his people as a whole; he prays for them with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” (Romans 9:2).
And, besides other things, I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches.
Here Paul speaks as a pastor. The care of souls is a heavier cross than any rod.
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The world boasts of strength; the apostle boasts of weakness, because there Christ’s power is seen.
but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall, and escaped from his hands.
An ironic ending. Roman soldiers were honoured for being first up an enemy wall; Paul’s “glory” is to have gone down a wall in a basket.
ch: St John Chrysostom loved Paul above all the saints and preached seven homilies in his praise; he marvels that this one man, weak in body, carried the care of the whole world in his heart (in substance, Homilies in Praise of St Paul). Pope Benedict XVI, in the Pauline Year 2008–2009, taught that Paul’s sufferings show that the apostle is united with Christ crucified, and that his strength came from Christ alone (in substance, General Audiences on St Paul). The Church honours Peter and Paul together because both gave their lives for Christ in Rome; St Clement of Rome, writing within a generation, already holds them up as examples of endurance (in substance, 1 Clement 5).

r.h: Feed my sheep
set: The risen Jesus has appeared to seven disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. After a night of catching nothing, they have hauled in a great catch at his word, and he has given them breakfast of bread and fish on a charcoal fire (21:1–14). The only other charcoal fire in the Gospels is the one in the high priest’s courtyard where Peter denied him three times (18:18). Now, beside a charcoal fire again, Jesus heals Peter’s threefold denial with a threefold question of love.
str: vv. 15–17: three times: “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Three times Peter answers, and three times Jesus entrusts his flock to him.
v. 18: the prophecy: when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will fasten a belt around you.
v. 19: the meaning: the death by which Peter would glorify God; then, “Follow me.”
kw: Jesus twice asks with agapaō; Peter answers with phileō, and the third time Jesus also uses phileō. Some Fathers and preachers have found a lesson here, but many scholars think John varies the words for style, since he uses both of the Father’s love for the Son (3:35; 5:20). Either way, the heart of the scene is the threefold question.
Two verbs: to feed and to shepherd, to guide and protect. Peter receives the whole care of the flock, lambs and sheep alike.
The flock remains Christ’s. Peter is a shepherd under the Good Shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).
vv: Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?
Jesus calls him by his old name, as at the first call (1:42). Peter had once boasted that he would never fall away (Mark 14:29). Now he does not compare himself with the others.
Peter felt hurt because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”
Peter no longer trusts his own word. He appeals to the Lord’s knowledge of his heart. Humility has replaced boasting.
But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.
Early Christian writers understood this of crucifixion. Tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, and Origen, as reported by Eusebius, says he asked to be crucified head downward.
After this he said to him, “Follow me.”
The last words of Jesus to Peter in John are the first words of every vocation. To shepherd is to follow, all the way to the Cross.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter, and that after his Resurrection he confirmed it: “Feed my sheep” (CCC 553). The First Vatican Council and the Second Vatican Council cite this passage in teaching that the Lord made Peter the shepherd of the whole flock, and that this ministry continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome (Lumen Gentium 18, 22; CCC 881–882). St Augustine notes that the threefold confession answers the threefold denial, so that the tongue might show as much love as it had shown fear (in substance, Tractates on John 123). He adds that Peter is told to feed Christ’s sheep, not his own.

r.h: Love is the fulfilling of the law
set: These verses follow Paul’s teaching on the civil authorities. After saying “Pay to all what is due them,” he turns from debts that can be paid to the one debt that is never paid off: love.
str: v. 7: pay all their due: taxes, revenue, respect, honour.
v. 8: owe no one anything except love; the one who loves has fulfilled the law.
vv. 9–10: the commandments are summed up in “Love your neighbor as yourself”; love is the fulfilling of the law.
kw: Paul plays on the word: settle every debt, but keep this one always open. We can never say we have loved enough.
Love does not cancel the commandments; it fills them up and brings them to their goal.
vv: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.
A debt of love grows the more it is paid.
Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore, love is the fulfilling of the law.
Each commandment Paul lists protects the neighbour. Love does all that the commandments ask, and more.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it shows how Jesus and the apostle sum up the Decalogue in the twofold commandment of love (CCC 2055), and it teaches that charity is the soul of all the virtues (CCC 1827). On the feast of the two apostles, this is fitting: both Peter and Paul learned that love is the whole of the law, and both gave their lives for love of Christ.

r.h: In Peter’s house
set: This is the first day of Jesus’ ministry in Mark, a sabbath at Capernaum. He has taught in the synagogue and freed a man from an unclean spirit (1:21–28). Now he goes straight to the house of Simon and Andrew. Pilgrims from the fourth century onward venerated a house in Capernaum as Peter’s, and the remains of an early house church, later covered by an octagonal church, can be seen there today.
str: vv. 29–31: in Simon’s house Jesus raises up his mother-in-law, and she serves them.
vv. 32–34: at sunset the whole town brings the sick; he heals many and silences the demons.
kw: The verb Mark will use for the Resurrection (16:6). Jesus’ touch already brings the life of Easter.
From the word diakonia. The one who is healed becomes a servant, like the Son of Man who came to serve (10:45).
vv: Now Simon’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever, and they told him about her at once.
Peter was married. The first healing in his house is for his family. The disciples bring a need to Jesus at once: this is the first form of intercession.
He came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. Then the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
Three gestures: he comes, he takes her hand, he lifts her up. Healing leads to service.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a sign that God has visited his people, and that he wants to heal the whole person, body and soul (CCC 1503). St Jerome, preaching on this passage, prays that Jesus may come to our house too, take our hand and lift us up from the fever of our sins, so that we may rise and serve (in substance, Homilies on Mark).

qa: Why are Peter and Paul honoured on the same day?

Both were martyred in Rome under the emperor Nero, in the mid-60s, according to ancient tradition: Peter crucified, probably near the Vatican hill, and Paul beheaded on the road to Ostia. The Church in Rome has kept their common feast on 29 June at least since the fourth century. Together they stand for the two sides of the apostolic mission: Peter the shepherd and rock of unity, Paul the apostle to the nations. Very different men, sometimes in sharp disagreement (Galatians 2:11–14), they were one in faith and in love for Christ.
Did Peter really have authority over the other apostles?

The Gospels show Peter named first in every list of the Twelve (Matthew 10:2), given the name “Rock” (Matthew 16:18), asked to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32), and entrusted with Christ’s flock (John 21:15–17). In Acts he leads the first community (Acts 1:15; 2:14; 15:7). The Church teaches that this authority comes from Christ, and that it is a service of unity and love, continued in the bishop of Rome (CCC 881–882).
Why did Jesus ask Peter three times?

St Augustine and many others saw the threefold question as healing Peter’s threefold denial beside another charcoal fire (John 18:18). Each question gives Peter a chance to say with his lips the love that fear had silenced. And each answer is followed by a mission. Christ does not only forgive; he trusts again.
rite: In the East Syriac tradition, Peter and Paul are honoured within the Season of the Apostles, the season after Pentecost that celebrates the Church sent to the nations. The Syro-Malabar Church, which traces its faith to Mar Thoma Shleeha, rejoices in the communion of all the apostles: the faith Thomas brought to India is the same faith Peter and Paul sealed with their blood in Rome. Our Church lives in full communion with the successor of Peter, the bishop of Rome, and prays for him in the Holy Qurbana.

The reading from Acts is close to every parish: Tabitha’s needle and the widows’ tears speak of the many quiet works of charity in our homes and parishes. Like Peter, we kneel and pray first, then reach out a hand to lift others up.
study: Elisha and Peter both shut the door and prayed before acting. What place does quiet prayer have before I try to help others?
The widows showed Peter the clothes Tabitha had made. What will people show of my love when I am gone?
Paul boasts of his weakness, and his greatest burden is his care for all the Churches. How can I share that care through prayer and support for my parish and eparchy?
Jesus asked Peter, “Do you love me?” before saying, “Feed my sheep.” How does my love for Christ show in the way I care for those entrusted to me?

lead: Both readings ask where our true belonging lies. Paul tells the Corinthians to live out God’s call in the condition in which it found them, for whether slave or free, they belong to the Lord who bought them with a price. In Luke, Jesus teaches that we cannot serve two masters: wealth must become a servant of love, used faithfully and shared, or it will become a master. Whatever our state in life, we have one Lord.

r.h: Remain with God
set: In chapter 7 Paul is answering questions about marriage and celibacy. In the middle of that discussion he states a general rule, with two examples: circumcision and slavery. Some new Christians at Corinth seem to have thought that conversion required them to change their outward state: to leave a marriage, to undo or seek circumcision, or to gain release from a master. Paul answers that what matters is the call of God and obedience to his commandments.
str: v. 17: the rule: lead the life the Lord has assigned, as God called you; this is my rule in all the Churches.
vv. 18–20: first example: circumcised or not, it is nothing; keeping God’s commandments is everything.
vv. 21–23: second example: slave or free, each belongs to Christ; you were bought with a price.
v. 24: in whatever condition you were called, remain there with God.
kw: For Paul the “call” is first of all God’s call to faith in Christ. Our outward state is the place where we answer it.
A freed slave in Rome still had ties to his former master. Paul turns the picture around: the Christian slave is truly free in the Lord, and the free Christian is a willing servant of Christ.
Paul repeats 6:20. The price is the blood of Christ. No human master can own a person whom Christ has bought.
vv: let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you.
Holiness does not wait for a different life. God’s call reaches us where we are.
Were you a slave when called? Do not be concerned about it. Even if you can gain your freedom, make use of your present condition now more than ever.

The Greek of the last sentence is short and can be read two ways: “make use of your freedom” or “make use of your present condition”. The NRSV puts the first reading in its note; the Malayalam POC follows it. Many interpreters prefer it, since Paul plainly values freedom (v. 23).
You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human masters.
No one may treat another person as property, and no Christian should hand over his conscience to any human master.
ch: Paul did not set out to abolish the social order of his day, but he planted the seed that would undo slavery: in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28), and he asked Philemon to welcome back Onesimus “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The Second Vatican Council lists slavery among the infamies that poison human society (Gaudium et Spes 27), and the Catechism teaches that enslaving human beings, buying and selling them like merchandise, is a sin against their dignity (CCC 2414).

r.h: You cannot serve God and wealth
set: Jesus has just told the parable of the dishonest manager, who, about to be dismissed, used his master’s accounts to make friends who would receive him (16:1–8). The master praised his shrewdness, not his dishonesty. Now Jesus draws lessons for his disciples about the use of money. Luke, more than the other evangelists, gathers Jesus’ teaching on riches and the poor.
str: v. 9: make friends by means of dishonest wealth, so that they may welcome you into the eternal homes.
vv. 10–12: faithful in little, faithful in much; who will give you true riches?
v. 13: no slave can serve two masters; you cannot serve God and wealth.
vv. 14–15: some Pharisees, lovers of money, scoff; God knows your hearts.
vv. 16–17: the law and the prophets until John; now the Kingdom is preached; yet not one stroke of the law will fall.
kw: An Aramaic word for property or riches, perhaps from a root meaning “that in which one trusts”. Jesus speaks of it almost as a rival lord.
Literally “mammon of unrighteousness”. Not that all money is stolen, but that wealth belongs to this passing world and easily leads to injustice.
Literally “eternal tents”. The poor whom we help become friends who welcome us into the dwellings of God.
vv: Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much
Daily honesty in small sums is a test of the heart. God entrusts great things to those faithful in small ones.
No slave can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.
A slave belonged wholly to one master. Wealth can be a good servant, but it will not be a second lord beside God.
but God knows your hearts; for what is prized by human beings is an abomination in the sight of God.
Outward respect can hide inner greed. God judges by the heart.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 13 when it warns against idolatry of money (CCC 2113) and when it teaches that any system that makes profit the only norm of economic life is morally unacceptable (CCC 2424). The Fathers read verse 9 as a call to almsgiving: by sharing with the poor, we make friends who will intercede for us. Luke’s “Pharisees, who were lovers of money” describes those who mocked Jesus on that occasion, not all Pharisees or the Jewish people; the same warning is for every disciple whose heart is divided.

qa: Does Paul approve of slavery when he tells slaves to remain as they are?

No. Paul writes to a society in which slavery was everywhere and Christians had no power to change the law. He tells slaves that their dignity before God does not depend on their status, and he encourages them to take freedom if they can (v. 21, as many read it), and warns all not to become slaves of human masters (v. 23). His teaching that slave and free are brothers in Christ worked like yeast, and the Church came to teach plainly that slavery is a grave offence against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414).
study: Paul says, “In whatever condition you were called, … there remain with God.” How can I live my present state of life as a calling from God?
Jesus says I cannot serve God and wealth. What does my use of money this month say about which master I serve?
